Series: Gaṅgānāthajhā-Granthamālā, Volume 13 Commentaries: ‘Rāmānandī’—Sanskrit commentary by Ācārya Śrī Rāmānanda

*Samantapāsādikā*, Part 1,
Pages 1–200 (Main Text from Page 145)
In the work composed by the venerable great seer Vyāsa: [Pt 1 Page 145]
In the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa,
the first chapter:
We recognize him as Maheśāna, the beloved child of Maheśānī.
Gaṇeśāna, whose face is like that of the lord of the elephant-herds, who is free from all ailment. || 1 ||

Though situated on the earth, she is not "earth" (bhū); though standing below, she is higher than the third heaven; she who is bound to the ground is the giver of liberation; and in her, living beings who die become immortal.
May that Kāśī—the royal city of the enemy of Tripura—protect the world from calamity; it is eternally resorted to by the gods on the banks of the river that purifies the three worlds. 2.

Salutations to that Great Lord, the Master of the three worlds, through whose guise of the three junctions of day and night the inhabitants of the three worlds incessantly perform their coming and going.
The son of Satyavatī, the author of the eighteen Purāṇas, recounted before Sūta this narrative that dispels all sins. [Pt 1 Page 159] 4.
Once, the illustrious Nārada, having bathed in the waters of the glorious Narmadā and having worshipped the glorious Oṃkāra, which bestows everything upon all embodied beings, [proceeded]. ||5||
Vyāsa said:
As he was traveling, he beheld before him the Vindhya mountain, the upholder of the earth.
It dispels the torments of saṃsāra and is adorned by the waters of the Revā.
He also made this earth, known by its true name, resound with a twofold form— both stationary and moving— and endowed it with great splendor.
It was a repository of flavors with its mango trees, a remover of grief with its Aśoka trees;
it was graced everywhere by Tāla, Tamāla, Hintāla, and Śāla trees.

With *khapura* fruits it was indeed like a *khapura*, with *śrīphala* fruits it was truly a *śrīphala*; with *aguru* it possessed great splendor, and with *kapittha* fruits it was tawny like a monkey.
It was enchanting with *lakuca* trees shaped like the breasts of the Forest’s Beauty (*vanaśrī*),
and it was made fragrant by plantains that seemed to be fashioned from the very essence of the fruit of nectar.
It possessed the splendor of a pavilion of limbs with oranges and citrons,
and it was filled with reeds, jambīras, and bījapūras.
It truly acted as a hallīsaka dance for the kaṅkola creepers swaying in the wind,
and it was indeed the abode of the playful dance through the graceful movements of the lavalī and javalī vines.
With the gentle swaying of the leaves of its camphor plantain trees, it seemed to beckon travelers overcome by fatigue for the sake of rest. (13)
Like a *punnāga* tree with its *punnāga* sprouts, he seemed to be holding a cluster of jasmine blossoms as breasts with his trembling, sprout-like hands.
Displaying its interior like one full of passion through its split pomegranates, it seemed as if embracing the *mādhavī* creeper in the form of a lover within the forest. (15)
With its *udumbara* trees, which possess infinite fruit and are like the expanse of the sky, it seems to bear millions of cosmic eggs on all sides, appearing as if it were infinite. ||16||
It was covered with *panasa* trees resembling the noses of forest-dwellers, with *śukanāsa* trees,
and with *palāśaka* trees that seemed to have shed their leaves as if out of grief for those separated from their lovers. (17)
Seeing the *kadamba* trees as if they were bristling with horripilation,
it shone on all sides with clusters of *kadamba* blossoms.
It shone with *nameru* trees like the lofty peaks of Mount Meru,
and with *rājādana* and *madana* trees like the palaces of lovers.
On every bank, the high reed-thickets,
covered with cloth-like tents and shining with clusters of *kuṭaja* flowers, appeared as if inhabited by cranes.
It shone with thousands of hands reaching out to welcome supplicants— hands formed by *karamardaka*, *karīra*, *karañja*, and *karambaka* trees. (21)
It was as if consecrated by the radiant buds of the royal *campaka* trees,
and with its flowering *śālmali* trees, it surpassed the beauty of a lotus pond.
In some places shining with tall trees having trembling leaves, in some with golden ketaka flowers, in some with kṛtamāla and naktamāla trees, and in some places with katha trees.
It was resplendent with *karkandhu*, *bandhujīva*, and *putrajīva* trees,
and with *tinduka*, *iṅgudī*, and *karuṇa* trees, which were the very abode of compassion. (24)
Constantly worshipping Hara, who bears the form of the Earth, with full-blown madhūka flowers and pearls released from their own hands, they dwell in celestial chariots. 25.
As if being fanned by fans made from the seeds of *sarja*, *arjuna*, and *añjana* trees;
as if holding an umbrella in the sky made of coconuts together with dates. 26.
With *āmalaka*, *picumanda*, *mandāra*, and *kovidāraka* trees; with *pāṭala*, *tintiṇī*, *ghoṇṭā*, *śākhoṭa*, and *karahāṭaka* trees.
It was also marked with *uddaṇḍas*, *śehuṇḍas*, *eraṇḍas*, *guḍapuṣpas*,
*bakulas*, and *tilakas*, its summit adorned with *tilaka* trees.
It was adorned with *akṣa*, *plakṣa*, *śallakī*, *devadāru*, and *haridruma* trees,
as well as trees and creepers that always bear fruit and always bear flowers.
It was covered with groves of cardamom, cloves, black pepper, and *kuluñjana*, and adorned with rose-apple, *asnātaka*, *bhallāta*, *śelu*, and *śrīpaṇa* trees. ||30||
It was delightful with groves of *śāka* and conch trees, and with *candana* and red *candana* trees; it was adorned with forests of *harītakī*, *kaṇikāra*, and *dhātrī* trees. (31)
Grapevine, betel vine, long pepper vine, and śatāvarī;
jasmine, yūthikā, kunda, and fragrant madayantī. ||32||
Adorned with *mālatī* flowers and swarms of bees, it seemed as though Kṛṣṇa had arrived there in the guise of the bees to repeatedly satisfy the gopīs. (33)
It was crowded with various herds of wild animals, resounded with the cries of various birds,
and surrounded by various rivers, lakes, streams, and ponds.
It was inhabited on all sides by various classes of gods who, like those who have returned after abandoning the land of heaven due to its hollow splendor, were intent upon diverse enjoyments.
It seemed to be scattering offerings of leaves and flowers here and there, while with the cries of peacocks from afar, it was as if offering a formal welcome.
Then the mountain saw Nārada in the sky, shining like a hundred suns and illuminating the heavens; he went out from afar to meet him.
The splendor of the body of the son of Brahmā had driven away all darkness;
beholding him approaching, Mānasa abandoned that [darkness].
Filled with awe born from the majesty of Brahman, he performed a proper act of hospitality.
Even though it is hard, it is said that it abandons its hardness and assumes softness.
Seeing his gentleness even amidst his dual nature, that Nārada rejoiced exceedingly; for the virtuous have minds that are won over by humility. (40)
Upon seeing a teacher or even one who is not a teacher returning home, he who is not a teacher yet offers salutation is a true teacher; he who does not is no teacher at all. (41)
In response, that mountain, though its peaks were high, bowed its neck very low;
with its crest touching Ilā, it prostrated before the great sage.
Having raised him up with the tips of his hands and greeted him with blessings,
he took the seat indicated by him, which was loftier even than the mind.
He worshipped him with curd, honey, clarified butter, water-moistened unbroken rice and dūrvā grass,
sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and flowers— namely, with these eightfold offerings. (44)
Having received the fee, the mountain, who was weary, spoke while bowing down after perceiving that [the guest] was no longer fatigued due to the massaging of his feet and other services. (45)
Today, the external dust has been instantly removed by the dust of your feet,
and the internal darkness has also been suddenly dispelled by the splendor of contact with your body.
O Sage, today has become fruitful for me, and today is a truly auspicious day;
today, my long-accumulated past merits have finally borne fruit. (47)
"Today, my status as a mountain among mountains shall be honored," having heard this, the sage then stood for a moment with a slight sigh of relief.
[Pt 1 Page 176]
The best of the Kulis, his mind filled with agitation, spoke again:
"O Brahmin, skilled in all matters, tell me the cause of this sigh. (46)
That which has never been seen before is now seen by us, O you who are desired throughout the three worlds;
if there is compassion for me here, please speak, for I am bowed down before you.
Though my voice is thickened by the abundance of joy born from your arrival and I am unable to speak repeatedly, nevertheless, I shall say this one thing. (51)
The capacity to support the earth was previously attributed to Meru and other such beings;
however, that which was described as a collective attribute, I alone now uphold the earth.
Because he was the father of Gaurī, because he was the lord of the Himavat among the mountain kings,
and because he was the kinsman of Paśupati, he alone was the one honored by the virtuous. (53)

Is Mount Meru esteemed by me anywhere as venerable because it is filled with gold, or because its peaks rise up with jewels, or even because it is the abode of the gods? For are there not hundreds of other mountains whose play consists in supporting the earth? (54)
In this world, there are those worthy of honor among the virtuous, yet they are honored only within their own domains.

When the sun is sluggish, the Niṣadha mountain— though it possesses medicinal herbs and is not itself set, even as the sun has set— becomes the sole refuge for those whose doubts are dispelled by laughter and who rely on its singular compassion.
Nīla, Nīlīnilaya, Mandara, Mandalocana,
Sarpālaya, Samalaya, and Raivata do not know wealth. (57)
"Hemakūṭa, Trikūṭa, and others have 'Kūṭottara' as their suffix;
Kiṣkindha, Kauśva, Sahya, and others are not capable of bearing the burden of the earth.
Having heard these words of Vindhya, Nārada reflected thus in his heart.
Association with unabated pride does not lead to greatness.
Are there not mountains here, foremost among them Śrīśaila, possessing stainless splendor? [Pt 1 Page 179]
For the virtuous, even the mere sight of their peaks and so forth leads to liberation.
Thinking, "Today his strength must be observed," the sage said:
"Truly has it been spoken by you, as you reveal the very essence of the mountain. (61)
"Furthermore, among the mountains, Meru, the king of mountains, holds you in contempt;
I have sighed about this, and it has been reported to you as well. (62)
"Or rather, what concern is this for great-souled ones such as myself?
Saying, 'May it be well with you,' he departed by way of the sky. (63)
When the Sage had departed, Vindhya, his mind deeply distressed and his desires frustrated, censured his own counsel and fell into great anxiety. (64)
Vindhya said:
"Fie on the life of one devoid of the sciences and arts; fie on the life of one who has abandoned his exertion!"
Fie on the life of one defeated by his kinsmen; fie on the life of one whose desires are in vain! (65)
How does he eat by day? How does he sleep at night? What is his secret pleasure, he whose very existence is the subjugation of his enemy?
Alas! The torment of the forest fire does not afflict me as much as this does.
But just as the continuous succession of the heat of anxiety afflicts the mind, so too [does it afflict the body]. ||67||
It has been rightly said by those who know the past: "The extremely terrible form of anxiety is not pacified by medicines, nor by fasting, nor by any other means. (68)
The fever of anxiety robs humans of their hunger, sleep, and strength;
it takes away their beauty, energy, intellect, fortune, and life—of this there is no doubt. (66)

When a fever has passed six days, it is here called a chronic (jīrṇa) fever; this is an intense fever of anxiety that returns to a state of novelty every day. Here, Dhanvantari is fortunate, for Caraka does not practice medicine in this place.
Even the two Nāsatyas (the Aśvins) are indeed not present here in this fever of anxiety.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? How can I conquer Meru?
Having leaped, I shall fall upon its summit; I shall not fall elsewhere.
Formerly, by someone of our own lineage who provoked Śakra, he was rendered wingless; fie upon the conduct of one who lacks allies! [73]
Or rather, how could he rival me, who am so high as Mount Meru?
For those who bear the burden of the earth generally become objects of delusion. (74)
Or else, how could falsehood be possible in the case of Nārada—he who is a celibate student, a knower of the Vedas, and a resident of the world of truth? (75)
Furthermore, deliberation on what is appropriate or inappropriate is of no use for one such as me; it is only the minds of those incapable of valor that indulge in such reflection. (76)
[Pt 1 Page 183] Or rather, what is the use of these futile reflections? I shall seek refuge in the Lord of the Universe, the Creator of the universe; He will grant me wisdom. (77)
The protector of the protectorless, the lord of all, he is indeed celebrated as the Lord of the Universe (Viśvanātha).
Having reflected upon this for a moment in the mind, it will undoubtedly become so:
"I shall do exactly this; delay is not desired. (78)
The wise should not overlook these two enemies while they are still increasing.
"The Sun, along with his host of planets and constellations, surely circumambulates Meru every single day, considering it to be superior in strength.
Having thus resolved, that Vindhya mountain, intent on battle, began to grow.
With their peaks as if reaching to the end of the infinite sky. ||81||
One should not engage in conflict with anyone at any time;
if it must be done, one should do so with such effort that people do not laugh at one.
With the path of his enemies blocked, the king of mountains became as composed as one who has accomplished his task;
for the future of living beings is indeed dependent upon destiny.
Whomever the Maker of Yama sends today as his sacrificial fee,
he shall be of noble birth, he shall be illustrious, he shall be great, and he shall be honored.
As long as he is not capable of being touched—even if one is capable—so long must he be avoided by all, like a fierce, blazing fire. (65)
Thus, having cast off the great burden of anxiety, he remained firm in his resolve,
awaiting the rising of the sun like a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Growth of the Vindhya," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa.
Thus ends the first chapter in the glorious Kāśī-khaṇḍa, according to the commentary composed by Śrī Rāmānanda.
[Pt 1 Page 185] Now begins the second chapter.
Vyāsa said:
The Sun, the soul of this moving and stationary world and the enemy of darkness, rose upon the mountain of sunrise with his pure, spreading rays—
increasing the virtues of the righteous and suppressing the state of ignorance.
Awakening his beloved Padminī, whose face was closed like a bud during the night,
he proceeded with the offerings for the gods (havya), the ancestors (kavya), and the oblations for the spirits (bhūtabali).
Manifesting the time for activities of the forenoon, afternoon, and midday;
indicating the presence of darkness in the hearts and mouths of the wicked;
and reviving the world once again, as it were, at the onset of night.
When he has arisen, there occurs a perfect manifestation of merit for all beings;
oh, if you say that helping others does not bear fruit immediately! (5)
Having set in the evening, how might the sun live again at dawn?
Having consoled the eastern quarter, who has been left desolate, with the touch of his affectionate rays.
Having enjoyed the night, she then approached the southern quarter, which was as if blazing with the fire of separation,
adorned with cloves, musk deer, moonlight, and sandalwood.

Her lips were reddened by the dye of betel leaves; her beautiful breasts were like clusters of grapes; her creeper-like arms were like *lavalī* vines; and her fingers were like the tender sprouts of the *kaṅkolī*.
She whose breath is the Malaya breeze, whose excellent garment is the waters of the Milky Ocean, whose body is composed of gold and jewels from Mount Trikūṭa, who has Mount Suvela for her hips,
whose shanks are the Kāverī and Gautamī rivers, and who is clothed in the silken garments of the Colas and Cōlas.
She has the Sahya and Dardura mountains for breasts, is adorned with the Kāntī river as a girdle,
and is enchanting with the graceful play of the exceedingly soft Mahārāṣṭrī language. [Pt 1 Page 189]
Even today, Great Fortune (Mahālakṣmī) does not abandon her who possesses such excellent virtues.
The Lord of the Quarters set out toward the auspicious and skillful southern direction;
meanwhile, all his horses traversed the sky of the Sun with ease.
They were unable to proceed further ahead, whereupon Anūru made his request.
Anūru said:
"The Vindhya mountain, puffed up with pride, stands obstructing the sky."
Desiring to perform the circumambulation granted by you, he vies with Mount Meru.
Having heard the words of Anūru, the Sun reflected within his heart.
"Alas! Even the path of the sky is obstructed—what a great wonder!
Vyāsa said: "What could even a hero do while standing on a desolate road? What indeed could a hero do while standing on a desolate road?"
Who, even if possessed of a voice, could alone cross a path that is blocked? || 16 ||
Rāhu, whose arms were severed and who could not remain still for even a moment, was obstructed on the empty path; what could he do? Fate is powerful.
He who travels two thousand, two hundred, and two yojanas in half a blink of an eye— even he remains there for a long time. (18) [Pt 1 Page 191]
When a great deal of time had passed, those from the east and north were severely afflicted; tormented by the falling mass of rays from the fierce-rayed sun,
the westerners and southerners had their eyes sealed with sleep.
Even while lying down, they gaze at the sky filled with stars and planets.
"Aha! Is this not night due to the absence of the sun, yet it is not day because of the moon? Since the constellations have set from the sky, what time is this that cannot be discerned? (20-21)
"How indeed will the cosmic egg meet its dissolution so prematurely,
and why have the oceans not yet overflowed here and there? [1.192.22]
On the surface of the earth, which was deprived of the utterances of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*,
the three worlds trembled due to the omission of the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*).
All rituals, beginning with the sacrifice, proceed from the rising of the sun.
Through them, the sacrificial eaters are satisfied; Savitṛ is the cause therein.
Citragupta and all others know time through the Sun;
Ravi alone is the cause of maintenance, creation, and dissolution.
Because the movement of the sun was thus obstructed, the three worlds were brought to a standstill;
whatever remained there stood as if entirely depicted in a painting.
On one side, due to the darkness of night, and on the other, due to the heat of the day, the destruction of many occurred; the world became utterly bewildered, not knowing where to turn.

Thus, while the world—including gods, asuras, humans, and serpents—was thrown into confusion, the people cried out, "Alas! What is this that has occurred so unexpectedly? The world is being violently overwhelmed! (28)
Then, having all looked upon one another, they went to Brahmā for refuge;
praising him with various hymns, they cried out, "Protect us! Protect us! (2.9).
The gods said:
"Salutations to the one of golden form, to Brahman who has the nature of Brahman;
to him whose true essence is unknown, to the absolute liberation and the immortal. (30)
Salutations to that Self of Consciousness, which the gods do not perceive, wherein even the mind is blunted, and where speech does not extend. 31.
Salutations to that glorious Brahman, whom yogis, remaining motionless through their resolve, behold as a form of light within the space of the heart. (32)

Salutations to the one who transcends time, to the time itself, and to the Supreme Person; salutations to the one whose nature consists of the three qualities and who takes the form of primordial matter (prakṛti).
Salutations to Viṣṇu, who is the form of *sattva*; to Brahmā (*Vedhas*), who is the form of *rajas*;
and to Rudra, who is the form of *tamas*, the cause of preservation, creation, and destruction.
Salutations to Him whose nature is the intellect (*buddhi*) and salutations to the threefold *ahaṃkāra*.
Salutations to you who consist of the five subtle elements (tanmātras), whose nature is the five organs of action;
salutations to you whose form is the mind, whose nature is the five organs of perception;
salutations to you who possess the five forms beginning with earth, whose nature is the objects of the senses.
Salutations to the one whose form is the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), salutations to the one who dwells within it;
salutations to you, whose universal form encompasses both the near and the far.
Salutations to You, whose form is both impermanent and eternal, the Lord of existence and non-existence;
O You who have manifested Your body by Your own will out of compassion for all devotees!
The Vedas are Your breath, and the entire universe is Your sweat.
All beings were your feet; from your head the sky evolved. From your navel came the intermediate space, and the trees were your body hair.
The moon was born from your mind, O Lord, and the sun from your eye;
you alone are everything, and in you, O God, is everything. You alone are the praiser, the praise, and the object of praise here.
O Lord, all this is indeed pervaded by you; let there be salutation again and again, salutation unto you!
Having praised him thus, Brahmā and the gods prostrated themselves on the ground like staffs;
then, being well-pleased, Brahmā replied to the inhabitants of heaven.
Brahmā said: "O gods, I am pleased with this hymn of praise that accords with reality; you have bowed down before me.
Arise, for I am gratified; choose an excellent boon."
Whoever, being faithful and pure, shall praise me, Hara, or Viṣṇu every day with this hymn—we shall always be pleased with him. (44)
We shall grant all desires: sons, grandsons, cattle, wealth,
good fortune, long life, health, fearlessness, victory in every battle,
as well as worldly and otherworldly enjoyments and imperishable liberation.
Whatever is most dear to him, all that shall come to pass.
Therefore, with every effort, this supreme hymn should be recited;
for this hymn is renowned as the bestower of desires and the granter of all perfections.
Then the Creator spoke again to those gods who had risen after prostrating:
"O you, remain at ease; why are you still so agitated even here?"
These Vedas have assumed embodied forms, as have all these branches of knowledge;
here are the sacrifices accompanied by sacrificial fees, truth, dharma, austerity, self-restraint,
celibacy, compassion, and this goddess of speech.
These people have realized the true meaning of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the Itihāsas.
[Pt 1 Page 201] Here there is neither anger, nor envy, nor greed, nor lust, nor lack of fortitude, nor fear.
Violence, crookedness, pride, censure, envy, and impurity are found nowhere [among them].

Those Brāhmaṇas who are devoted to the Brahman, established in austerity, whose wealth is penance, and who observe virtuous vows such as fasting for a month, six months, or the four-month period (Cāturmāsya), etc., [are truly Brāhmaṇas]. || 51-52 ||
"Behold these women devoted to their husbands, and these others who are celibate students; yet look at these gods, who are eunuchs toward the wives of others!
These are devoted to their parents, while these were killed for seizing cows."
In vows, charity, recitation, sacrifice, self-study of the Vedas, and the satiation of the twice-born;
in sacred fords, austerity, service, and in acts such as virtuous conduct—[in all these, one should act]. (54) [Pt 1 Page 202]
Those people are these very ones whose minds do not long for the fruits [of action]:
those devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī, dedicated to the Agnihotra sacrifice, donors of two-faced cows, and intent upon the gift of Kapila cows. || 55–56 ||
Those who are free from desire, those who drink the Soma, those who drink the water from the feet of the twice-born,
those who have died at the holy ford of the Sarasvatī, those who serve the twice-born,
those who are capable of receiving gifts yet remain free from accepting them— [all these attain the highest state].
These Brahmins are dear to me, who have abandoned accepting gifts at holy fords;
they are those pure-souled ones by whom the month of Māgha was spent bathing at dawn in Prayāga.
When the sun is situated in Capricorn, these [planets] are pure and possess the brilliance of the sun. || 5.9 ||
Having bathed for three days at the Pāśvanada in Vārāṇasī during the month of Kārttika, those of immeasurable merit, possessing pure bodies and being exceedingly stainless,
having bathed in the Maṇikaṇikā and gratified the Brāhmaṇas with wealth, [attain their goal].
Rich in all enjoyments, these shall dwell in my city for an eon.
Then, having reached Kāśī, impelled by that merit and through the grace of Viśveśvara, they will undoubtedly attain liberation.
Whatever action, even if it be very slight, is performed by men in Avimukta—
Its ripening is liberation in the form of the highest good, even in future births;
"bathed at dawn" means brought to completion by the morning bath.

*Pāñcanadam* means "at the five rivers" (*pañcanada*). The suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). Alternatively, the reading is *pañcanada*. || 60 || A *kalpa* is two *parārdhas*. || 61 ||
The ripening of that is the fruition of that karma. What is it? He says: "Liberation. Regarding its neuter gender—[Page 204 of Pt 1]:
"O, in the sacred field of Vaiśveśvara, we have no fear even of death."
Where everyone awaits death as if it were a beloved guest;
those by whom pure wealth was given to the Brahmins at Kurukṣetra—
these very ones, with their limbs made stainless, now stand in my presence.
Those by whom their grandfathers were fed in the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa after they had approached the Grandfather (Brahmā) at Gayā—those [offerings] are for them; those are their grandfathers.
O gods, my world is not attained through bathing, nor by giving gifts, nor by recitation, nor by worship; it is attained by the satiation of the twice-born.
[It includes] houses with their furnishings, such as pestles, mortars, and so forth.
"These palaces indeed belong to those by whom [these gifts] were given together with beds. (68)

Those who cause a hall for sacred knowledge to be built, who teach the Vedas, who provide the gift of learning, and who cause the Purāṇas to be recited; [those who give] houses together with their furnishings, household implements, and ornaments—or indeed, along with all such equipment—[attain the highest state]. 68–69.
A *brahmaśālā* is a house for the purpose of Vedic study; or rather, there is a reading *purāṇam*. Those who give ancient [texts], that is, those who even give books of the Purāṇas.
Those who give treatises on Dharma shall dwell here in my city.

There, the Lord of Lakṣmī himself comes from Vaikuṇṭha to [bless] human beings.

Through the form of the illustrious Mādhava, one leads [the soul] to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. It is recited by the Vedas that those whose limbs have bathed there in the two excellent rivers, the white and the black, truly become immortal; this is certain.
"From the world of Śiva, from the world of Brahmā, again from the excellent world of Umā, from the world of Kumāra, from Vaikuṇṭha, and from Satyaloka on all sides"—

the phrase "having ascended which" refers to the intention of the distinction between different *kalpas*. Alternatively, "having ascended which" refers to [the path] by which one situated within the belly of the Lord [reaches] the one situated in the banyan tree.
The Blessed One said "so be it" with the intention of expressing the non-difference between himself and the banyan tree.
|| 51-52 || The supreme state is liberation (kaivalya).
And Tapoloka, Maharloka— all these dwellers of the heavenly worlds [came],
as well as from Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, and the entire Nāgaloka. 17.9–56.
The immovable mountains, headed by Himavat,
and the celestial trees such as the Kalpavṛkṣa, come to Prayāga at dawn during the month of Māgha to bathe. 57.
Even the breezes of Prayāga, for which the women of the quarters long, shall purify us; what can we do? For we are like the lame.
Furthermore, the sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha are [surpassed] by the dust of Prayāga.
It was weighed by Brahmā;
even those sins accumulated over many lifetimes, reaching into the very marrow, were not equal to that dust.
By merely hearing the name of Prayāga, [all sins] are utterly destroyed and [the mind] becomes exceedingly agitated [with devotion].
This is the true field of dharma; this is the supreme field of ultimate meaning;
this is the field that fulfills all desires; and this is certainly the field of liberation. || 60–61 ||
The meaning is: even the winds belonging to that Prayāga, which is possessed of such power. To the question "What do they request?", he says:
"Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin roar within embodied beings."
"As long as they do not bathe in Māgha at Prayāga, which removes all sins, so long the wise do not behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
this is what is recited repeatedly in the Veda concerning Prayāga. (62-63)

Sarasvatī is of the nature of *rajas*, the Kalindajā (Yamunā) is of the nature of *tamas*, and Gaṅgā here is of the nature of *sattva*; together they lead one to the Brahman that is beyond all qualities (*nirguṇa*).
This braid is indeed a ladder for a living being whose body has been purified— who, though immersed in both faith and lack of faith— is about to proceed upon the path of Brahman.
"Embodied beings roar"— this is the ellipsis.
[Pt 1 Page 323] "Kāśī."
There is a certain woman established throughout the worlds, whose eyes are as restless as the sun and Keśava;
her pair of arms is this Varaṇā river, and her braid of hair is that which is called here the Akṣayaśarmabhūmi.
Agastya said:
Who here is capable of describing the virtues of that jewel of mountains, Prayāga, the king of holy places, which is frequented by all sacred sites? (67)
Now, describing the boundaries of Kāśī starting from Prayāga, he characterizes Kāśī in the form of a woman:
"Alas! Whatever sins belong to sinners have been forcibly washed away! [Pt 1 Page 324]
Because it is sought by sacred fords (*tīrtha*) for the sake of that purification, Prayāga is superior to them.
Having learned the virtues of Prayāga, the wise brahmin Śivaśarman stayed there during the month of Māgha and then reached the city of Vārāṇasī.
Upon entering, she beheld the Liṅga of Vināyaka together with his body, and then she devoutly smeared it with a paste of ghee and vermilion.
She offered five sweetmeat balls (modakas) while deceiving her own people.
Then, from amidst the multitude of great calamities, she entered the inner sanctuary;
she whose characteristic is such—though in some places the reading is *sadharmiṇī* (having a common dharma). || 67 || || 71 ||
For the purification of those sins—that is, for their cleansing and destruction—O, my beloved! 68.
Having arrived and seen the celestial river flowing northward at Maṇikarṇikā, he—
Having bathed without delay in the pure water with his clothes on— surrounded by groups of men whose merit and demerit had been exhausted, as if by hosts of Sthāṇu— he,
a knower of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), being possessed of pure intellect, offered oblations to the divine sages, humans, and the celestial ancestors, as well as to his own forefathers.
And having performed it instantly. || 73 ||

Having worshipped Viśveśa at the five holy fords, he then repeatedly gazed upon the city of the Enemy of Tripura according to his own inclination; yet, wondering whether this was the one he had previously beheld, he was filled with amazement.

The city of heaven cannot bring about an equal correspondence with this city, even through its own proper and correct nature, due to the difference in their continuity—just as a copy from a separate manuscript [differs] because of the breaking of the excellence of the fine script.
(75) Having determined that it was "beheld later," he describes Kāśī with eight verses beginning with *na svaḥ purī*. That [city] is heaven...

The city Amarāvatī, however, by a certain examination of this city Kāśī—whether from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛśā*), or even from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāradṛśā*) as indicated by the word "api"—does not attain, nor can it reach, equality with it. This is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). [This holds true] when examined from both perspectives.
The use of the word *pratisāmya* (counter-similarity) embedded within the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the absence of similarity.

By means of an investigation from both perspectives, he states the reason residing in both [cases] simultaneously (*tantreṇa*) for the absence of similarity: "because of the difference in continuity" (*prabandhabhedāt*).
*Prabandha* is a continuous connection, a composition, or a sequence; it is because of the difference therein. For Amarāvatī is [constructed] by Brahmā every day...
It is being constructed, whereas this [city] is created all at once. Even there, that city is built by Brahmā, while this one is by the Lord himself.

Furthermore, that city is inlaid with a collection of small jewels and is of modest height, whereas this one is fashioned from a heap of priceless gems and rises to the height of the sky. Alternatively, it is due to a difference in composition (*prabandha*); for *prabandha* means a superior binding (*bandha*) for those residing in the celestial city. Moreover—

The meaning is that *saṃsāra* consists of the nature of repeated birth, death, and so forth; however, for those residing in Kāśī, there would be "prabandha," meaning the bond (*bandha*) has departed (*pra-gata*)—thus, it refers to the difference between these two states of bondage. Alternatively, *prabandha* means intense bondage (*prakṛṣṭo bandhaḥ*).

Due to the difference—that is, the abundance—of such [bondage] among those residing in Amarāvatī, whereas for those residing in Kāśī, there is the breaking apart (*vidāraṇa*) of that intense bondage. Thus is the meaning.
He provides an illustration for the fact that even Amarāvatī cannot equal Kāśī:
"Even the water here possesses such inconceivable majesty that those dwelling in heaven [envy it]. (185) [Pt 1 Page 327]
It is drunk in vain;
for if this milk had been drunk, then the water from the breasts of the mother would not have been drunk.

In this city, by the power of the Lord’s contemplation, people are free from affliction; even those who perform virtuous deeds do not act otherwise here, and they emulate the attendants of Śarva on all sides—except for the wielder of the Pināka bow himself. Indeed, by whom can this Kāśī be described? For when a living being residing here reaches the time of death, [it attains liberation].
The Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) causes the syllable *Oṃ* to resound for those who have ripened the burden of their ordinary merits.

Since Śiva suddenly utters that *Tāraka* [mantra] into the ear of a virtuous person at the time of death— He who is the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) here for those wandering in *saṃsāra*— it is therefore celebrated as *Maṇikaṇikā*.
This jewel at the base of her two lotus feet is the great throne-stone of the Goddess of Liberation; therefore, people call it Maṇikarṇikā. (80)

Those dwelling here—namely the viviparous, the oviparous, the soil-born, and the sweat-born—are indeed not equal [to others] in attaining liberation; they find liberation difficult to perceive, even compared to the gods (tridaśa).
Alternatively, the word "maṇi" may be supplied [at the beginning of the verse].

He states another derivation for the word *Maṇikarṇikā*: "The Fortune of Liberation" (*muktilakṣmī*). The construction is to be understood by supplying the words "that which [people] call Maṇikarṇikā is this very one. Why is that? Because it is the great seat (*mahāpīṭha*)—the great throne or the great abode—of the Fortune of Liberation, the *mokṣalakṣmī*; it is a "jewel" (*maṇi*) because it is of that nature, being the most excellent of all.
My birth has been in vain, for I am a man of evil conduct and dull intellect;
until this very day, I have not visited Kāśī, the illuminator of liberation. (82)
Making that field his guest again and again with his eyes, he—
though it was wondrous and pure— did not attain satiety.
Indeed, among the seven cities that bear the foremost burden [of sacred sites], I honor Vārāṇasī, which is expert in bestowing perfect liberation;
nevertheless, the other four have not been brought within the range of my vision by me.
"Even after learning of their power, I shall come back again, performing a pilgrimage every single day for a full year;
yet I did not reach all the holy sites, for in Kāśī, there is a sacred place at every grain of sesame. (85-86)
Having seen Kāśī, he regrets that "so much time of mine has passed in vain," thinking, "My birth [has been in vain].
As long as Kāśikā was not seen by me—not seen, not beheld, not observed—so long my birth was born in vain. Thus...
[Page 331]
O Goddess, although that twice-born man knew the supreme qualities of this sacred field, he nevertheless departed, intent on various other measures; alas! 87.
O beautiful one, what indeed can even authoritative scriptures accomplish?
He who, by his own divine play, brings the entire universe to an end at the end of every kalpa— [what can they do against him]?
Having measured that time, he who indeed became Mahākāla [appeared]. 9.1.
Protecting against evil, she is called "The Protectress of the Universe" (Viśvāvantī);
in every age she bears another name, and in the Kali age she is known as Ujjayinī.
Even a living being who has met his end there clearly attains the state of a corpse [only to be restored].
One does not encounter a foul odor, nor does one ever rise up [to rebirth] anywhere.
Indeed, the messengers of Yama never enter that place; there,
millions upon millions of Liṅgas exist at every step.
Hāṭakeśa, Mahākāla, and likewise Tārakeśa—
this single Liṅga, having become threefold, remains pervading the three worlds.
Those twice-born ones who behold that light here at Jyotis-Siddhavaṭa, [attain liberation].
Alternatively, those who have seen that liṅga of Mahākāla anywhere, even while suffering from hardships, are heaps of merit bestowed by Śrī Mahākāla;
they are not touched by great sins, nor are they beheld by the fierce minions of Yama.
Touched on their backs by the flames from Mahākāla’s banners, the horses momentarily cause the dawn-red light to flicker in the sky as if struck by a whip.
"Mahākāla, Mahākāla, Mahākāla!"— thus constantly,
perpetually, and repeatedly remembering [the two] who are the creator of Smara and the ender of Smara.
Having thus propitiated Mahākāla, the Lord of Beings, the twice-born [man] then...
He went to the lovely city of Kāntī, which was more beautiful than even the three worlds.
There, the Lord of Lakṣmī himself, dwelling among living beings, certainly makes them beloved by Śrī both in this world and the next. 100–101.
Having beheld Kāntī, who was radiant and frequented by those full of splendor, he too became radiant;
there was no one there who lacked luster.
There, having performed whatever duty was to be done, he who knew all duties stayed for seven nights and then departed for the city of Dvāravatī.
"Of those who remember, contemplate, and meditate"—that is, of the devotees. "Of him who remembers," meaning he gazes with eyes moistened by compassion.
"Wherein the gates of the classes [of beings] are on all sides."
Therefore, it is called Dvāravatī by the wise who know the truth.
(104) Oh, even the bones of living beings there are marked with the discus; what wonder is there that hands marked with conchs and discs do not exist there? (105)
The Ender.
Thus he repeatedly instructs his own messengers:
"Those by whom even the name of Dvāravatī is uttered must be abandoned.
Where is that fragrance in sandalwood? Where is such a color in gold?"

Where indeed is that purity found as it is in this Gopīcandana at the sacred ford? [Verse 107] He explains the etymology of the name Dvāravatī: "Of the four," etc. It refers to the four goals (vargas) of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
According to the reading "of the castes" (varṇānām), the word "also" (api) implies others as well. [Verse 104]
O messengers, listen: even one whose forehead is marked with Gopīcandana should be avoided with great effort from afar, like a blazing firebrand. 108.
O soldiers, those who are adorned with *tulasī*, those who chant the name of *tulasī*,
and those who protect a *tulasī* grove— these must be avoided from afar.
In age after age, plundering the treasures from every side in Dvāravatī,
Andhī Ratnākara is even today celebrated throughout the worlds. Those living beings who, impelled by Time, perish in Dvāravatī—
In Vaikuṇṭha, they were four-armed and wore yellow garments. There too, having gratified the ancestors along with the gods, sages, and humans, he bathed tirelessly in all those sacred fords.

Then he reached Māyāpurī, which is difficult for evildoers to attain; there indeed that Vaiṣṇavī Māyā does not bind with her snares. [Regarding verse 108: "Like a blazing linga," "like a glowing fire," or in some readings, "like burning coals. [This concludes] the incidental discussion.
Some said, "Haridvāra is the door to liberation," and others than them [said the same].
Being a foreigner, alone, and afflicted by a severe fever, he fell into great anxiety: "What is this that has come upon me? (11.9)
He became submerged in an ocean of anxiety, having lost all hope for his life and wealth, like a sea-faring merchant whose ship has been wrecked in the fathomless great ocean.
"Where is my field? Where is my wife? Where are my sons, and where is that wealth? || 120 ||
Where is that wonderful mansion, and where is that collection of books?
Even now my life-span is not exhausted, nor have grey hairs appeared upon me;
yet this terrible fever has come, and the Knower of Time is most cruel.
Death has made its dwelling upon one's head, while one’s own residence remains far away;
when fire has reached the very roof of one’s house, one digs a well right here.
"What is the use of these futile anxieties that cause me such intense torment?
I shall instead contemplate Hṛṣīkeśa and Śiva alone, who bestows auspiciousness.
Or rather, indeed, one single means for liberation has been properly practiced by me. (124)
These seven cities of liberation have been brought within the range of one's own vision.
Indeed, of heaven and final liberation, one must certainly be accomplished by the wise; for if neither of these is achieved, one later suffers with remorse.

Or rather, what is the use of this anxiety of mine regarding such a miserable state? Death in battle or here at a sacred ford is better for me than this. Why should I, like one of ill fortune, now seek out some woman on a street?
With this body, which is but a collection of skin and bones,
I shall certainly attain death here; through that, I will surely achieve the supreme perfection of liberation.
As he was thinking thus, an exceedingly terrible pain arose within him; he reached a state like that of one bitten by ten million scorpions.
He forgot everything that ought to be remembered, and knew neither "where am I" nor "who am I."
Having remained for seven times seven days, he passed away;
at that moment, a celestial chariot arrived from the realm of Vaikuṇṭha,
upon which a very lofty banner marked by Tārkṣya was raised.
It was presided over by a thousand beautiful maidens dressed in golden silk garments, their hands busily occupied with chowries, and it was exceedingly vast. || 133 || [Pt 1 Page 341]
Adorned by the two hosts, Puṇyaśīla and Suśīla,
and graced by two four-armed, beautiful-faced [deities] garlanded with networks of small bells—
having ascended that celestial chariot, he, four-armed and clad in yellow garments, [proceeded].
That twice-born one, adorned with divine ornaments, graced the path of the sky.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Seven Cities," in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
"Adorned with a network of tinkling bells" means that it has become garlanded by a multitude of small bells. || 134 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the commentary on the Kāśīkhaṇḍa composed by Śrī Rāmānanda.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Lopāmudrā said:
"O Lord of my life, I do not reach satiety upon hearing this meritorious narrative concerning the holy city, as it is uttered from your own lotus-like mouth. (1)
"In Māyāpurī, the city of liberation, there was an excellent brahmin named Śivaśarman; though he died there, he did not attain release. O Lord, tell me the reason for that.
Agastya said: "O sweet-spoken lady!"
Liberation is not directly attained in these cities;
with reference to this very matter, I have heard this historical narrative concerning those seized by Piśācas,
Guhyakas, Gandharvas, and Vidyādharas.
In the eighth [chapter], the five worlds beginning with Saṃyaminī are described.

At the end of the preceding chapter, by the words "having ascended that celestial chariot," the liberation of Śivaśarman as a *sārūpya* (attaining the same form as the deity) was stated; [the author] now asks about the cause of that, expressing his own lack of satisfaction regarding the story told therein, on the grounds that such liberation is impossible. [He addresses him as] "O Lord of Life."
By means of the two; liberation is union.
Listen, O beloved, to this wondrous tale that destroys all sins,
as told by Puṇyaśīla and Suśīla to Śivaśarman.
Śivaśarman said:
"O meritorious attendants of Viṣṇu, with eyes like lotus petals, I desire to ask something, with my hands joined in reverence. (5)
Indeed, I do not know your names, nor do I know anything of your conduct;
yet you two must surely be Puṣyaśīla and Suśīla by virtue of your appearance. (6)
The two attendants said:
"What is unknown to those endowed with devotion to the Blessed One, such as yourself? For this very name of ours has been spoken by you, the illustrious one. (7)
Whatever else you wish to ask in your mind, O one of great wisdom, inquire about it without hesitation; we shall explain it with pleasure.
Having heard these words spoken by the attendant of the Blessed One,
which were exceedingly pleasing and heart-pleasing, he then replied to the two of them.
The divine bird said:
"Who is this world of meager splendor, inhabited by people of such scant merit? And who are these beings of deformed appearance? Tell me this."
The two Gaṇas said:
"This is the world of Piśācas; here dwell flesh-eaters who, having given, feel regret, and do not give even when they have made a promise."
"O friend, these are Piśācas who, though possessing pure minds, have worshipped Śiva only once incidentally; thus, due to their meager merit, they possess but little fortune.

Proceeding from there,
he saw [a place] filled with happy and well-nourished people,
[guarded by men] with large bellies, thick thighs, and voices as deep as the rumbling of clouds.
Inhabited by the worlds.
The world is covered with dark-limbed, hairy ones;
for they know only that single twice-born man who is worthy of worship by his family.
They bestow cows upon him; clearly, they accept his word.
For even here, the Guhyakas, possessing great prosperity through that merit, enjoy heavenly pleasures like the gods, free from fear from any quarter.
Then he beheld that world which bestows bliss upon the eyes, [thinking]:
"Who are these people, and what is the name of this world, O two speakers? The two attendants said: "This is the world of the Gandharvas, and these are the Gandharvas of auspicious vows."
For these wandering minstrels are indeed the singers of praise for the gods. || 21 ||
Those skilled in song please kings with their exquisite singing, and those deluded by greed for wealth praise the wealthy. (22)
Fine garments and wealth obtained through the favor of kings,
as well as fragrant substances such as camphor in great abundance;
They bestow [wealth] upon the Brahmins while singing songs day and night;
their minds are fixed solely on the Vedas, though they have exerted themselves in the science of dramaturgy (Nāṭyaśāstra). 24
By that merit, the world of the Gandharvas is distinguished for them,
since the Brahmins were indeed gratified with wealth acquired through the science of song.
This is by the power of the science of song.
The great celestial sage Nārada is indeed venerable in the world of Vaiṣṇava; he is exceedingly dear to the illustrious Śambhu.
Both Tumburu and Nārada are extremely difficult for even the gods to attain.

Śiva is directly the embodiment of Nāda; indeed, those two are knowers of the reality of Nāda. If a song is ever sung in the presence of the illustrious Hari and Hara, they say that its fruit is liberation or else their very presence.
Those by whom effort has been exerted in the treatises on dramaturgy (nāṭyaśāstra) are such [persons]. || 24 ||
If one who knows song does not attain the supreme state through singing,
he becomes an attendant of Rudra and rejoices together with him.
"In this world, at all times, this traditional teaching is proclaimed:
'The two gods, Hari and Hara, are always to be worshipped with a garland of those [lotuses].
Hearing this, he instantly reached another enchanting place."
Then Śivaśarman asked: "What is the name of this city? The two attendants said: "O you who are experts in various sciences, this is the city of the Vidyādharas."
These [sages] provide food, sandals, clothing, and woolen blankets for students;
indeed, they also give medicines that alleviate their ailments.
Free from pride in their own learning, they instruct them in various arts and sciences.
He clarifies the second position with the words "one who knows song. The mention of "Rudra's" is also an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for Viṣṇu's as well. || 2.9 ||
They look upon the disciple as a son with garments, betel, and food.
And they marry virtuous maidens who have been adorned, in accordance with dharma. || 34 ||
"Constantly worshipping their chosen deities with a longing mind,
these excellent Vidyādharas dwell here by virtue of these merits.
While they were thus engaged in conversation, the Lord of Saṃyaminī arrived.
The King of Dharma arrived amidst the sounds of celestial drums;
seated in his aerial chariot, he possessed a serene form and was surrounded by those who know the Dharma, along with three or four servants skilled in the duties of service. || 36-37 ||
The King of Dharma said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly intelligent Śivaśarman, best of the twice-born! You have set forth that which is appropriate for the lineage of Brāhmaṇas. (38)

In the past, you studied the Vedas and satisfied your gurus; you have observed the Dharma within the Dharmaśāstras and Purāṇas and have honored it. [The phrase] "from Dharma" means on account of Dharma, with reference to Dharma. [The phrase] "with a mind of longing" refers to desire—
The body of one who departs swiftly from the City of Liberation is cleansed.
You alone are truly wise regarding life and that which lies beyond it.
This body, which always reeks of impurity and is a vessel for filth,
has been perfectly fashioned by you as a sacred bathing place through the merchandise of merit.
For this very reason, the wise hold learning in high esteem;
for those sages do not waste even a single moment.
Indeed, living beings in the mortal world certainly breathe for only five or six moments.
Even there, they would not engage in base and censurable actions;
for the body is always subject to certain decay, whereas wealth does not remain at the time of death.
Why then, being so deluded, do you not strive for a mature undertaking as you yourself would? 44.
Quickly.
Life is transitory and the world is overwhelmed by sorrow;
therefore, O most righteous one, you should direct your mind toward Dharma just as I have.
This is the ripening of your virtuous deeds; indeed, both you and I are worthy of praise.
"Since these two devotees of the Blessed One have attained friendship with you, let my command be given; therefore, what assistance may I provide?
Whatever ought to be done by those like me has indeed already been performed by you."
Today I am most blessed here, since the two attendants of the Blessed One have been seen;
let my service always be made known in the presence of their illustrious feet.
[Pt 1 Page 352]
Then, dispatched by those two, Yama entered his own city.
When Yama had departed, the Brahmin questioned those two attendants.
Śivaśarman said: "He has a most gentle appearance."
Surely this Dharmarāja is the Dharma itself personified, for his very words are pleasing to the mind;
and this city of Saṃyamanī possesses exceedingly auspicious characteristics.
"Even hearing his name, sinners tremble excessively.
People in the mortal world describe the form of Yama in one way, yet he has been seen by me in quite another; O two Gaṇas, tell me the reason for that. (51-52)
The two attendants said:
"Listen, gentle one; he appears here as very gentle indeed to those such as yourself."
By his very nature, he is the embodiment of Dharma, free from doubt through his masses of merit.
Indeed, this very one has tawny eyes, with the corners of his eyes red with wrath;
his face is formidable with fangs, and he is terrifying like a flickering flash of lightning.
With hair standing erect and limbs exceedingly black, his voice was like the roar of the clouds at the dissolution of the world;
he held the staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa) uplifted in his hand, and his face was contorted with a frown. || 56 ||
"Bring him here! Strike him down! Bind him! Release not, O Unconquerable One!
Slay this one of wicked conduct with fierce iron clubs upon his head!
(57) Seizing the feet of this evil-doer, strike him against the surface of a stone!"
"Pluck out his eyes, placing your foot upon his throat!
(58). Speaking thus, they gave the answer to the first question and then stated the answer to the final question, beginning with "Listen, gentle one," and so forth (54).
Indeed, this very person is Yama; such talk is heard from afar and seen by the wicked—thus [ends] the thirty-fifth [verse].
212. Split open!
Quickly pierce his two swollen cheeks with a razor.
Bind his neck with a noose and hang him from a tree;
split open his head like a piece of wood with a saw,
and crush his mouth with terrible blows of your palms.
"Cut off the hand of this sinner that reaches out toward another's wife;
sever the feet of him who goes to another's wife's house.
Pierce his body on all sides with needles in every pore."
Upon the limbs of the wicked man who has left nail-marks on the body of another's wife;
spit into the mouth of him who has kissed the face of another's wife;
and thrust a sharp stake into the mouth of him who speaks slander against others.
The two parts below the cheeks are the *gaṇḍas* (jowls); the meaning is: "suspend him so that [the noose] does not touch them, but rather keep him bound. || 5.9 ||
Roast him like chickpeas in heated sand and earthen pans; roast this one who causes suffering to others in a frying pan until his face becomes hideous! 64.
O Krūralocana, you constantly cast blame upon the innocent;
with your tongue, you immerse his face in the mire of pus and blood.
You seize the sprout-like hands of those who have not given away the property of others.
O Utkaṭa, repeatedly plunging him into oil and cooking him over glowing coals;
O Bhīṣaṇa, thrust red-hot iron rods into the mouth of one who utters slander against his guru or reviles the gods.

Granted that he had conquered the three worlds with the mere fall of his glance, yet he reduced Brahmā and the other gods to the state of bodilessness as they gazed upon him. (111)
"O son, go for refuge to that Śiva, the sole creator beginning with Brahmā, whose vehicle is the cloud, the infallible one who is the jewel for the protection of the universe.

He reached Kāśī, which is difficult to attain even for Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and the other gods; a place protected by Viśveśvara and rendered radiant by the celestial river, which, like a sacrificial pole, shines upon its neck-like regions amidst the heat of the great dissolution.
She was resplendent with manifold virtues and white as a pearl necklace or frost;
she warded off the suffering arising from the masses of people tormented by the heat of many transmigrations with her protective shield, and severed it with the edge of her sword.
Having reached Kāśī, that householder beheld Maṇikarṇikā with his own eyes before him; he proceeded,
perfectly causing it to blossom.
Which the wise have called Kāśikā. || 117 ||
With eyes scorched by the heat of saṃsāra, which were fixed from ear to ear, he beheld it;
first, he went to Maṇikarṇikā.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite and beheld the omnipresent Lord Viśveśvara,
the protector of all living beings in the three worlds,
he prostrated himself before him.
Beholding that linga again and again, he rejoiced greatly in his heart;
this is clearly known as the root of supreme bliss, of this there is no doubt.
"Oh, no!
There is no one more blessed than I in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, since today I have beheld the glorious and all-pervading Lord Viśveśvara. (120–121)
"This is indeed the very essence and all the wealth of the three worlds condensed into one;

Is this the first sprout of the light of self-realization?
Or is it the root-stalk of the bliss of Brahman? Or perhaps the elixir of Brahman—that which is said to be formless and residing in the lotus-heart of the yogi? (123)
Did it assume that form through the artifice of a logical mark? (124)
Or it is the vessel of the cosmic egg filled with a multitude of various jewels;

Is this mass of hair adorned with beautiful flowers the cluster of blossoms from the jasmine vine of liberation that grants the desires of those who praise it?

Is he the sun that shatters the darkness of delusion regarding saṃsāra? Or is he the beautiful mirror of adornment for the auspicious lady? 128
For all embodied beings, there would be nothing else known;
this marvelous citron is the seed-vessel for their manifold karmic seeds.
Of all [the gods]. || 126 ||
Because the dissolution of all seeds known as karma occurs within this source of nirvāṇa, this is therefore the "liṅga" (sign) of the universe when dissolved therein.

Regarding the term *keśapāśa*: it means a mass of hair or a crest; according to Amara, "the crest, the tuft, and the mass of hair" are synonyms. In the reading *supuṣpyate*, it means "it blossoms beautifully."
By the very rise of my good fortune, the great sage Nārada arrived and spoke thus; because of that, I have achieved my purpose.
Having thus prepared the nectar of bliss, he indeed performed his breaking of the fast; then, on an auspicious day, having installed the Liṅga that bestows all benefits,
he undertook severe vows difficult for those of unrefined self to perform.
Having bathed Śiva every day with one hundred and eight jars filled with the flowing waters of the Gaṅgā, that pure-souled man, using cloths purified by fire,
offers a garland made of blue lotuses to Him daily.
Having fashioned [the Linga] out of one thousand and eight *sumanas* flowers, he remained for half a fortnight and then for six months subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits.

Because dissolution (*laya*) and destruction (*nāśa*) occur in this Linga, it is therefore called the *viśvaliṅga*. However, in another reading, [it asks]: "But how [can this be so] if it is limited?"
There is the dissolution of all seeds of the nature of karma; regarding that, he says: "It is spread" (*tataṃ*). The meaning is "completely full.

In this manner, by means of the nectar-like essence of bliss—the liquid of the ambrosia of happiness—for those of unpurified self whose senses are unsubdued; [he becomes] a purified self, a cleansed self; day after day, every single day.
Regarding the phrase "with its wings": that Vaiśvānara, having pervaded six months, together with half a wing—
For seven days he subsisted on bulbs, roots, and fruits, using *sumana* flowers and blue lotuses.
For six months he subsisted on withered leaves;
for six months he lived on air, and for six months he consumed only drops of water.

in the twelfth year from his birth, those words spoken by Nārada were fulfilled.

"Whether sitting, standing, or existing—that is, being present—Śaṅkara himself, in the form of Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, has indeed terrified you, just as I have, in the form of Indra. Thus he will say.

"Arise, arise! May it be well with you! he said, as if his touch were restoring life;
for they had remained like those who have slept through the end of a day, with their lotus-eyes closed.
And rising up, he beheld before him Śambhu, who surpassed a hundred suns in brilliance upon his forehead.
Beholding him whose eye is fire, who bears Kāla upon his neck, whose banner is the bull,
who has the Daughter of the Mountain seated upon his left side, who is the moon-crested Lord,
shining with his matted hair, and whose weapons are the trident and the Ājagava bow. (148)

Having recognized Mahādeva through the words of his guru and from the scriptures— as one whose limbs are as white as shimmering camphor and who is draped in an elephant hide— [he prostrated]. || 14.9 || [Pt 1 Page 452]
Overcome with tears of joy, his voice choked and his body covered in horripilation,
he stood for a moment as if paralyzed, like a painted or artificial puppet; thus perfectly absorbed, he even forgot himself.
When there was no one capable of praising, bowing down, or even making any request,
Śaṅkara then smiled and spoke.
Īśvara said:
"O child, householder, you have been recognized by me; you are afraid of Śakra with his thunderbolt raised in hand. Do not fear! Your desire for knowledge has been fulfilled by me.
For one devoted to me, neither Śakra, nor the thunderbolt, nor even Antaka (the God of Death) has power. (153)
"For you were indeed terrified by me, appearing in the form of Indra.

(154) In what state was he? He was overwhelmed by tears of joy; for that very reason, his throat was choked and his voice faltering, and his body was covered with a "mantle" consisting of the bristling of his hair. (150)
Just as an artificial son might be painted on a wall or elsewhere with variegated pigments, so too did he become [such a one]; this connects with the preceding or the following two lines.
When, having forgotten himself—and by the word "and" (ca), others as well—he was unable to perform even the slightest action, then he smiled.
The meaning is that Śaṅkara, having made a slight smile, spoke.
(152) Neither Antaka nor Yama [could do so]; in some places the reading is "capalāpi ca" (and even the fickle one).
"You shall become the mouth of all the gods.

"This Liṅga established by you shall be known by your name;

For the devotees of Agnīśvara, there is no fear arising from lightning or fire;
nor is there ever any illness caused by weak digestion, nor any untimely death anywhere.
Having duly worshipped Agnīśvara in Kāśī, which bestows all prosperity,
even one who dies elsewhere by fate is honored in the world of Agni.
Then, having reached Kāśī again at the end of the kalpa, he shall attain liberation.
To the east of Vīreśvara and on the western bank of the Gaṅgā.

The two attendants said:

though they are Rākṣasas by birth alone, these people are holy beings (puṇyajana) by their conduct.

At the end of the previous chapter, it was said: "O Śivaśamana, the nature of Agni has thus been described to you; what else do you wish to hear? Speak that, and I shall tell it. Even among the most excellent castes, those who follow the path of the Smṛtis and the Śrutis do not at any time disregard what is prescribed in the Smṛtis regarding food and drink.
Averse to violating another's wife, seizing another's property, or harming others,
they follow their merit even when born into the lowest castes.
Those who sustain themselves by means acquired through devotion to the twice-born—
And they always keep their limbs contracted when conversing with the twice-born and in similar situations.
When summoned, those women with faces veiled by their garments speak in the presence of the twice-born, exclaiming, "Victory! Live long! O Blessed One! O Lord! O Master!
They are constantly devoted to bathing at sacred fords and eternally dedicated to the gods.
They are always bowed down before the twice-born, preceded by the announcement of their own names.
Self-restraint, charity, compassion, patience, purity, control of the senses, non-stealing, truthfulness, and non-violence are the causes of dharma for all.
"And those castes are low"—the meaning is "even among those of the lowest caste. "Not mentioned in the Smṛtis" means not stated in the Smṛti scriptures.
"Always intent upon the necessary duties" [is the meaning]. 315. [Pt 1 Page 457]
Those who are born anywhere whatsoever,
provided they are enriched with all enjoyments, dwell here in this supreme city.
The Mlecchas, ten.
Even those who commit suicide at excellent sacred bathing places (sutīrtha),
having abandoned Kāśī, enjoy [their fruits] here after attaining liberation at the end;
whereas those people who are self-destroyers enter into blinding darkness.
Having experienced thousands of hells, they shall become fierce boars.
Therefore, a wise person should never commit suicide under any circumstances;
for those who take their own lives find no auspicious results either in this world or in the next.
Some who have realized the truth say that death at one's own will occurs at Prayāga, the king of all sacred fords, which grants all desires. (14)
Even those of the lowest castes who follow the dharma of compassion and are devoted to helping others—those most excellent beings dwell here. (15)

We shall describe his true nature; listen for a moment, O Lord of the Quarter. In the midst of the Vindhya forest, among the people dwelling in a village of hunters, there was a fierce leader of a settlement known as Piṅgākṣa.
On the bank of the Nirvindhyā river, there was a hero who turned his back on cruel deeds;
though stationed at the gateway, he would strike down those who waylaid travelers and diligently slew tigers and other wicked beasts. || 17-18 ||
He lived by the dharma of a hunter,
yet even therein he was devoted to compassion.
One should not kill birds or deer that are trusting, nor those that are asleep, nor those engaged in mating; nor those greedy for water,
nor infants, nor those characterized by pregnancy.
Knowing the Dharma and turning his back on the nature of birth, he causes [suffering] to be destroyed; he grants rest to travelers afflicted by fatigue.
He removes the hunger of those tormented by hunger, being himself one who possesses sandals for those without sandals.
The deer skin, exceedingly soft, is surrendered by those who are destitute of clothing;
it follows the travelers on the road through the wilderness and the vast desert.
He does not desire wealth from them, but grants them freedom from fear;
my name, "The One Who Removes the Fear of the Wicked," should be taken up by me throughout the Vindhya forest. (23)
He constantly visited all the fortune-tellers along with his son,
and they, in turn, offered him beneficial blessings at every sacred ford.
Thus, while the tawny-eyed one remained there, that forest became like a city;
out of fear, no traveler would obstruct another on the road.
Once, by his paternal uncle, who resided in a nearby village—
For he had heard that a caravan of pilgrims, a great-sounding multitude, was approaching. Greedy for their wealth, that base hunter set himself to destroy them;
going ahead, he blocked that path while remaining deeply concealed.
Then, while a portion of his lifespan still remained, Piṅgākṣa went out hunting;
he stayed that night in that forest near the path.
They offer blessings; they bestow benedictions.
"Nagarāyitā" means that which has become like a city. "Adhvanīne" means for one traveling on a road; "adhvanīna" is [the term used for such a person].
[Pt 1 Page 461]
If one were to harm the vital breaths of others, men’s desires would not be fulfilled;
this entire universe is protected by the Lord of the Universe through His auspiciousness,
so one should not contemplate undesirable things.
Therefore, there can never be any cultivation [of merit], since that which is seen by the rules will result only in defilement. (30)
Therefore, one who desires the happiness of the Self should not contemplate the desirable or the undesirable;
if one must contemplate, then one should contemplate the means to liberation and nothing else. (31)
Then, when the night had dawned, a great clamor arose:
"Kill them! Strike them down! Strip them naked quickly, O soldiers! (32)
"Do not kill us! Save us, soldiers! We are but petty traders.
Plunder us without effort and take whatever we possess! (33)
"We are travelers without a protector, with Viśvanātha as our sole refuge;
by him we are truly protected, while any other traveler remains far from true protection. (34)

"Trusting in Piṅgākṣa, we always travel back and forth on this path without fear from any quarter; yet he is far away from this forest. Having heard these words spoken by Kārpeṭika, the soldier Piṅgākṣa then [reflected].
"Do not fear, do not fear! he cried from afar as he approached.
Drawn by the threads of his past karma, the Bhilla, who was fond of the pilgrim, arrived there in an instant, as if drawn by the very thread of his own lifespan. (37)
"Who is this? Who is this ill-behaved one, while I, Piṅgākṣa, am alive—this one who wishes to plunder the travelers who are as dear to me as my own life-breaths and *liṅga*?
In that matter, we have Viśvanātha as our protector; he, however, is far away. [We seek] the state of being a protector from those who beg for their own protection—"
The meaning is that, due to the power of false perception (*duradṛṣṭa*), it appears as if situated at a distance.
(34) Furthermore, "we" [are as follows].
Tārākṣa was his paternal uncle.
Out of greed for wealth, the wicked Piṅgākṣa conceived an evil thought: "This disgrace to the family lives having cast aside the family dharma."
"I have long contemplated this; today I shall undoubtedly kill him. (40)
Having reflected thus, that evil-minded one, out of anger, commanded his servants:
"First, let them kill this man, and then these merchants. (41)
Then all those men of wicked conduct fought with him alone; somehow or other, he led them to the vicinity of his own dwelling.
Equal to the mobile *prāṇaliṅga*s worn by living beings, they were like the *śivaliṅga*s being carried by them.
[Pt 1 Page 464] Indeed, his bow was severed, his quiver was cut away by arrows, and his armor was shattered.
If I had been the Lord, I would have brought them to perfection. || 43 ||
Desiring [to save] his life, he gave it up for the sake of another;
those pilgrims also reached that hamlet, their fear gone.
For whatever the state of mind at the time of death may be, the destination follows accordingly.
"Thus he attained the lordship of the quarters and became the Lord of the Nairṛtas in the southwest (Nirṛti).
In this manner, his true nature has been described by us both to you.
To the north of this is the wonderful world of Varuṇa."
The builders of wells, tanks, and lakes with pure wealth [attain merit]. (323)
In this world, those who possess the splendor of Varuṇa are honored in the realm of Varuṇa.
Those who provide water in waterless places, who remove the suffering of others,
and who bestow upon supplicants variegated parasols and water-pots— these are the builders of water-sheds. (48)

Those who assist with trees on the road should provide various articles of utility and also offer "Dharma-pitchers" filled with fragrant water. (4.9) Those who perform the watering of the Aśvattha tree on the road are benefactors of living beings.
They are the builders of rest-houses who dispel the fatigue and suffering of travelers. || 50 ||
At the onset of the heat, even palm-leaf fans,
decorated with peacock feathers that ward off the summer’s fever, are distributed.
They diligently distribute delicious, fragrant, and cooling drinks that satisfy the thirst of those suffering in the heat;
they even prepare and give fields of sugarcane to the Brahmins.
Likewise, those who provide many various kinds of sugarcane products,
as well as dairy products, and those who give cows and buffaloes;
those who construct water-shed pavilions and those who create shaded pavilions.
Those who provide multi-streamed water-pots in temples, or those who remove tolls at a holy ford, or those who clear the path to the ford; || 55 ||
Those who, with hands upraised in distress, grant fearlessness to those afflicted by fear,
dwell and shine joyfully in the world of Varuṇa, free from fear.
Those meritorious ones who release from their throats the nooses with which they have been bound by those of evil conduct.

O twice-born one, those citizens who rescue travelers from rivers and other waters by means of boats and other vehicles dwell in this world without fear from any quarter; they likewise rescue others from the ocean of suffering. (58)

Those men who construct embankments with stones and other materials for rivers of merit and the like, for the sake of achieving the happiness of those seeking water, are the "enjoyers" (bhoginaḥ) in this world. 5.9.
Those meritorious ones who quench the thirst of the thirsty with cool waters, by that very act they become partakers of a continuous stream of happiness in the world of Varuṇa.
"Vipāśayanti" means they cause them to be free from bonds; that is, they release those whose necks are bound by nooses. "Kaṇṭhapāśitān" means those [bound] around the necks.
Of all reservoirs of water, this is one of the foremost lords.
Pracetas, the lord of aquatic creatures, is the witness to all ritual acts.
Listen to the origin of this lord of Varuṇa, the high-souled one: there was a sage of immeasurable soul, [the son] of the progenitor Kardama. (62)
He had a son known as Śuciṣmān, who was well-bred and endowed with qualities such as steadfastness,
sweetness, and fortitude, and who was beneficial to others.
He went with the boys to bathe in a clear lake;
while he was absorbed in playing in the water, a crocodile seized him.
When he had been carried off by those children who foretold a great calamity, they gathered together and related it before his father,
who was seated in worship of Hara, his mind motionless in meditative absorption.
And despite hearing of the calamities that befell the young, his mind did not waver from Hara.
He practiced even more intensely his devotion to the omniscient, three-eyed Lord,
beholding the fourteen worlds in the presence of Śambhu.
The various beings existing within the cosmic egg,
as well as the moon, the sun, the constellations, the stars, the mountains, the rivers, the trees,
the oceans, the islands, the forests, and the lakes.
And he saw various classes of gods and the city of Bahvādiviṣadā.
[He saw] many ponds, wells, tanks, canals, and lotus-pools;
[and] at a certain lake, those intent on water-sports— then,
immediately after that, when the son of the sage had been taken away from that lake (the implication being that he was taken by a crocodile).
And many young sages by means of plunging in and out of the water,
and by being sprinkled with streams of water released from the hollows of her hands. (71)
Thus, many boys were engrossed in water-sports, making sounds by clapping their hands and filling the quarters with the noise of the water. || 72 ||
Then, remaining absorbed in meditation, Kardama beheld among them his own infant being carried away by a porpoise, utterly distressed.
Then, a certain goddess of the waters forcibly led him away from that cruel aquatic creature and saw him delivered to the ocean.
Having rebuked the Lord of Rivers with words such as "O Trident-bearer! by someone possessing the form of Rudra, whose face was drawn taut with rage;
thus, the grammatical connection is that he was looking at many boys and the sons of sages, both those who were engaged and those who were not—thus.
"Released by them" means abandoned; "by those showers" means by those consecrations—this is the meaning. || 71 ||

The sounds produced by those waters and fluids struck by hands, as well as the noises from the quarters of the sky and the like, and by means of water-sports—that is, aquatic games—[were heard]. || 72 ||
Without knowing [this] of the highly fortunate and wise Prajāpati Kardama. || 76 ||
Having heard those words, the ocean, trembling with fear, waited for a long time to manifest the power of Śiva;
then, having adorned the boy with jewels, he [offered him]. (77)
Having bound that Śiśumāra and brought it as an offering,
he presented it in the presence of the lotus feet of Śambhu.
Having bowed down, I address you: O Lord, I have committed no offense, O Lord of the Universe, Protector of the helpless, Destroyer of the calamities of devotees!
O Śambhu, the wish-fulfilling tree for devotees, by this [creature], O Śambhu, by this wicked aquatic monster—
O Lord, I did not lead the child who was devoted to you through the cycle of existence.
Then, having understood the intention of Śambhu, that Gaṇa bound that aquatic creature with a noose and delivered it into the hand of the boy.
