"Accept this, your own son, O attendant, by the command of Śaṅkara; go to your own abode, my child," saying this, that Kardama, of noble intellect, heard all of it while in a state of meditative absorption. 82.
As soon as he opened his eyes and released his meditative concentration,
he beheld a child standing before him; and at his side, he saw one holding a porpoise and adorned with earrings.
Embracing him— who had moistened his crow-feather-like locks with water, whose corners of the eyes were stained with collyrium, who was slightly parched, whose skin was agitated,
and whose mind was deeply moved— she kissed his lotus-face after he had offered his salutation.
He felt as if he were born again, looking at him again and again.
[The two and a half verses beginning with] "Take [him]" constitute the speech: while the attendant of Śaṅkara, by the Lord's command, was saying to Śuciṣmat, "O child!
Go to your own home," and likewise saying to Kardama, "Take this, your own son."

Hearing what was previously mentioned—that "Kardama, at the time of his meditative absorption"—he released his resolve, one-pointedness, and concentration; opening and widening his eyes, as soon as he looked before him, he beheld a child by his side.
[Pt 1 Page 473]
For Kardama, who remained steadfast in his vow while worshipping Śambhu, those [aeons] then passed away.
And Kardama also understood that momentary union at that time,
for Time has no power in the presence of Mahākāla.
Then,
having questioned his father and prostrated before him,
the son went quickly for the sake of asceticism to the illustrious city of Vārāṇasī.
Having performed severe penance there, he installed a Śāmbhava Liṅga and remained for five thousand years, as motionless as a stone.
Then Mahādeva appeared, pleased by that austerity, and said to Kārdama: "Speak; what supreme boon shall I grant you?"
Kārdami said:
"O Lord, compassionate toward your devotees, if you are pleased with me,
grant me sovereignty over all waters and even over the aquatic creatures."
"Met for a moment" means he realized or understood that they were together for only a brief instant; the reason for this is given by the word "yataḥ" (since).
[Pt 1 Page 474]
Having heard this, Maheśāna, the Lord who grants all desires,
consecrated him there in the supreme station of Varuṇa,
[the lord] of jewels born from the ocean and of the oceans as well as the rivers.
Furthermore, be the sovereign of lakes, ponds, and the waters of wells and streams;
be the lord of all reservoirs of water and of the western quarter as well, O beloved of all the immortals, with noose in hand.
I grant another boon as well, which shall bring benefit to all:
this Liṅga installed by you shall be known by your name.
Known as Varuṇeśa, it bestows excellent siddhi in Vārāṇasī;
it is situated in the southwest direction of the Maṇikarṇeśa Liṅga.
Constantly propitiated by men, it destroys all dullness;
for those who are devotees of Varuṇeśa, there is no fear of me anywhere.
They have no fear of suffering, nor do they ever suffer misfortune or death.
There is no fear of dropsy at all, nor indeed any fear of thirst anywhere.
They will become full of flavor; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having spoken thus, Śambhu vanished, and Varuṇa also, together with his kinsmen,
remained there from that time forth, adorning this world, O twice-born one.
This true nature of the realm of Varuṇa has been described to you.
Having heard which, a man is never again afflicted by difficult calamities anywhere.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the World of Fire," in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the commentary on the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa* composed by Śrī Rāmānanda.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.

"O gentle one, this Liṅga has been established by you, which bestows intelligence upon all, removes evil-mindedness, and grants residence in your world. (64)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Śambhu vanished right there;
and by the grace of the God of gods, Budha went to the celestial realm (Svarloka).
The two attendants said:
Indeed, having entered the bottomless ocean of saṃsāra, a man whose intellect has not been attained through the worship of Budheśvara in Kāśī would sink,
even if he possesses the moon-like luster that delights the eyes of the virtuous.
One shall dwell here in this world with a beloved face.
Having seen the Budheśvara Liṅga to the east of Candreśvara,
a living being is never deprived of intelligence, even at the time of death.
It bestows intelligence and produces knowledge; in some places, it is said to increase the intellect. || 64 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the commentary on the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa* composed by Śrī Rāmānanda.
In this manner,
the two groups conversed for as long as they wished,
reaching the world of the wise.
Just then, the celestial chariot reached the unsurpassed world of Śukra.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worlds of the Nakṣatras and Budha," in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
[Pt 1 Page 544] || Now begins the sixteenth chapter. ||
The two attendants said: "O Śivaśarman of great intelligence, this world of Śukra is wonderful;
here dwells Kavi, the preceptor of the Dānavas and the Daityas. (1)
Having drunk for a thousand years the most difficult-to-bear smoke of grain-husks,
he obtained from Hara the great vidyā known as Mṛtyusañjīvanī.
Even the preceptor of the gods does not know this most difficult-to-master lore,
except for Mṛtyuñjaya, Skanda, Pārvatī, and the elephant-faced one.
Śivaśarman said: Who is this one known as Śukra, whose world is so excellent?
And how was the Mṛtyu-sañjīvanī (the life-restoring) lore obtained by him from Hara?
In the sixteenth [chapter], the excellent jewel of living beings, the city of Bhārgava, is described.

[This is] the description of the world of Bhṛgu, which has come in due order, belonging to the preceptor of the lords of the Asuras, who possesses incomparable splendor. [The verse begins: "Śivaśamaṃ... [and continues: "Kaṇāḥ kaṇḍitāḥ taṇḍulatuṣāḥ... (The husks are the threshed grains of rice...)
"Smoke produced from that [fire], namely soot-smoke. (2) "Difficult to perform, difficult to attain. "And Vākpati," as it appears in some versions.
(3-4) [Pt 1 Page 545] Thereupon, the two of them said to the Goddess:
The supreme narrative of Śukra.
Having heard it, those endowed with faith are freed from untimely deaths; furthermore, no fear arises from ghosts, spirits, or demons.
This occurred during the battle that was unfolding between Andhaka and the Enemy of Andhaka (Śiva).
[He was the lord] of the two who possessed the adamantine arrays and mountain-like formations that were impenetrable.
Then, having withdrawn from the battle and approached the presence of Śukra, Andhaka descended from his chariot and spoke as follows.
O Blessed One, having taken refuge in you,
we consider even the gods with their followers— including Rudra, Upendra, and the others— to be equal to blades of grass.
"Let them tell," they said. "From untimely deaths—that is, from premature deaths—from sinful deaths—like elephants from lions, or like serpents from Garuḍas. [Pt 1 Page 546]
O Teacher, the gods fear us because of your grace.
The Daityas and Dānavas entered the impenetrable Vajravyūha formation,
having shaken off the host of Pramathas like those afflicted by heat enter a lake.
Having come for refuge to you, we remain as immovable as mountains.
"Abiding thus, we move about without fear in this great battle between Brahmā and Indra.
With a spirit of total trust, we, together with our wives and sons, serve your feet—which grant us happiness—day and night. (12-13)
O Brahmin, being pleased, you have graciously protected those who have come to you for refuge;
now behold Huṇḍa, Tuhuṇḍa, Kujambha, and Jambha!
Pārka, Kārtasvana, Vipāka, Pākahārin, Candradamana, Śūra, and Śūrāmaravidāraṇa—[these were his sons]. || 15 ||
Having drunk [the blood] of those who were slaughtered and fallen, like sandalwood trees by the Dravidians... || 16 ||
Indeed, in the past, after a thousand years, you obtained this excellent knowledge through the smoke of chaff; now the time for its fruit has arrived. (17) Now, the fruit of that knowledge:
Let all the Pramathas behold these Daityas being restored to life by you as you intend to bring them back to life. || 18 ||
Having heard these words of Andhaka, the sage Bhārgava, firm in intellect,
then smiled slightly and spoke to the lord of the Dānavas.
O Lord of the Dānavas! 16 ||
Everything you have spoken is true; indeed,
this acquisition of knowledge was undertaken by me for the sake of the Dānavas,
through the Dravidians— people born in the land of the Dravidas.

If it is asked, "This being so, what can be done by me?", he says: "Having drunk... and so forth. Having drunk the extremely difficult-to-bear smoke of grain-chaff for an autumn—that is, for a year—or indeed for a thousand years.
This knowledge, obtained from Īśvara, brings happiness to one's kinsmen.
"By means of this knowledge, I shall raise up those who have been crushed in battle by the Pramathas, just as a rain-cloud revives withered crops. (22)

"O King, in this very moment you shall see the Dānavas risen— free from wounds, free from pain, healthy, and as if they had merely awakened from sleep. Having spoken thus to the lord of the Dānavas, Kavi invoked the Vidyā-mantra.
Aiming at each individual demon, they rose up, grasping their weapons.
Like the Vedas constantly studied, or like clouds at the proper time, or like wealth given with faith to Brahmins during a great calamity;
[these] wither and dry up. (22) 25.
But seeing those great asuras, Tuṇḍa and the others, restored to life, [he said: 407. [Pt 1 Page 549] Seeing those great asuras, Tuṇḍa and the others, restored to life...
Those ancient gods roared like clouds filled with water.
Seeing those Dānavas restored to life by Śukra, the lords of the Gaṇas spoke thus to one another, addressing the Lord of the Gods: "This must indeed be reported [to him]. || 26-27 ||
While that sacrifice of battle, so wondrous in form, was thus proceeding among the lords of the Pramathas,
Śilāda’s son, indignant at having witnessed the deeds of Bhārgava, approached Maheśa.
Having cried out "Victory!", Nandin spoke to the fierce source of victory, who was as radiant as gold:
That which is difficult even for the lords of the Gaṇas, for the gods of war, and even for the gods led by Indra;
just as clouds that have perished before the rainy season rise up in the sky when appointed by Parjanya during the rains;
and just as wealth given with faith to Brahmins rises up to grant fruit to the givers in times of great calamity. In times of great calamity...
Or "given"—the meaning is that it is just like that. || 25 ||
The former gods were the Asuras. || 26 ||

"Vijñāpyam evam evaṃprakāram vijñāpanīyam" means "this is to be made known in such a manner. In some places it appears as "vijñāpyam etat. Since the word "evam" (thus) is used without repetition due to a difference in grammatical construction (*anvaya-bheda*), there is no tautology. || 27 ||
O Lord, that which has been done today by Bhārgava for us is in vain; let our enemies, who died in battle, be restored to life.
O Master, having effortlessly mastered the science that grants life to the dead, revive each one of them individually.
The great lords of the asuras, such as Tuhuṇḍa, Huṇḍa, Kujambha, Jambha, Vipāka, and Pāka,
having returned today from the abode of Yama, roam about putting the Pramathas to flight.
For if he were to restore those foremost Daityas here again and again once they have been cast down, [the gods would be lost].

"O Maheśa, how shall victory be ours, and how indeed can there be peace for the lords of the Gaṇas? Thus addressed by Sanandin, the lord of the Pramathas, the God, the lord of the lords of the Pramathas, then spoke laughingly to Nandin, the king of all the lords of the Gaṇas.
"O Nandin, proceed with extreme haste! Having snatched him from the midst of the sons of Diti—the lords among the twice-born—bring him here quickly, just as a hawk seizes a young quail."
In such a way that it may be easy and graceful. || 30 ||
Having plunged into the army, he who was the lamp of the Bhārgava lineage proceeded swiftly;
and as he was being guarded by all the sons of Diti, who held nooses, swords, trees, stones, and mountains in their hands—

Having agitated the Daityas, the powerful Nanda seized Kāvya like a Śarabha seizing an elephant. As he was being carried off by the strong one— his garments slipping, his ornaments falling away, and his hair disheveled—
the enemies of the gods followed him, uttering lion-like roars as if intending to liberate him.
Like clouds pouring forth fierce rain, the lords of the Dānavas rained down thunderbolts, tridents, swords, axes, towering discuses, and stones upon Nandīśvara.
With a roar like that of a bull and a sound superior to the lion's, he [the lion]— having agitated and shaken the *śarabha* (the eight-legged mountain beast)—
[attacked] the *ibha* (elephant).
Having encountered that descendant of Bhṛgu, the Lord of the Gaṇas, having burnt hundreds of weapons with the fire from his mouth,
arrived at the side of Bhava while the great war between the Asuras and the gods was raging, with the enemy forces distressed.
"This is that Śukra, O Blessed One," he quickly reported this to Bhava.
And that God of gods accepted Śukra as an offering presented by the pure one.
Without saying a word, that protector of beings indeed hurled the lord of poets into his mouth like a fruit;
then all those asuras let out a loud cry of "Hā! Hā! and a great clamor of "Alas! Alas! (hahaha).
When the poet had been swallowed by the Lord of Girijā, the Daityas became devoid of hope for victory,
like lordly elephants deprived of their trunks, or like bulls bereft of their horns.
Just as the qualities of a being are without effort, or as efforts are devoid of fortune;
just as women are deprived of a husband, or as volleys of arrows are without their feathers;
just as lives are deficient in merit, or as sacred learnings are lacking in virtuous conduct. (43–44)
Just as masses of ritual actions become deficient in their own fruits without the one power of majesty,
so too did the Daityas become averse to any hope of victory without that one best of the twice-born.
When Śukra had been carried off by Nandin and swallowed by Viṣādin, [the demons were despondent].
The Daityas fell into despair, their enthusiasm for the festival of battle waning.
Seeing them bereft of energy, Andhaka addressed them:
"By Nandin, who has displayed his prowess and led us away, we have been brought under control."
Today, by him, the life-breaths of all of us have been taken from our bodies;
[so too have been taken] your fortitude, your valor, your refuge, your fame, your courage, your splendor, and your prowess. (48)

[Pt 1 Page 554] "When one Bhārgava was taken away, everything was seized all at once. Fie on us, by whom even a single most excellent member of the family— the one honored by the lineage— has been lost!"
"The Guru is all-powerful and our protector; he has not been saved from calamity.
Therefore, relying on his fortitude, fight here against the enemies!
I myself shall destroy all the Pramathas along with Nandin."
"Today, having slain these helpless ones along with the gods including Indra,
I shall release Bhārgava from his life, just as yoga releases one from karma.
And even if that yogi himself is a master through his yoga,"
"Let our remaining protection issue forth from his body!
Hearing this, the Dānavas, with voices like the rumbling of clouds, [spoke].
Having resolved that they must die before being conquered,
they did not [fear] death; for as long as their life-force remains true, the Pramathas could never overcome them by force.
If life is no more, what is the point of departing and abandoning one's master in battle?
Those people who value honor above all else and depart from the battlefield, leaving their master behind,
will certainly go to the abode of Andhatāmisra.
It proclaims their infamy and darkens them extensively; those who are broken on the field of battle will find no happiness, neither in this world nor in the next. (56)

What is the use of gifts, what is the use of austerities, and what is the use of bathing at sacred fords, if one has bathed in the sacred ford of the Earth (dharātīrtha), which removes the impurity of rebirth? Those for whom high esteem alone is their wealth are "those whose wealth is high esteem" (bahumānadhanāḥ). 55–57.

The very disposition is the darkness of ignorance; by that darkness of disposition, they—those Daityas and Danujas—having thus deliberated with one another, [sought] renown and fame. [Page 556] "Having reflected," they said to each other.
The Pramathas churned [the enemy] in battle, sounding the war-drums;
there, with floods of arrows, swords, and thunderbolts made of jagged stones,
and with *bhuśuṇḍīs*, *bhindipālas*, spears, javelins, and axes— || 58–59 ||
Striking one another with skull-topped staffs, sharp-edged spears, tridents, axes, and maces, they wrought a great slaughter.
Of the drawn bows and of the falling arrows—
The sound of *bhindipāla* and *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons and the shouts of battle arose. With the blare of war-trumpets, the frequent trumpeting of elephants,
and the neighing of horses, a great tumult occurred.

With stones consisting of *kaṭaṃkaṭa* rock— that is, with stones from rocks characterized by the word *kaṭaṃkaṭa* used as mechanical projectiles— and with *bhuśuṇḍīs* and *bhindipālas*: here, *bhuśuṇḍīs* are everywhere covered with iron spikes at the bottom—

Between heaven and earth,
a great bristling of hair arose among both the brave and the timid, as the sound of the thunderous cries of elephants and horses was silenced.
With their banners and flags broken, and their weapons exhausted; with their horses,

The thirsty troops indeed fainted on both sides upon seeing the army being crushed here and there by the Pramathas;
then Andhaka himself, mounting his chariot, rushed toward the Gaṇas.
By those strikes of the arrow-vajras and by those vajra-blowings, the foremost mountains perished as if they were waterless clouds scattered by the winds. || 67 ||
Beholding him as he went and as he came, whether at a distance or standing nearby,
Andhaka then pierced him with arrows equal in number to each of his body hairs.
Their ears— the organs of hearing— were clearly bursting and splitting from the great roars of the elephants and horses.
By Vināyaka, Skanda, Nandin, Somanandin,
Naigameya, Śākha, and the powerful Viśākha.
By these and other fierce hosts, Andhaka was likewise blinded by the falling torrents of showers from volleys of tridents, spears, and arrows.
Then a great clamor arose between the armies of the Pramathas and the Asuras.
At that great sound, Śukra, who was staying within the womb of Śambhu,
then wandered about searching for a hole like the wind, which has no fixed abode;
he beheld the seven worlds along with the netherworlds (pātālas) within the body of Rudra.
The diverse worlds of Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, Indra, the Ādityas, and the Apsarases, as well as the battle between the Pramathas and the Asuras.
Wandering all around within the belly of Bhava for a hundred years,
he did not see any opening there, just as a wicked man finds no flaw in the pure.
Then, by means of the Śāmbhava yoga in the form of semen, Bhārgava descended; he bowed down, and was then addressed by the Lord:
"Since you have emerged like semen (śukra), therefore, O descendant of Bhṛgu, you shall be known as Śukra."
"By this very act, you are Śukra; you are my son. Depart! (76)
When the semen emerged from his belly, even the god rejoiced greatly:
"It is well for me that the twice-born one wandered away; he did not die within my belly. (77)
Thus addressed by the god, Śukra, whose splendor was like that of the sun,
entered the army of the Dānavas as the moon enters a mass of clouds.
From the rising of Śukra, that great ocean of Dānavas attained joy.
Just as the great ocean, garlanded with waves of joy, [rises] at the rising of the moon;
a *randhra* is a hole or aperture. By the *śāmbhava*—that is, by the yoga or means obtained through the grace of Śambhu—in the form of *śukra*, that is, in the form of semen; as for *śukra*...

He emerges through a fissure in the path; that is to say, by that manner. He leaped forth—that is, he went outside—while the great battle between Andhaka and the Slayer of Andhaka was indeed taking place.
Thus, by name, he became Śukra, the delighter of the Bhṛgus.
And listen, O observer of noble vows, to how Kāvya obtained that supreme knowledge of reviving the dead through the grace of Śambhu.
The two Gaṇas said: [He went to] the city.
Long ago, that descendant of Bhṛgu went to Vārāṇasī,
which bestows [liberation] upon the world of beings born from eggs, sweat, soil, and wombs.
Having installed the linga of Śrī Śambhu and having constructed a well in front of it,
he performed austerities for a long time, meditating upon the Lord Viśveśvara.
With *rājacampaka*, dhattūra, karavīra, and kuśeśaya flowers; with *mālatī*, *kaṇikāra*, kadamba, *baṃkula*, and *utpala* flowers. || 84 ||
He concludes the answer to the question "Who is this Śukra? with the words: "Thus he became known by the name Śukra. (80)

He provides the answer to the question, "How was the vidyā obtained by him? following an introductory restatement: "Just as with *aśoka*, *karuṇa*, *puṣpa*, *punnāga*, and *nāgakesara* flowers... [Pt 1 Page 561] || 85 ||
With *kṣudrā* and *mādhavī* vines,
with *pāṭala*, *bilva*, and *campaka*; with *navamallī*, *vicikila*, *kunda*, and *samucukundaka* flowers.
With mandāra, bilva leaves, īśvara, droṇa, marubaka, and baka flowers;
with granthiparṇa, damanaka, and the sprouts of surabhī and uśīra; and with tulasī, devagandhārī, bṛhatpatrī, and kuśa shoots— || 87 ||
With *nandyāvarta*, *agastya*, *śāla*, and *devadāru* trees; or [the word] *dada*. In the masculine, *padma*, *nalina*, *aravinda*, and *mahotpala* [mean lotus].
"A thousand-petaled lotus, a hundred-petaled [lotus], and a kuśeśaya," according to Amara.
Mālatī, Jāti, Kaṇikāra, Drumotpala; Kadamba, Halipriya; Vaṅkula, Kesara;
with Kāñcanāras, Kurubakas, sprouts of Dūrvā grass, and Kuraṇṭakas.
With each of these flowers, as well as with other sprouts.
With hundreds of thousands of leaves, he worshipped Śaṅkara;
and with great effort, he bathed the Lord of Gods a hundred thousand times with five *droṇa* measures of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and many fragrant ablutions.
A thousand times he anointed the Lord of Gods with sandalwood and yakṣakardama pastes;
following these fragrant ointments, he honored the Lord of Gods with songs, dances, offerings, and many hymns of praise as prescribed in the Vedas.
With thousands of other names and hymns, Śukra praised Śaṅkara,
thus worshipping him for five thousand years.
When she did not see the God looking even slightly toward her with favor,
she then undertook another formidable vow that was exceedingly difficult to endure.
Having repeatedly purified that jewel of a mind through meditative cultivation along with the senses, and having offered it to the wielder of the Pināka bow, || 65 ||
The sage drank a thousand autumns of the mass of smoke from grain-particles.
Then the Lord,
whose splendor exceeds that of a thousand suns, emerged from that liṅga and,
being Virūpākṣa himself— the husband of Dākṣāyaṇī— became gracious toward the high-souled Bhārgava and spoke.
"O Bhārgava, treasure of asceticism, I am pleased; choose a boon.
Hearing these words of Śambhu, the lotus-eyed twice-born one, his body covered with horripilation born of a surging mass of bliss, [spoke].
Satisfied, with the corners of his eyes blossoming with joy, he praised the Eight-bodied One, placing his joined palms upon his head and crying out, "Victory! Victory! (100).

The connection between the two verses is as follows: having washed away and removed the great impurity, the poet Śukra, pervading a thousand autumns, thoroughly drank—the verb *papau* meaning "drank"—the mass of grain-smoke, that is, the collection of smoke from rice-husks. By what means? By those very clouds of contemplation and meditation (*bhāvanādhyāna*).
[Page 564]
Bhārgava said:
"By these rays of yours, having overcome all darkness,
you lead to its setting the desires of the night-stalkers."

O Lord of the World, O Sun, you shine intensely in the sky for the welfare of the three worlds; therefore, salutations to you. In this world, with your exceedingly great splendors beyond measure... 101.
O moon for the frost-like delusion of my son, you who have dispelled all darkness, you who create the joy of the autumnal moonlight and the vast ocean of delight,
and you who are filled with a flood of nectar— to you, our son, we offer our salutations.
The hero of the Bhṛgu lineage praised the Blessed Lord Īśa, whose forms are the sun, moon, wind, fire, water, space, earth, and the self,
with four verses in succession.
On the pure path, you are always the refuge and the one to be worshipped.
Who here could live, sustaining the life of the world, without you—O you who satisfy all beings throughout the universe when they are oppressed by the stiffened winds; salutations to you! 103.

O Inner Soul of the Universe! Alas, this world breathes only because of Your singular power as the purifier of the Purifier of Viśvakapa; otherwise, O Immortal One, how could this divine work exist, being as it is like nectar?

O Supreme Lord, whose form is water, who purifies the world, salutations to you, the one who bestows tranquility and who has fire as your first step. 104. [Pt 1 Page 566] O Supreme Lord, whose form is water, who purifies the world, salutations to you,
O Lord of the Universe, you surely perform wondrous and diverse virtuous deeds;
for indeed, by drinking from or bathing in you, this entire world becomes pure and stainless—therefore, I bow down to you. 105.
This entire universe, the Lord, expands here by providing space both within and without through its ethereal form;
it always breathes with you as its very nature of compassionate respiration.

Therefore, I bow to you, for the world does not live without the singular power of your fire—that is, without the preeminent purifying capacity associated with you; this should be understood as being due to the kindling of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*). Of what nature is the world? It is the divine effect of nectar, and the gods are [born] from nectar.

The divine senses, their functions, and the elements— due to their state of oneness, O Amṛta, the divine function, the cosmic whole (viśva), exists here, O All-pervading Lord, as the presiding deity, the internal self, and the external world.
Thus, having been saluted by these eight forms of Umā,
O most venerable one, whose form is dear to all people, may you be victorious!
O You who are spread out, well-expanded, and who have brought all the multitudes of goals for those who bow down to the ultimate truth—O Source of all things, I bow before You. 106.

Having thus praised the Lord with the eight-fold hymn of the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*), Bhārgava bowed down again and again, his head touching the ground, to Bhaga, who dwells within the inner self of all beings—the inner self of all whose ignorance and its effects have been destroyed.
(110) O Hara! O destroyer of ignorance and its effects! O you who reside within the inner self of all! [The inner selves of all are their internal organs...]

This is an address to Him whose abode or refuge is those [forms]. Likewise, "O You of corresponding form" (*pratirūparūpa*): that which corresponds to each form (*rūpaṃ rūpaṃ prati*) is "corresponding" (*pratirūpa*), meaning having the nature of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) according to each limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); this is the address to Him. And so says the Śruti: "Just as tiny sparks fly up from a fire, even so from this Self... and "He became the counterpart of every form; such is His form for every form. Regarding that, it is said: *tadasyarūpaṃ prati*.
Having raised him from the ground and supported that prostrate twice-born man with his two arms,
he spoke, with the moonlight of his teeth—

The Chapter on the Aggregates (Khandha-niddesa), pp. 601–770. [Main Text from Page 1] **Chapter I: The Aggregates** **1. The Five Aggregates** *Aggregates* (khandhā) are so called because they heap up (rāsi) or accumulate (puñja). There are five aggregates: the aggregate of form (rūpa-khandha), the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-khandha), the aggregate of perception (saññā-khandha), the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhāra-khandha), and the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇa-khandha). **2. The Aggregate of Form** Form (rūpa) is that which is subject to transformation (ruppana). It consists of twenty-eight kinds: the four primary elements (mahābhūtā) and the twenty-four derivative forms (upādāya-rūpa). The four primary elements are: the earth element (pathavī-dhātu), the water element (āpo-dhātu), the fire element (tejo-dhātu), and the air element (vāyo-dhātu). The twenty-four derivative forms are: the five sense faculties (indriyāni)—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; the four objects (visayā)—visible form, sound, odor, and flavor; the three characteristics of matter—gender (liṅga), life-force (jīvita), and physical nutriment (āhāra); the two communicative intonations—bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti) and vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti); the three spatial qualities—limitedness (pariccheda), cohesion (santati), and lightness (lahutā); the three plastic qualities—malleability (mudutā), wieldiness (kammaññatā), and integration (upacaya); the three sustaining qualities—continuity (santati), decay (jaratā), and impermanence (aniccatā). **3. The Aggregate of Feeling** Feeling (vedanā) is the experiencing of the result of contact. It is of six types according to the sense base: feeling born of eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact. These are further classified as pleasant, painful, or neutral. **4. The Aggregate of Perception** Perception (saññā) is the grasping of the specific marks (nimitta-ggāha) of an object. Like feeling, it is of six types according to the sense base: perception of visible form, sound, odor, flavor, tangible objects, and mental phenomena. **5. The Aggregate of Mental Formations** Mental formations (saṅkhārā) are volitional activities (cetanā) and other concomitants of consciousness that construct (abhisankharonti) kamma. They are divided into fifty-two factors: the seven universal (sabba-citta-sādhāraṇā), the six object-determining (pakinnaka), the fourteen unwholesome (akusala), the nineteen wholesome (kusala), and the eight indeterminate (abyākata). **6. The Aggregate of Consciousness** Consciousness (viññāṇa) is the act of cognizing (vijānana). It is of eighty-nine types, categorized by way of plane (bhūmi), root (hetu), and object (ārammaṇa). **Summary:** Thus, the five aggregates are the basis for the designation of a "being" or "person. They are empty of a permanent self (attā) or anything belonging to a self (attaniya). Understanding these aggregates is essential for realizing the nature of suffering and attaining liberation. *** **Chapter II: The Bases and Elements** **1. The Twelve Bases (Āyatana)** Bases (āyatana) are the doors and objects through which consciousness arises. There are twelve: the six internal bases (ajjhattika-āyatana)—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—and the six external bases (bāhira-āyatana)—visible form, sound, odor, flavor, tangible objects, and mental phenomena. **2. The Eighteen Elements (Dhātu)** Elements (dhātu) signify the different modes of existence.
There are eighteen:

[He] asks to hear the greatness of Kāśī in detail, saying, "O Lord," and so forth; it shines exceedingly (atirocate).

That sacred field is not attached to the earthly realm (bhūrloka) but resides in the intermediate space (antarikṣa);

O Brahmin, he who should dwell there with a restrained self and a concentrated mind—
Even one who eats at the three times of day becomes equal to one who subsists on air alone.
For he who possesses supreme devotion at Avimukta for even the duration of a single blink of an eye has performed great penance, endowed with the practice of celibacy.
But that steadfast man who dwells for a month, eating light food and with senses subdued,
by him the entire divine Pāśupata vow has been performed.
Dwelling there for a year, having conquered anger and subdued the senses,
another [person] with unemaciated limbs, avoiding the food of others— there,
in Avimukta, perfection is present; the reason for that is "there it is eternal," as indicated by the word "where."
Sometimes. || 57 ||
"Endowed with celibacy" means properly engaged in the practice of celibacy.
|| 60 || "But another [is one] whose limbs are not nourished by another's property"—that is, one whose body is not made fat by the wealth of others.

Elsewhere, he performed great austerities for a thousand years; however, that man who dwells in this sacred field for as long as he lives, knowing its majesty, [attains the same merit].
Having abandoned the fear of birth and death, he attains the supreme goal.
The goal attainable through yoga cannot be reached even in hundreds of other births;
yet, by the grace of the Lord, it is attained here with ease.
Indeed, even a slayer of a Brahmin who goes to the city of Vārāṇasī by divine providence [attains that goal].
By the greatness of that sacred field, the sin of killing a Brahmin is averted.
For one who does not leave Avimukta until the fall of the body,
not only the sin of killing a Brahmin but even primordial nature (prakṛti) itself ceases to exist.
He who, with undistracted mind, does not abandon that field,
abandons old age, death, and the most unbearable dwelling in a womb.
Nature is ignorance.
A wise man who desires not to undergo rebirth on earth should resort to Avimukta, which is frequented by hosts of gods and sages. (66)
One should never leave Avimukta, which grants liberation from the fear of saṃsāra;

Even after committing thousands of sins, it is better here to attain the state of a piśāca.

But heaven, which cannot be attained even by a hundred sacrifices, is not possible without the city of Kāśī. (71) At the time of death, when the vital organs of men are being torn asunder and they are being pierced by the wind [of death], no memory whatsoever arises. (72)

He states the answer to the first question with the following section of the text, beginning from "mahāpralaya" up to, but not including, "skanda": "mahāpralaya..."

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: at the time of the elemental dissolution (*prākṛta-pralaya*), the entire universe was composed of darkness (*tamomaya*). He describes the nature of the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) with the words "when the stationary and moving have perished" (*naṣṭe sthāvarajaṅgame*). "Perished" means having gone out of sight. "Composed of darkness" means having the nature of ignorance (*ajñāna*). By the word "darkness" (*tamas*), which denotes a single part of the qualities (*guṇa*), *prakṛti*—which consists of the totality of those qualities—is expressed. And the mention of "darkness" is because, at that time, the universe has a deluded nature.
Because it is easily established as being of that nature; and thus Manu says: "This was then enveloped in darkness.

Or rather, "consisting of darkness" (tamomaya) means pervaded or covered by *tamas*, which is ignorance (*ajñāna*) characterized by concealment; and thus the Śruti says: "By death indeed was this covered."
It is not within the range of the mind, nor can it ever be made an object of speech;
it is devoid of name, form, and color, being neither gross nor subtle.
Neither short nor long, neither light nor devoid of weight; wherein there is no accumulation whatsoever, nor likewise any diminution. || 13 ||
Furthermore, the Śruti describes with trepidation that which exists as "Being," as well as the supreme light of bliss,

The use of the term "blinding darkness" (*andhatamas*) for ignorance is intended to convey its impenetrability except through the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). For this very reason, it is described as being pierceable only by a needle:
"immeasurable, supportless, changeless, and formless."
It is devoid of qualities, accessible to yogis, all-pervading, and the sole cause;

if he does not take refuge on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, which are so easy to enjoy.
Of what use is long life, or health, or even a blossoming fortune?
Or what is the use of pure intellect if one does not serve the Gaṅgā?
That man who causes a temple to be built as a likeness of the Gaṅgā shall enjoy worldly pleasures and, after death, attain residence in the same world as the Gaṅgā.

The meaning is that the formal declaration (*saṃkalpa*) regarding the lunar day, the asterism, the directions starting with the east, and so forth, need not be observed. In the reading *parvādī*, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the specific day and other such details.
The bank of the Bhāgīrathī is a field of spiritual accomplishment (*siddhikṣetra*). Thus it has been said: "A mendicant should dwell constantly on the bank of the Gaṅgā."
Those who constantly and with devotion listen to the greatness of the Gaṅgā obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā by pleasing the reciter with wealth. (63)
Whoever bathes a Liṅga with the waters of the Gaṅgā for the sake of the Pitṛs,
his ancestors shall be satisfied, even if they have gone to a great hell.
The wise have declared that bathing with fragrant water from the Gaṅgā, purified by cloth and over which mantras have been recited eight times, is superior even to the bath of clarified butter.
Whoever [offers] even once water from the Gaṅgā mixed with eight substances, measuring a Māgadha-prastha and placed in a copper vessel; || 66 ||
One should offer an oblation to the Sun together with one's own ancestors;
he is glorified in the world of the Sun by means of a celestial chariot of supreme splendor.
Water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, clarified butter, honey, and the curd of cows— [these are the offerings].
"Red *karavīra* flowers and red sandalwood as well"—this means by means of wealth and substances that satisfy the reciter; that is, by satisfying the reciter. 9.3.

This eight-limbed worship (aṣṭāṅga-pūjā), performed with the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya" or with the twenty-syllable Gaṅgā-mantra to be described hereafter, is declared to be extremely pleasing to the Lord.
O Viṣṇu, it should be known that [the merit] from the Gaṅgārva rivers is multiplied ten millionfold, provided it is not obstructed by others.

The wise person who, according to their own capacity, should construct a temple on the bank of the Gaṅgā, shall obtain a fruit ten million times greater than the consecration of a shrine at any other sacred ford.
Whatever fruit is obtained by planting trees such as the aśvattha, vaṭa, and āmra, as well as by means of wells, step-wells, tanks, water-stalls, shelters, and the like; || 101 ||
Whatever merit might arise elsewhere, that would be attained by the sight of the Gaṅgā;
and even more than that is gained from touching the Gaṅgā with flower gardens and other such offerings.
Whatever merit is gained from the gift of a daughter in marriage, and whatever merit is gained from the gift of cows and food—
that merit shall become a hundredfold by drinking a mouthful of water from the Gaṅgā.
O Janārdana, whatever merit might accrue from a thousand Cāndrāyaṇa fasts,
one obtains even greater fruit than that by drinking the nectar of the Gaṅgā.
O Hari, what other fruit can be said for bathing in the Gaṅgā with devotion? Even an imperishable residence in heaven, or perhaps even liberation (nirvāṇa).
That man who constantly worships the pair of sandals of the Gaṅgā—
One obtains long life, merit, wealth, sons, heaven, and liberation.
There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā for destroying the impurities of the Kali age;
O Hari, there is no field equal to Avimukta for bestowing liberation.
Upon merely seeing a mortal devoted to bathing in the Gaṅgā, the servants of Yama flee in the ten directions, just as deer do upon seeing a lion. (108)
By drinking a mouthful of the Gaṅgā— that is, by drinking even a mere handful of the Gaṅgā’s water—
for one who is habituated to honoring the Gaṅgā and who dwells upon the banks of the Gaṅgā.
By performing the *arjā* rite according to the prescribed rule, one obtains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
By the devout gift of cows, land, and gold on the auspicious bank of the Gaṅgā,
a man is not born again in this cycle of existence fraught with suffering.
Longevity is obtained through the gift of garments, and knowledge through the gift of books;
prosperity is attained by the gift of food, and ten million daughters through the gift of a daughter in marriage.
Furthermore, whatever action is performed elsewhere—whether it be a vow, a gift, recitation, or austerity—[bears fruit].
But on the bank of the Gaṅgā, O Hari, all that becomes ten millionfold.
O Viṣṇu, he who gives a cow with its calf on the bank of the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rite shall possess all prosperity for as many yugas as there are hairs on the cow's body.
By the gift of a wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu), one enjoys all desires—many and various kinds of divine things—in Goloka or in my own world. || 114 ||
The two verses beginning with "gaṅgābhajanaśīlasya" constitute a single syntactical unit.
Regarding "duḥkhasaṅkaṭe" and "duḥkhasambādhe," [the meaning is] in a crisis of suffering and a confinement of suffering.
In the four words ending in the accusative case, such as "dīrghāyuṣyam" and so forth, the word "prāpnoti" (obtains) is to be supplied. [The verb] "labhet" (may obtain) [is also used].
Having enjoyed even those things unattainable for the gods together with his kinsmen,
ancestors, and friends, he was adorned with all kinds of jewels. (115)
Thereafter, one is born into a noble family abounding in wealth and grain, endowed with jewels and gold, and possessed of virtuous conduct and learning. || 116 ||
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures together with his sons and grandsons,
he again reached the Ganges at Kāśī, which flows toward the north.
Having propitiated Viśveśvara due to the impressions (vāsanā) from previous births,
and upon reaching the end of the body in due course of time, one then attains Brahman.
Even during the two periods of transition on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, [one attains the same].
Listen to the fruit of the merit of that man who gives with devotion. || 11.9 ||
Having enjoyed mind-pleasing delights in the worlds of Mahendra and Candra for as many yugas as there are atoms in that [earth],
by virtue of the gift of the previously mentioned wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu)— in some versions, it is stated "surrounded by a multitude of wish-fulfilling cows."
In that Goloka, he should be understood as being surrounded by a multitude of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu), just as in my own world he is surrounded by my attendants (gaṇas). Or, in both places,
having become the lord of the seven continents (saptadvīpa), he is devoted to the highest dharma.
O Hari, may you cause all those who dwell in hell to attain the third heaven.
Having liberated all the ancestors residing in heaven, that one of great luster finally severed the ignorance pertaining to the five elements with the sword of knowledge.
Having attained supreme dispassion and practicing the highest yoga, or having reached Avimukta, he attains the Supreme Brahman. || 123 ||
He who bestows even a mere measure of gold as gold upon Suvarṇa on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, O Hara, [attains great merit].
In a beautiful, all-pervading celestial chariot inlaid with gold and jewels,
endowed with all sovereign powers and honored in all the worlds, he—
having liberated [them] and having granted liberation, [liberated] ignorance which has transformed into the form of the five elements consisting of the five gross elements— [attains this state].

"Having cut" means having abandoned the conceit of "I" regarding the body. Regarding the reading *pañcaparvikām*, the meaning is: "that which has five joints," namely those mentioned in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa as "darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and utter darkness (andhatāmisra). || 122 ||

"Yuñjānaḥ" means practicing, striving, or performing; "yogam" refers to the union of the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman). The adjective "uttamam" (supreme) is used for the sake of distinguishing it from the eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga). Alternatively, having attained the "Avimukta" (the Unreleased), one reaches supreme liberation at the end of the body.
O Viṣṇu, enjoying delightful pleasures within the various worlds of the cosmic egg and honored by all until the dissolution of all beings,
he shall thereafter become a powerful sole sovereign in Jambūdvīpa.
Then, having reached Avimukta, one attains the state of Nirvāṇa.
But when a bath is performed with devotion in the Gaṅgā on one's birth-star (janmarkṣa), one is instantly liberated from the flood of sins accumulated since birth. || 127-128 ||
A bath in the Gaṅgā during the months of Vaiśākha, Kārtika, and Māgha is very difficult to obtain.
On the new moon day (darśa), the merit is a hundredfold; on the sun's passage into a new sign (saṅkrānti), it is a thousandfold.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, it is a hundred-thousandfold; but during the Vyatīpāta yoga, it is infinite.
Ten thousandfold at the equinoxes, and indeed a hundred thousandfold during the two solstices.

The connection is with "in all the worlds situated within the cosmic egg. A lunar eclipse occurs on a Monday, and a solar eclipse on a Sunday, lasting until the dissolution of all beings (ābhūtasaṃplavam).
And that [place] is called Cūḍāmaṇiparva; bathing there is of innumerable merit.
O Viṣṇu, whatever bathing, giving, chanting, or fire-offerings are performed here on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī according to the Cūḍāmaṇi [Kalpa], all that becomes inexhaustible.
Having bathed in the Gaṅgā with faith and endowed with devotion, one attains the ultimate treasure-store.
Even a slayer of a Brahmin would be purified, how much more so any other sinner!
Even worms, insects, moths, and the like that die on the bank of the Jāhnavī, and even the trees that fall from the bank, attain the supreme goal. (133-134)

On the tenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, when it is conjoined with the asterism Hasta, a man or a woman on the bank of the Gaṅgā, through a spirit of devotion, [performs an act] which produces a result whose merit is beyond counting; that is to say, it generates a fruit of incalculable measure. (135) (131)

In this world, on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī—that is, on both banks of the Gaṅgā—one should perform a vigil at night before the Gaṅgā according to the tenfold method of worship. On that bank, the distance is three hundred bows.
[Pt 2 Page 106] One should keep a vigil at night before the Gaṅgā through the tenfold rite dedicated to Hari.
With fragrant flowers, food offerings, and ten fruits of each kind,
and having fashioned an image of Gaṅgā out of gold or silver according to one's means— || 136 || [Pt 2 Page 107]
[He should place it] upon a full water-pot whose mouth is covered with a cloth. || 141 ||
Having consecrated the Goddess, who has been purified with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should worship her—
she who has four arms and three eyes, who is attended by rivers and streams,
and whose slender body is drenched in the flowing nectar of beauty.

Then one should meditate upon her who is exceedingly gentle, possessing the luster of ten thousand moons, holding in her excellent hands a full water-jar, a white lotus, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
being fanned with chowries and adorned by a white parasol. || 143-144 ||

Having meditated upon her, whose surface of the earth is flooded with nectar, who is anointed with divine fragrances, whose feet are worshipped by the three worlds, and who is praised by the celestial sages;
and having worshipped her with mantras through offerings of incense and lamps—
And [salute] me, you, Vidhi, Bradhna, Himavat, and Bhagīratha.

She is purified and bathed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). He describes the visualization (*dhyāna*) with three and a half verses beginning with "four-armed" (*caturbhujām*). First, one must understand the first quarter of the second verse: "Then one should visualize.
(Verse 142) *Lāvaṇya* is beauty; that itself is the nectar (*amṛta*), and its *niṣyanda* is its flowing forth. Even in the reading *niṣyandeti*, it means the same.

She whose very body is a slender staff because she meditates upon that very object; she who is accompanied by a full water-jar and white lotuses, and whose hands—which dispel the fear of devotees—grant boons and bestow fearlessness.
Having worshipped an image fashioned from sandalwood and unbroken grains (akṣata) before [the deity],
one should respectfully give ten prasthas of sesame seeds to ten Brahmins.
A pala, a kuḍava, a prastha, an āḍhaka, and a droṇa—these should be understood, according to the measure of grain, to increase fourfold in succession. (148)
Fish, tortoises, frogs, crocodiles, and other aquatic creatures;
swans, kāraṇḍavas, cranes, cakravākas, ṭiṭṭibhas, and sārasas—
these should be fashioned according to one's ability from gold, silver, or copper.
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, the observer of the vow should cast them into the Gaṅgā.
(150) Demonstrating the measure of a *prastha*, he states the measure of all four, beginning with the *pala*: "And the *pala*... These [are as follows].
[Pt 2 Page 109]
Having performed it according to this procedure, free from stinginess regarding wealth and observing a fast, one is liberated from the ten sins that will be described hereafter:
taking what has not been given and violence contrary to the prescribed rules.
And serving another's wife is recorded as the threefold physical [karma].
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every respect, and incoherent prattle constitute the fourfold verbal [karma]. (152–153)
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind, and adherence to falsehood—these are recorded as the threefold mental [karma]. (154)
By these ten kinds of sins arising from ten births, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this, O Gadādhara—this is the truth, the absolute truth.
One shall uplift ten ancestors and ten descendants from the terrible hells.
One should recite this hymn, which is about to be told, with faith before the Gaṅgā.

Harshness (*pāruṣya*) is indeed harshness; it means rough speech. Incoherent prattle (*asambaddhapralāpa*) is verbal discourse that serves no purpose. (153) False attachment (*vitathābhiniveśa*) is persistence in matters that are unreal. (154)
Oṃ, salutations to Śivā, to Gaṅgā; salutations again and again to her who bestows auspiciousness.
Salutations to you whose form is Viṣṇu; let there be salutations to you, the embodiment of Brahmā. (1) 157.
Salutations to you who possess the form of Rudra; salutations again and again to you, the consort of Śaṅkara.
Salutations to her who embodies all the gods, whose form is the supreme medicine.
Salutations be to you, the best of physicians for every single disease.
Salutations to you, the destroyer of poison produced from both stationary and moving beings. ||3||15 9 ||
Salutations to you, the destroyer of the poison of saṃsāra and the giver of life;
salutations again and again to you, the mistress of the vital breath who dispels the threefold affliction. ||4|| 160 ||
Salutations to you, the one who brings about the lineage of peace; salutations to you of pure form.
Salutations to the one who effects universal purification; salutations to the embodiment of the enemy of sin. || 5 || 161 ||
Salutations again and again to the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, the giver of auspiciousness;
salutations be to you, Bhogavatī, the giver of worldly enjoyments and their experience. (6) 162.
Salutations to you, O Mandākinī; salutations again and again to the giver of heaven.
Salutations to the ornament of the three worlds; salutations again and again to the one who flows through the three paths.
Salutations again and again to her who abides as the three white ones, to her who is endowed with patience;
salutations again and again to her who abides as the three sacrificial fires, to her who is possessed of splendor. || 8 || 164 ||
Salutation to Nandā, the bearer of the *liṅga*; salutation to you whose nature is a stream of nectar.
Salutation to you, the foremost of the universe; salutation again and again to you, Revatī. (6) 165.
Salutations to you, the Vast One; salutations be to you, the Sustainer of the World.
Salutations to you, the Friend of the Universe; repeated salutations to Nandinī. (10.166)
Salutations again and again to you, Pṛthvī, Śivāmṛtā, and Suvṛṣā; salutations again and again to you, Tārā, who are enriched by hundreds of higher and lower [manifestations]. ||11||167||
Or rather, it is she whose perfect abiding consists of that which is white, pure, and of the nature of Brahman throughout the three periods of time.
As it has been said: "That very Lord Janārdana, who is stainless and whose nature is consciousness (citsvarūpī), is himself the water of the Gaṅgā in liquid form; there is no doubt in this."

Or, she who is established upon the Himalayas—the moon-mandala of Maheśvara—or upon the Kailāsas, which are "three-fold white" (triśukla); or she whose form (saṃsthā) is like that of the three-fold white, resembling a conch, a jasmine flower, or the moon. Thus it is heard in the *Gaṅgāstotra*:

"White as a conch, a jasmine flower, and the moon, she is the destroyer of great sins. To her who is patient (kṣamāvatī), the performer of forgiveness (kṣamākārī), and who has the form of the three sacrificial fires (trihutāśana).

Salutations to you, the indivisible one, who cuts through the net of bonds; you in whom the three fires—the Dakṣiṇāgni, Gārhapatya, and Āhavanīya—are established, and who are full of splendor and radiant. 8.164 [Pt 2, p. 113]
Salutations again and again to Śāntā, to the most excellent, and to the giver of boons. (12) 168.
Salutations be to you, O Ugrā, to the consumer of happiness, and to Sañjīvinī;
salutations again and again to Brahmiṣṭhā, to the giver of Brahman, and to the destroyer of evil. (13) 169.
Salutations to you, the Mother of the World, who utterly shatters those who bow down;
salutations again and again to Maṅgalā, the adversary of all calamities. (14) 170.
O Goddess Nārāyaṇī, who are solely intent on protecting those who have come for refuge, the wretched, and the distressed, and who remove all calamities—salutations be unto you! || 15 || 171 ||

Salutations again and again to you, the cutter of the net— the twenty-four principles themselves— which is a snare because it is the cause of bondage; to the indivisible one, the untainted one, the destroyer of difficulties, the skillful one.
And to Gaṅgā, who is both supreme and non-supreme, the bestower of nirvāṇa. || 16 || 172 ||
O Gaṅgā, may you be before me; O Gaṅgā, stay behind me;
O Gaṅgā, come to my sides; O Gaṅgā, let my stability be in you. (17)

O auspicious one, you are at the beginning, at the end, and in the middle; you are everything, like the Ganges. You alone are the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), and you indeed are the supreme Puruṣa.
O Gaṅgā, you are the Supreme Self; O Śivā, salutations to you, O Auspicious One!
|| 18 || 174 || Whoever recites this hymn or listens to it with purity shall be liberated tenfold from the sins arising from body, speech, and mind. || 16 || 175 ||
To the stainless one, who is free from ignorance and its effects; to the destroyer of Durga, the slayer of the Asura named Durga;
to the capable one—[one] situated in disease shall be liberated from disease, and one beset by calamities from calamities.
The bound is released from bondage; the fearful is liberated from fear. ||20||176||
He attains all desires and, after death, goes to the third heaven;
ascending a divine celestial chariot, he is fanned by divine women. ||21|| 177||
For one who always keeps this written in their home or wears it [as an amulet], there is no fear of fire or thieves, nor any fear of snakes and the like anywhere. (22) 178.
On the tenth lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
conjoined with the asterism Hasta and joined with Wednesday, one shall destroy the threefold sin.
On that tenth day, standing in the waters of the Gaṅgā, one should recite this hymn.
Whoever should recite it ten times, even if they are poor or lacking in strength.
He too obtains that fruit which is proclaimed as resulting from worshipping Gaṅgā with effort according to the previously mentioned procedure;
for as is Gaurī, so is Gaṅgā, and therefore [the merit is the same] in the worship of Gaurī.
Whatever [rite] has been correctly prescribed by rule, that too [is accomplished] through the worship of the Gaṅgā. ||26||182 ||
When that [night] is well-known, it means when it has occurred during the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha. || 24 || 180 ||
Then, perceiving the Goddess's intention that she was superior even to himself, the Blessed One said: "As for Gaurī...
and so forth; since it is thus, therefore, "of Gaurī" (gauryās-tu). || 26 || 182 || [Pt 2 Page 116]
"O Viṣṇu, as I am, so are you; as you are, so indeed am I.
As Umā is, so is Gaṅgā; the fourfold form is not divided. There is no difference between Viṣṇu and Rudra, nor is there any difference between Śrī and Gaurī. (27) 183.
He who speaks of a difference between the Gaṅgā and Gaurī is indeed a person of deluded intellect. || 28 || 184 ||
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Daśaharā Hymn," preceded by a Description of the Greatness of the Gaṅgā, in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
Then, perceiving Viṣṇu’s intention that "I alone am the most base," Viśveśvara speaks: "As I am...
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa-ṭīkā* composed by Śrī Rāmānanda.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
Umā said: "O Lord, desiring to ask something for the sake of dispelling my own doubts,"
Speak, O you who are skilled in the knowledge of the three times, if you have no weariness!
Where was King Bhagīratha then, and where was the Bhāgīrathī,
when Viṣṇu performed penance on the bank of the Cakrapuṣkariṇī?
Śiva said:
O large-eyed one, O ever-pure one, no doubt should be entertained here;
in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas, the three divisions of time are proclaimed.
In the twentieth [chapter], the eightieth, following the narrative of the Vāhīkas, the great majesty of the Gaṅgā is described by Śambhu to Hari. || 1 ||

In the portion beginning with the previous chapter, it was stated by the Lord that Bhagīratha, having heard that the oceans had been consumed by fire, went to the Himavat mountain desiring to propitiate Gaṅgāmātā; now, to dispel the doubts of ordinary people regarding that matter, Bhavānī, while herself still doubting, questions Viśveśa with the two verses beginning with "kiñcit. || 1 ||

According to the principle that "the metaphorical treatment of what is yet to be as if it were already existent," even that which is future is indicated as if it were past; with this intention, [it is said]:
"Do not vainly entertain doubt regarding what is past, what is yet to be, or what is currently occurring."
Having spoken thus, the Lord again spoke of the supreme majesty of the Gaṅgā.
Agastya said:
O son of Pārvatī, speak again concerning the greatness of the celestial river (Gaṅgā) all around, just as it was then told by the God of gods regarding Hari.
Skanda said:
O Sage, son of Mitrāvaruṇa, listen now to the greatness of the river that flows through the three paths, which destroys all sins, exactly as it was spoken by the Lord.
Whoever, having reached the Trisrotas river, offers rice-balls even once,
by that act his ancestors are lifted from the ocean of existence by means of the water mixed with sesame seeds.
And as many sesame seeds as are taken up by mortals during the ancestral rite, [so many are they delivered].
For that many thousands of years, the ancestors dwell in heaven.
Since the gods together with the ancestors are always present in the Gaṅgā,
there is no need for the invocation or the dismissal of them there.
Kṛthāḥ means "do" (imperative). Yadvat means "just as.
Trisrotas means "she whose stream flows through the three worlds"; [refer to] her, Trisrotas.
Pitṛkarman refers to rites for the ancestors, such as libations (*tarpaṇa*) and so forth.
Those who have died in the paternal lineage, and likewise in the maternal lineage;
those who have died among the gurus, fathers-in-law, and kinsmen, as well as other relatives; || 10 ||
Whosoever have not yet cut their teeth, and those who were aborted in the womb, as well as those killed by fire, lightning, or thieves, and by tigers or fanged beasts; || 11 ||

Those who died by hanging, those who fell [from a height], and those who committed suicide; those who sold themselves, thieves, as well as those who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice (ayājya-yājaka);
those who sell liquids (such as wine), and others who suffer from sinful diseases—[all these are excluded].

Those who set fires, those who administer poison, and those born in one's own lineage who kill cows; those who have gone to the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana) and to the Pot-cooking Hell (Kumbhīpāka);
and those who have gone to Raurava, Andhatāmisra, and Kālasūtra. || 13-14 ||
Those who, by their own actions, wander through thousands of different births—including those of birds, wild animals, insects, trees, and creeping plants—[attain this state]. (15)
Countless and innumerable women have entered the womb, while those who were counted as auspicious have been brought to the realm of Yama by the most terrible servants of Yama.
The connection with the subsequent [text] is as follows: "having recited these mantras beginning with 'And those who have died in the paternal lineage'...
(10). "Those afflicted by disease" means those suffering from leprosy, or those whose illness is caused by sin (13).
The five specific hells beginning with Asipatra. || 14 ||
Among those who are reckoned as inauspicious, and even among those such as birds and other creatures who are reckoned as auspicious, there are those who are inauspicious and inferior;
whether they be kinsmen or non-kinsmen, they were kinsmen in another birth.
Those who are ignorant of the Vedas, those who have no sons, and those born of their own lineage;
those who have been killed by poison, those who have been struck down by horned animals;
those who are ungrateful, those who kill their gurus, and likewise those who kill their friends. || 17–18 ||
Those who kill women and children, those who are betrayers of trust, those devoted to falsehood and violence, and those who are always intent on evil; (16)
Those who sell horses, those who steal the property of others, and those who are helpless, wretched, and miserable—such as these are unable to attain human birth. || 20 ||

Even those who have been scorched by the waters of the Jāhnavī but bathe there once according to the prescribed rite go to heaven; and even those who are already dwellers of heaven shall attain liberation.
He who, having recited these mantras, performs the libation for the ancestors (pitṛ-tarpaṇa),
the ancestral rite (śrāddha), and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa-pradāna), is here called one who knows the ritual procedure.
Whatever sacred fords exist in the three worlds that bestow desired objects, they all reside in Kāśī at the north-flowing river.
The word *abāndhavāḥ* is to be split as *a-bāndhavāḥ*. 17.
[Pt 2, p.
121] The celestial river (Sindhu) is meritorious in every respect and removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O Viṣṇu, this is especially true in Kāśī, where the river flows toward the north.
The hosts of gods, sages, and ancestors indeed sing this verse:
"May we behold, even within our range of vision, those who flow northward in Kāśī, who are satiated by the nectar of that place and are freed from the threefold suffering. (25)
By the grace of Viśvanātha, may we truly become immortal. || 26 ||
O Hari, the Gaṅgā alone is determined to grant liberation on all sides;
