Itihāsa means ancient history and Śruti means the Veda; that whose purpose or goal—whether the object to be praised or the human aim—is laudable by both of these is "itihāsa-śrutīḍyārthā. Furthermore, because she bestows auspiciousness, happiness, and liberation both in this world and in the next world, she is "ihāmutra-śubha-pradā. Gaṅgā is the giver of happiness and the giver of liberation; like Gaṅgā, she is the supreme refuge.
Having ascended the path of the sky, she who dwells in the world of the divine serpents, bearing the earth as a water-pot filled with blue lotuses, flows from the feet of Upendra. 100.30.
It is the cause of the ocean's putridity, the obstructer of noble enthusiasm, the destroyer of agitation, the pacifier of heat, and the beloved of the son of the Sun. || 31 ||
She by whom the risen one has been made to reach the path of the sky is Uditāmbaramārgā; she is Goddess Uttrā, the illuminator,
the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction, who moves above.
"Ūrjavahā," "Ūrjadharā," "Ūrjāvatī," and "Oghamālinī";
"Ūrdhvaretas," "Priyordhvādhvā," "Amilā," and "Ūrdhvagatipradā"; "Ṛṣivṛndastuta," "Ṛddhi," and "Ṛṇatrayavināśinī. (32-33)

She is the bestower of the *ṛtambharā* superknowledge, whose own nature is the *ṛc*, who is fond of the straight path, who carries the stars along the path of the constellations, and who reveals the straight path.
(34) She is the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction, and her form is that of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; this is the meaning. Above the earth!

She whose nature it is to move above the heavenly world (*svargaloka*) or the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is *uparicāriṇī*. She who carries forth vigor (*ūrja*) is *ūrjavahantī*, [appearing] in the form of mantras such as "the nectar, the clarified butter" (*amṛtaṃ ghṛtam*). She who sustains vigor—meaning strength, vitality, or breath—is *ūrjadharā*. She possesses vigor, meaning she possesses strength or the sustaining of life-force, and is thus *ūrjāvatī*. She is also *ūrmimālā*, a garland of waves.

That which possesses waves is *ūrmimālinī*. She is the beloved (*priyā*)—the desired one—of those who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*), namely the mendicants (*bhikṣuka*); thus she is called *ūrdhvaretaḥ-priyā*. And so it has been said:
"A mendicant devoted to liberation should dwell constantly on the banks of the Gaṅgā."
"That should be known as a field of accomplishment (siddhikṣetra) for as far as three hundred bow-lengths. Thus it is said.
It is so called because it takes up or receives (lāti) the waves (ūrmī)—namely grief, delusion, old age, death, hunger, thirst, and so forth—or the superimposition (adhyāsa) of the body.
[Pt 2, Page 151]
She who increases all dharma and artha, yet bestows death upon each [of her foes] alone;
she whose nature is to be kindled by sacrifice, and who has conquered all sins;
she who is the embodiment of both sovereignty and its opposite, and who is the traditional lore as well as the lunar radiance.
She is the field of medicinal herbs full of vitality, the bestower of vigor, and the giver of gifts. 140. 36.

You are the giver of the height of nectar to the lips, the medicine for those diseased by worldly existence; you are the consort of Upendra, radiant with generosity, the fierce one, and she who possesses the form of Umā.
She by whom both Dharma and Artha—entire and complete—are increased and fully attained; she is thus "she who has sought all Dharma and Artha.
Furthermore, she is "one," meaning preeminent or peerless, or "without a second," according to the Vedic scripture: "One only, without a second.

She is the "bestower of the singular nectar"—the bestower of that nectar which is the one, non-dual Brahman. (Verse 130) She is of a nature that is "to be nourished," meaning she is to be increased or expanded.

That whose nature is such is "edhanīyasvabhāvā" (of a nature that increases). Those from whom sins tremble or shake are "ejāḥ"; she who is virtuous toward them is "ejyā," meaning worthy of worship. She by whom all sins without exception have been shaken or caused to tremble is "ejitāśeṣapātakā.
[Pt 2, Page 152]

She who flows through the path of the sky, the daughter of Ambaṣṭha, she whose garland is excellent, whose eyes are like lotuses, the Mother, the great source of water, the giver of feet, and the destroyer of darkness. || 38 ||
Aṃśumālā, Aṃśumatī, she who has accepted the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) [as her son], the destroyer of the Andhatāmisra hell, Dhurañjanā, and Añjanāvatī. || 3.9 ||
She is the doer of good, the desirable one, fragrant with the scent of lotuses and water-lilies;
she is the abode of white lilies, the bed of red lotuses, splendor itself, and the bestower of what is desired. 170.
40. [Pt 2 Page 153]
She has golden eyes, she is the wish-fulfilling cow, the creator of fame, and the destroyer of afflictions;
she is the most excellent of sacrifices, the fruit of sacrifice, and the breaker of the bonds of karma. || 41 ||
She has lotus-like eyes, she removes fatigue, and her radiance is like that of the scorching fire;
she is moist with compassion, auspicious, and the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age.
She can assume any form at will, she is the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and she wears garlands of lotuses and water-lilies.
She is immutably steadfast, compassionate, lovely, borne upon a tortoise, and possessed of all artistic perfections. 43.
She whose eyes are like gold is Kāñcanākṣī; she is the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), the milker of desires (Kāmadhuk), and Surabhi.
She is Kamalā, Kalpalatikā, Kālī, and the enemy of impurity (Kaluṣavairiṇī).
Her waters are desirable, her banks are beautiful, and she is adorned with shells like cowries.
She who pacifies the *kālakūṭa* poison, who is fond of the *kadamba* flower; she who is playful in her pastimes on the Yamunā (*kālindī*), whose garland is a series of sweet-sounding waves;
she who has traversed the three worlds, who is itching, and who is affectionate toward the son of Kaṇḍū.
Khajinī, who has the luster of a stream of nectar, Khagā, and she who bears the crescent moon. 210 || 46 ||
Moving through the sky, abiding in the sky, she who is fond of the crescent moon as her forehead mark;
she is the Sky-farer (Khecarī), worthy of worship by the Sky-farers, renown itself, and the bestower of renown. (47)

She who has shattered the flood of sins through prostration; she who destroys the intellect of the wicked; she who has uprooted the mass of the roots of evil; she who wields the skull-topped staff, the mendicant’s bowl, and the shield. 48.
The Gaṅgā, who allays the intense heat of the desert, who is a mine of nectar-like waters, who belongs to the Wind-god, who is fair-complexioned, and who is fond of the city of the Gandharvas. 4.9.

She who moves playfully through the sky (khe) is *khe-khelagāminī*. Or, "in the sky" (*khe*) means in Brahman; according to the Vedic scripture, "Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman. She who abides in the sky (or in Brahman) is *khasthā*. She who is fond of the crescent moon as her forehead mark is *khaṇḍendu-tilaka-priyā*, the beloved of the Lord of the Universe.
She who moves in the sky is *khecarī*. She who is worthy of worship by the *khecarīs*—the perfected women (*siddhāṅganās*)—is *khecarīvandyā*. She is *Khyāti*.

"Renown" (prakhyāti) means "establishment" (pratiṣṭhā). Alternatively, it consists of these five types of manifestation: misapprehension (ākhyāti), erroneous apprehension (anyathākhyāti), non-existent apprehension (asatkhyāti), self-apprehension (ātmakhyāti), and the apprehension of the indeterminable (anirvacanīyakhyāti); she is of that nature. She bestows renown and brings about establishment.
(47) She by whom the multitude of sins of those who have bowed down—that is, the devotees—is shattered and removed, is "she who has shattered the multitude of sins of those who have bowed down."
The intellect of the wicked is of a wicked nature, or rather, she is the destroyer of that intellect; she is dug out, uprooted, and eradicated.
She possesses deep limbs, is composed of virtues, is free from affliction, and is fond of movement.
The Mother of Gaṇeśa is praised in both prose and verse in this Gītā. || 50 ||
Gāndhārī is the pacifier of the womb; she bestows a state upon those who have lost their way.
Gomatī is the secret lore; Gau, Gau, the cow, is the one who moves through the sky.
She who causes the lineage to flourish, she who possesses virtues, she who transcends all qualities, she who leads the way for virtues;
Guhāmbikā, daughter of the mountain, born from the feet of Govinda;
she whose conduct is to be praised, Gāyatrī, beloved of Giriśa.
She is of hidden form, possessed of virtues, venerable, and the increaser of dignity.
She removes the affliction of the planets, she is the *gundrā* plant, the destroyer of poison, and fond of song.
She is the remover of heat, she possesses clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and she bestows satisfaction through *ghṛta*.

"Having herself fallen from her own state, she bestows a state upon others"—this is the figure of speech known as *viruddha* (contradiction). She is the river Gomatī, either residing at Dvārakā or in the Naimiṣa forest, appearing in that form. She is the secret knowledge, the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). She is "of the Cow" (*go-rūpā*), meaning she takes the form of the earth, or the Vedas, or Speech (*vāṇī*), or Heaven. She is the protectress, the guardian. She is one whose nature it is to move through the sky.
She is called Gotrā because she protects the earth (gām trāyate); Bhagīratha is so named because he has the habit of subduing the multitude of mountains (parvatavṛnda).
She is Ghrāṇatuṣṭikarī (the one who brings satisfaction to the sense of smell), Ghoṣā, Ghanānandā (she whose bliss is dense), and Ghanapriyā (she who loves density). || 55 ||
She who destroys [the cycle of existence], whose waters are swirling, who has rubbed away the succession of sins,
whose waters are drunk by ten million jars [of the gods' mouths], and who has brought about all auspiciousness.
Compassionate, a treasure-house of compassion, voracious, and sounding like an owl;

possessing a tawny body with matted hair, she is Ghargharā, whose voice is like the sound of a water-pot, and who is fond of the ringing of bells (Ghaṇṭāravapriyā); she is the destroyer of that terrible flood of sins.
She is moonlight, she is the water of the moonstone, and her radiance flickers with moving waves;
she is composed of consciousness, she is the very form of consciousness, and she possesses the faces of hundreds of millions of moons.
She has eyes like Campaka flowers, she is beautiful, she is the daughter of the mountain (Cārvati), and she moves with graceful gait;
she is the noble one, the abode of virtuous conduct, the creator of wonders, and possessed of variegated forms.
She is the prose-poem (Campū), pure as sandalwood and water, worthy of constant meditation, and eternally stable.
Abounding with beautiful garlands of campaka flowers, she has caused all misdeeds to be consumed;
she flows through the space of consciousness, is worthy of contemplation, and is fanned by shimmering chowries.
All sins have been entirely stolen away, and the entire circle of [virtuous] conduct has been practiced.
She who has cut away the entire flood of sins, the destroyer of deceit, the remover of guile;
she whose dominion over the three worlds is concealed, and who has snapped all bonds.
She who sprinkles streams of nectar, who moves according to her own will with severed fetters,
who has made the flocks of swans her parasol, and who has rendered her own nectar into a mere spray.

Consciousness alone is the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*); that which carries or brings one to it is the "carrier of the space of consciousness" (*cidākāśavahā*). She is to be contemplated, she is the object of meditation.

For the *Smṛti* states: "Nārāyaṇa, who dwells eternally in the center of the solar disc, seated upon a lotus throne; adorned with armlets, shark-shaped earrings, a crown, and a necklace; golden-bodied, bearing the conch and the discus—He is to be meditated upon."
The meaning is that she is shining and quivering with her own self-luminosity, according to the Vedic scripture: "In this state, this person is self-luminous.
The meaning is that she is fanned by chowries and served by yak-tail whisks. She is one by whom all sins have been stolen away.
Jāhnavī, Jyā (320), Jaganmātā, Japyā, Jaṅghālavīcikā;
Jayā, Janārdanaprītā, Juṣaṇīyā, Jagaddhitā (64);
Jīvana, Jīvanaprāṇā, Jagajjyeṣṭhā, Jaganmayī (330).
The creeper that is the peerless life-force of all living beings, which sustains one through birth after birth;
she who destroys dullness, the womb of the universe, and who is moist with water.
The lotus-born goddess, with eyes like lotuses, who generates bliss for the world. 340 || 66 ||
She is nectar for the eyes of the people, sporting upon the slopes of matted locks;
she is victorious, ever-reciting prayers, the embodiment of generated wisdom;
she is skilled in the playing of the jhallarī drum, and is enveloped by waters that roar with the sound "jhalajjhāl."
She who is to be worshipped by Jhiṇṭīśa, she who causes the sound *jhāṅkāra*, and she who possesses the *jharjhara* drum—350.
She whose nature is to effect the destruction of dullness (*jāḍya*), ignorance, or suffering; she is the Destroyer of Dullness (*Jāḍyavidhvaṃsinī*).
[Pt 2 Page 163]
O you who have carved out the remaining depths of the netherworld (pātāla), O you who split asunder the mountains!
O you whose great banks are to be approached, where the waves dance to the clanging sound [of your thunder]. 66.
A flowing torrent of ostentation, crowded with flocks of dejected royal swans,
with hands sounding the *ḍama-ḍḍumara* drum, and possessing great eggs as described in the *Ḍāmara*.
She who has offered all things for final liberation, whose waters are stirred by the sound of the *ḍhakkā* drum;
she who is the mother of the Lord of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa) who is difficult to overcome, and who has multiplied sins through her humming.

She by whom the entire Pātāla has been traversed and inhabited in the form of Bhogavatī is "Ṭokitāśeṣapātālā. She is "Ṭaṅkikā," taking the form of a specific stone-cutting tool for the purpose of cleaving—that is, splitting—asunder the mountains that are her very sins. She is "Ṭaṅkāranṛtyatkallolā," she in whose [waters] the waves dance with the sound of *ṭaṅkāra*.
She who satisfies, she who is the sacred ford of all sacred fords, she who flows through the three paths, the sovereign of the thirty gods;
she who is the lineage of the three worlds, the mistress of the waters, and she who is praised by the three worlds. (72)
She is the destroyer of the threefold suffering, the dispeller of heat, strength, and power;
she is the three-lakṣa Tārā, the savior, adorned by the hand of the Lord of Stars (the Moon).
She purifies the three worlds, is meritorious, the giver of contentment, and the embodiment of contentment herself.
She is the cutter of craving, the mother of the sacred ford (tīrtha), and she is born from the foot of Trivikrama. 380. 74.

She is *tarpaṇī* because she satisfies all, or because by means of her all [beings] are satisfied; thus she is the one who provides satisfaction (*tarpaṇī*). She is *tīrthatīrthā*, for she is the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) among all sacred fords—those watering places, pilgrimage sites, and rivers frequented by sages—which possess the status of being a *tīrtha*. As Amara says: "The word *tīrtha* refers to a watering place and a source of water, as well as to water frequented by sages and to a preceptor. She is *tripathā*, for her path (*panthā*) extends through the three worlds; thus she is the one whose way is threefold.
She is the sovereign of the thirty gods (tridaśa), thus "Tridaśeśvarī. An alternative reading is "Tridiveśvarī. She protects the three worlds;
she consists of austerity, her form is austerity, and she bestows the fruit of the mass of austerities.

She who pervades the three worlds, she who is satisfaction, she who bestows satisfaction, and whose nature is the ultimate reality (tattva). She who is beautiful in the three worlds, she who is the fourth state (turyā), she who grants the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). She who is the Fortune (lakṣmī) of the three worlds, she who consists of the three steps (tripadī), she who is truth, and she who is the moonlight that dispels darkness.
Containing splendor within, the essence of austerity, and the abode upon the head of the enemy of Tripura;
she is the embodiment of the three Vedas, slender of form, and the dispeller of fear for the son of the Sun. 400. 77.
She is a friend to those who have crossed over the ocean of existence, she has satisfied all her ancestors,
she is devoid of the scales of duality, and she is a fierce fire to the cotton-wool of evil deeds. (78)
She is the subduer of poverty, skillful, difficult to behold, and adorned with divine ornaments;
she possesses initiation, is hard to attain, and bears water as sweet as grapes. 410, 76.

She who displays manifold wonders, who removes the suffering that is difficult for the wicked to overcome, who destroys the sins of the heart of Vainya, and who was born from the lotus feet of the enemy of the Dānavas.

It is called *tari* because it crosses over ignorance and its effects; or alternatively, because it is the nature of a boat for the devotees across the ocean of *saṃsāra*. It is the enemy (*amitra*) of *taraṇija*, that is, Yama, because it destroys his jurisdiction; or alternatively, it is the friend (*mitra*) of *taraṇijā*, that is, Yamunā. The ancestors—the great-grandfathers of Bhagīratha and all the ancestors of all people—have been *tarpita*, meaning they have been brought to satisfaction. The ancestors are the *pitaras*.
Or, by saying "pitāmahādyāyayeti," she has satisfied all her ancestors without exception. The meaning is that she is "tulāvirahitā," which is to say she transcends all measure.
"Tulā" refers specifically to intense sins; the meaning is that she is the "tanūnapād-dāhikā"—the fire that burns those very sins.

She is "dāridryadamanī," the subduer of poverty, and "daurgatyacchetrī," the cutter of wretchedness. She is "dakṣā," skillful in bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and is the wife of Dakṣa.
She is the destroyer of the venom of biting snakes, the tearer asunder of the continuous flood of accumulated sins;
she is swift, covered by celestial trees, and the remover of irresistible obstacles.
She is to be grasped with firm resolve, the mother of the gods, the revealer of the divine world;
she is the goddess beloved by the God of gods, the bestower of the station of the guardians of the quarters. || 82 ||
She who bestows long life (430), she who is long, the milch-cow, free from blemish;
she who flows with milk and water, she who is to be milked, the divine one, the giver of the divine state. 83.

She is the destroyer of the poison of *daṇḍaśūka* snakes—those who bite with their fangs—and thus she is *daṇḍaśūkaviṣaghnī*. She is *dāritāghaughasantatiḥ*, meaning she by whom the succession of the flood of evils—the lineage of sins—is torn asunder and shattered. She is *drutā*, meaning she who flows with speed.
[Pt 2 Page 168]
The river Dhunadī is a refuge for the distressed, warding off the afflictions of the body;
it is exceedingly long, a destroyer of feverish heat, and one that has dispelled the succession of sins. 440, 84.
Wandering through distant lands, difficult to reach, beloved by the gods; the destroyer of evil conduct, unfathomable, the reservoir of compassion, and merciful. (450) 85.
Unassailable, characterized by generosity, the subduer, praised by Brahmā.

She is the purifier of the Daityas and Dānavas and the destroyer of evil intellect. (86) "The river of heaven" means the celestial Gaṅgā. She is the refuge for the wretched, providing shelter even to great sinners.
[Pt 2 Page 169]
She whose essence is generosity, whose essence is compassion, who pervades heaven and earth;
she who brings about the attainment of fruits both seen and unseen, who is worshipped by hosts of deities;
she who observes long vows, who possesses far-reaching vision, whose waters are radiant, and who is difficult to attain.
She is the wielder of the rod of punishment, established by the science of governance for the punishment of the wicked;
she is the destroyer of gambling dens, a forest fire to the [sins of] gambling, and the sole treasury of fleeing wealth.
She is the pacifier of the suffering of the miserable, the giver of gifts, and the enemy of affliction.
"Sāra" means essence. She whose essence is knowledge through the giving of gifts is "Dānasārā. She whose essence is compassion for those who [study] the recitation of the Vedas is "Dayāsārā.
She whose nature it is to pervade both heaven (*dyau*) and earth (*bhūmi*) is "Dyāvābhūmivigāhinī. [The fruit seen...]

The attainment of visible and invisible fruits—that which consists of worldly happiness and the like, and that which is the invisible fruit pertaining to the next world, such as heaven and liberation—is "the attainment of visible and invisible fruits. (460) She is "worshipped by hosts of gods," meaning she is praised or saluted by the multitude of deities; for it is stated in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*: "She is honored by all the gods. (87)

She whose vow (vrata) is long and great, characterized by the creation and so forth of the universe, is Dīrghavratā. She whose vision (dṛṣṭi)—that is, knowledge—is far-reaching is Dīrghadṛṣṭi, or she whose essential nature is unlimited knowledge. She whose water is radiant, shining like a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon, is [Dīptatoyā].
Devoted to rending the caves, self-controlled, beloved by the self-controlled;
she who has split the mountain slopes, Durgā, who wanders through difficult forests.
She whose essence is dharma, the bearer of the yoke of dharma, the cow, the stream, fortitude, and the eternal.
She who touches upon the fruit of the gift of a cow; she who bestows virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation;
she who carries the ocean of Dharma; she who is the foremost bearer of burdens; she who is the nurse; she who is the ornament of the nurse;
she who possesses virtue; she whose character is righteous; and she who provides protection at the tip of the bow.
She whose supreme intent is the rending of caves is *darīvidāraṇaparā*. This is stated in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*:

"She who pierces the rocks of the Vindhya mountains. She whose senses are subdued is *dāntā*. She for whom self-controlled people (*dāntajana*) are dear, or she who is dear to self-controlled people, is *dāntajanapriyā*. She by whom the mountain slopes were split apart is *dāritādritaṭā*. [She who destroyed] the one named Durga...

She is Gaurī because she slew the demon Durga; likewise, in this very context, there is the statement of the Goddess: "From this day forward, my name shall become renowned as Durgā," because she struck down the demon Durga in battle, making her exceedingly difficult to overcome (*atidurgama*). She is of that form, for it is seen in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "He who speaks of a difference between Gaṅgā and Gaurī is indeed of dull intellect. [Verse 480] In the forest of Durgā, that is, in the impenetrable woods.
Or she is Durgāraṇyā, whose nature it is to roam and strike in both the fortress (durga) and the forest (araṇya);
she is the remover of the sins of those who meditate upon her, the object of meditation, the one who runs, and the one who has shaken off all impurity. 500.
She is the stream of Dharma, the essence of Dharma, the giver of wealth, and the increaser of wealth.
She is the cutter of the qualities of merit and demerit, fond of the dhattūra flower,
the mistress of dharma, the knower of the treatises on dharma, and the bringer of abundance in wealth and grain.
She is obtainable through the Dharma, possessing the waters of the Dharma, and having the nature of giving birth to the Dharma;
her true form is accessible through meditation, she is the Earth, and she is honored by the Sustainer (Brahmā).
[65] With ten million bows [of distance], one reaches Brahmā’s world, and half of that is the water of the Jāhnavī (Ganges).
Half of that is the name of Hari, and half of that is for bathing and giving gifts.

(9.2) She is the remover of the sins of the person who meditates upon her; thus, "remover of the meditator's sins" (*dhyātṛ-pāpa-harā*). In some places, the reading is "remover of the creator's sins" (*dhātṛ-pāpa-harā*). She is to be meditated upon (*dhyeyā*) by those desiring enjoyment (*bubhukṣubhiḥ*) and those desiring liberation (*mumukṣubhiḥ*), and she is to be contemplated. She is the purifier (*dhāvanī*), meaning she makes things pure, or she is of a wandering nature. That which is shaken off or dispelled is *dhūtam*.
She by whom this impurity has been destroyed is "one whose stain is shaken off" (dhūtakalmaṣā).
In this fifth century of the *Thousand Names of Gaṅgā*,
whatever merit was not previously seen here has now been offered to Viśveśa.
Residing within the matted locks of Śiva, she is the blessed one who bestows the *dhāraṇā* known as *dhūḥ*;
she is Nandā, the mother of liberation, the daughter of Nandin, and the one who drives away sins. 520, 66.

She who has warded off the entire multitude of obstacles, who radiates her own bliss, who moves through the courtyard of the sky, she who is to be bowed to—the Goddess Nārāyaṇī—has been praised. 530.67.

She is stainless, known as the Stainless One, the destroyer of the wealth of asceticism, ever-restrained, the bestower of eternal bliss, and a great treasure-house of manifold wonders. Her true nature is attainable through meditation; thus she is "she whose nature is accessible by meditation. She is the Earth, the form of the world, and is worshipped by the elements (or by the body).

She is the mother of rivers, streams, and lakes; she is the celestial river of the gods (the Gaṅgā); she is the leader of heroes; she is the wise one who rescues those who have perished; and she is the bestower of joy upon the Nandana grove. 540, 66.
She has cleansed all the worlds; she is free from attachment, free from affliction, without support, devoid of phenomenal appearance, and has destroyed great impurities.
She is the mother of stainless knowledge and the remover of the suffering of all living beings. 550 || 100 ||
She is eternally festive, eternally satisfied, worthy of salutation, and stainless.
She is established in perfection, free from fear, untainted, and of an immovable nature;
she is irreproachable, effortless, and resides upon the head of the Blue-and-Red One (Śiva). 560, 102.
Praised by the hosts of Nandi and Bhṛṅgi, the daughter of the mountain is the joy of the Nāgas;
she is the unimpeded river of heaven and the long ship for crossing the ocean of hell. 570. 103.
Bestower of merit, containing merit within, meritorious, possessing waves of merit;
vast, yielding abundant fruit, full, the destroyer of the distress of those who bow before her;
possessed of steadfastness—meaning she possesses discipline (niyama)—and free from all affliction (ātaṅka).

She who gives life, the mother of all living beings, the mistress of life, whose form is life itself; she whose abode is the lotus, the supreme power, the most beloved of the Conqueror of Cities. 105.
She is the attainment of the higher and lower fruits, the purifier, and the nourishing;
she is supreme bliss, the most excellent goal, the foundation, and the supreme protector.
She is recited in the Purāṇas, she is the beloved, and her form is the syllable Om.

Pārvatī is endowed with love and is the liberator from the bonds of the individual soul (paśupāśa). She is Prāṇadā, for she bestows life upon her devotees or, alternatively, she destroys it in those who are not devotees; she is the mother of all living beings. [Pt 2 Page 176]
She is the very nature of the Supreme Self, illuminating the Supreme Brahman;
she is the quiescence of supreme bliss and the embodiment of atonement. She is the extinction of suffering in the form of water and is solely devoted to universal protection.
She is the forest fire to the fuel of sin, the enemy of evil, and the destroyer of sin.
She is the mother of supreme sovereignty, wisdom, and the intellect; she is both transcendent and immanent.
She is manifest Lakṣmī, the lotus-eyed one, the supreme ether, and the stream of nectar.
Whatever unseen merit has been acquired here in this exposition of the thousand names of Gaṅgā— twice three hundred [verses]— that is offered to Viśveśvara.
She is the very nature of the Supreme Self, characterized solely by the Supreme Brahman, illuminating the Supreme Brahman, and the radiance of the Supreme Brahman.
She is of serene form, the personified vow, pure, and a deity manifest before one's eyes;
she is supremely beloved by the wielder of the Pināka bow and possesses the water-pot of the Supreme Lord.
Born from the lotus-navelled Lord, she wears a garland of lotuses;
she bestows supreme sovereignty, brings nourishment, is wholesome, fulfills all desires, and is radiant.
She purifies, destroys the yellow-colored womb-disease, and shatters the mountain of sins.
She is Phalinī, holding a fruit in her hand, and her eyes are like blossoming lotuses. || 113 ||
She is *prasannarūpā*, one whose form (*rūpa*)—that is, her essential nature (*svarūpa*)—is serene and untouched by the impurity of the form of its effects.
She is *praṇidhi* because the entire collection of effects is deposited within her in an eminent manner at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*). She is *pūtā*, meaning she purifies;

thus she is of a supremely pure nature, according to the Smṛti: "He who is the purifier of purifiers. She is *pratyakṣadevatā*, the manifest deity, whose nature is immediate, direct consciousness (*caitanya*).

Because of the Vedic scripture stating, "That Brahman which is immediate and direct," [she is Brahman]. (620) She who is exceedingly dear to the wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva) and is the most beloved of Viśveśvara;

she who is the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) of Parameṣṭhin Brahmā by virtue of being his support—thus she is *Parameṣṭhikamaṇḍalu*. For it is said that at the beginning, water was the vessel for the ritual observances of the Primordial Grandfather. (111)

Born from the noble feet of Padmanābha and produced by the noble feet of Viṣṇu, she subsequently became the great field that shatters the darkness for the Lord who reclines upon the serpent, and the ornament of the world of the serpents.
With its waters driven forth by the guise of foam, it possesses the fragrance of blossoming white water-lilies.
Resembling streams of clear foam from the ocean, she has utterly eradicated all sins;
her waters are as sweet as molasses and are turbid with the salutary water of decoctions.

The Mother of the Universe, the Sovereign of the Universe, the All-pervading One, the beloved of the Lord of the Universe; she who is devoted to Brahman, the creator of Brahman, the power of Brahman (Brāhmī), most established in Brahman, possessing pure waters;
she by whom the great field of sins and evils has been ploughed and broken—she is Phālitainomahākṣetrā.

In the form of Bhogavatī, she is the ornament of the world of serpents; she is the adornment of the realm of the *phaṇi*s (serpents). She is "one by whom sins (*enāḥ*)—those evils that have been driven far away—are cast out under the guise of foam" (*phenacchala-praṇunnaināḥ*). She is "possessing the fragrance of the blooming white lotus" (*phullakairavagandhinī*), for her scent is like the scent of the blossomed *kairava* or *kumuda* lily. || 114 ||

640. *Phenilācchāmbudhārābhā*: that which has the luster (*ābhā*) or the nature (*svarūpa*) of a stream (*dhārā*) of clear water (*ambu*) that is foamy (*phenila*). *Phuḍuccāṭitapātakā*: she by whom sin (*pātaka*) is eradicated (*uccāṭita*) with the sound "phuḍ"—"phuḍ" being an imitation of a sound. *Phaṇitasvādā*: as sweet as *phaṇita*, a particular kind of cooked food.

She whose water has the sweetness of *phāṇita* (molasses) is "one whose waters have the taste of *phāṇita*. She whose waters are turbid with that water which is as wholesome as *phāṇṭa* (unstrained buttermilk) is "one whose waters are turbid with wholesome *phāṇṭa*-like water. || 115 ||

She is the mother of all (*viśveṣām mātā*) and the Mother of the Universe (*viśvamātā*). She is the Sovereign of All (*viśveśī*), meaning the Mistress of Everything (*sarveśvarī*). She is the Universal One (*viśvā*), whose nature is everything.

She is the Beloved of the Lord of the Universe (*viśveśvarapriyā*), or she is one for whom the Lord of the Universe is beloved. She is the Benevolent One (*brahmaṇyā*), being beneficial to Brahman—the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), Hiraṇyagarbha, the Veda, or the Brāhmaṇas. She is called "Brahma-" because she creates Hiraṇyagarbha and the others.
Vibhāvarī, Virajā, Vikrāntānekaviṣṭapā,
Viśvamitrā, Viṣṇupadī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Vaiṣṇavapriyā. (117)
She who acts for the pleasure of Virūpākṣa, whose manifestations face in all directions,
who is free from bonds, who belongs to the gods, who is to be known, and who flows with the essence of the syllables of the Vedas.
Knowledge is swift, venerable, and nourishing;
she is the speaker of Brahman,
the giver of boons, far-reaching, most excellent, and the purifier.
Vibhāvarī is the form of Night, or alternatively, she is the form of the wife of Bhūridyumna. Thus it is said in the Padma Purāṇa:
"The great king Bhūridyumna was the protector of the circle of the earth;
for him there were hundreds of thousands of lotus-eyed women."
The slender-waisted woman became the most excellent night. Thus [it is said].

She from whom dust has departed is *virajā*; the meaning is "one whose essence is pure. She by whom many worlds (*viṣṭapa*), that is, many realms (*bhuvana*), have been traversed and pervaded is *vikrāntānekaviṣṭapā*. She who desires the welfare of the world is *viśvamitrā*. From the foot of Viṣṇu...
[Pt 2 Page 180]
Vidyādharā, Viśokā, Vayovṛndaniṣevitā,
Bahūdakā, Balavatī, Vyomasthā, Vibudhapriyā,
Vāṇī, Vedavatī, Vittā, and Brahmavidyātaraṅgiṇī.
Its waters pervade ten million cosmic eggs, and it removes the sin of killing a Brahmin.

She who possesses the forms of Brahmā, Īśa, and Viṣṇu; she who bestows prosperity and power; she who grants the pleasures of the playful; she who is all-pervasive; and she who is the source of virtue (the fire-stick for the bull).
She is called Vidyādharī because she holds knowledge, or because she has the form of a Vidyādhara woman. [The suffix] *strī* is used in the formation of her name.

She who dwells upon the crest of the bull-bannered Lord's crown, she who destroys excessive calamity, she who is disciplined, she who is humble, she who is the daughter of the Sun, and she who is endowed with modesty. (123)
She is skilled in playing the lute, expert in the science of the flute,
bestowing splendor and strength, and having uprooted all impurities through her power.
Free from sin, devoid of fear, and abandoned by conceptual construction (710);
she who causes rain, whose waters are rain, and whose bonds are severed by ritual (125);
she whose abode and refuge is the crown of the head of the bull-bannered Lord whose emblem is the bull—she is Vṛṣāṅkamauli-...
She who is the form of the vow, the form of wealth, the destroyer of many obstacles;
she is the stream of riches (Vasudhārā), the earth (Vasumatī), the one of variegated limbs, and the radiant sun (Vibhāvasu). 126. [Pt 2 Page 182]
Vijayā, Viśvabījā, Vāmadevī, Varapradā, Vṛṣāśritā, Viṣaghnī, Vijñānā, and Aṃśumālinī. (127)
She is Bhavyā, Bhogavatī, Bhadrā, Bhavānī, and Bhūtabhāvinī;
she is the sustainer of all beings, the remover of fear, and the destroyer of poverty for her devotees. || 128 ||

She whose form corresponds to the vow and the resolve of her devotees is "Vratarūpā. She who bestows enjoyment and liberation on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) and other such occasions is "Bheśī," the giver of heaven and final emancipation to her devotees.
Bhāgīrathī (740), Bhānumatī, Bhāgya, Bhogavatī, Bhūti;
Bhavapriyā, Bhavadveṣṭrī, Bhūtidā, Bhūtibhūṣaṇā;
she who knows the feelings of the one with the eye on his forehead (Śiva), and the sovereign of the past, future, and present (750). 12–130.

She quiets delusive cognition, she who has shattered the pavilion of the universe, she who bestows abundant gifts, she who is easily attained through devotion, and she who comes within the range of vision for the fortunate. (131)
Gaṅgā bestows enjoyment and liberation; Gaṅgā grants worldly pleasure and final release; Gaṅgā is the giver of happiness and the giver of salvation; Gaṅgā alone is the supreme refuge.
She shatters the multitude of calamities and provides the joy of various kinds of food and drink.
She is the one to be sought as alms, the mother of the monks, the essence of all states of being (bhāva), and the embodiment of the nature of existence.
She is the Mandākinī, the river of great bliss, the Mother, and the wave-filled stream of liberation.
She is the source of great prosperity, the possessor of honeyed sweetness, the one of great merit, and the bestower of excellent gifts.
Praised by sages (77), the destroyer of delusion, the great sacred ford, the flowing stream of honey, the consort of Mādhava, the proud one, the venerable one, she who transcends the path of desires.
She by whom the multitude—the entire collection—of calamities and afflictions of her devotees has been broken and destroyed... [she is] Bhañjitā.
She is the giver of liberation, the giver of intelligence, and the foremost; she is resorted to by people of great fortune, possessed of great speed, pure, and adorned with great majesty. 135.
She of great majesty, the vast one, with eyes as tremulous as a fish; she who is filled with great compassion, possessing great splendor and great lotuses;
she who is the personified lover of Liberation, adorned with jewels and rubies.

She who is adorned with a necklace of pearls, who delights the mind and the eyes, and who possesses *māna*—whether that *māna* be the intensity of love or the state of indignation—is the *māninī*. That state of *māna* exists in her during the period when she was the wife of Śantanu.
[Pt 2 Page 186]
The destroyer of heaps of great sins, who took half [the body] of Mahādeva;
the Great Goddess Manonmanī, liberated from the garland of great waves. 138.
She who is attainable through the arising of great merit, the moonlight that dispels the darkness of illusion;
she is Great Knowledge, Great Illusion, Great Intelligence, and the Great Medicine.
She wears a garland, possesses great means, and is adorned with great serpents.
She who pacifies great delusion; she who is the most auspicious among all auspicious things (140);

she who destroys heaps of great sins; she who cuts through the multitudes of great transgressions; she whose nature it is to take half the body of Mahādeva—meaning she who exists in the form of Gaurī; she in whom a great garland of waves exists.
Moving within the orb of the sun, she is Mahālakṣmī, free from intoxication;
she is Yaśasvinī and Yaśodā, the worthy one who is served by those with disciplined minds. 820 || 141 ||
She bestows the perfection of yoga, she who is to be worshipped, she who is fulfilled by the Lord of Sacrifice;
she is the Mistress of Sacrifice, the giver of the fruits of sacrifice, she who is worthy of worship, and the bringer of glory.
She is to be served by the ascetics, the source of yoga, the Yoginī, the giver of disciplined intellect.
She bestows the knowledge of yoga, is disciplined, and is joined with the eightfold limbs of yoga beginning with restraint (yama).
She who moves within the solar orb is the "Mover in the Solar Orb" (Mārtaṇḍamaṇḍalacarī). In the form of the celestial Gaṅgā,
she restrains the flow of the multitude of sins within the solar orb and wards off the realm of Yama.
She quiets the coming and going [of rebirth] and cuts asunder all forms of torment. || 144 ||

She is the moon of the night, the one with cool and pure waters, free from the dharma of the ages; she is Revatī, the creator of delight, the beautiful one, the one whose womb is filled with jewels, the goddess Ramā, and Rati herself.
She is the object of love for the ocean of jewels, the knower of flavors, and the embodiment of aesthetic essence.
And there was a most delightful river within the interior of a jeweled palace. || 146 ||
She by whom the movement of the multitude of sins—the flood of evils—is restrained is "yantritāghaughasañcārā";
she whose nature is to ward off the world of Yama is "yamalokanivāriṇī. "Yātāyāte" refers to death and birth.

She is the jewel, the delight of Rudra, the destroyer of passion and hatred; she is Ramā, the beautiful woman of lovely form, who is the life-giving medicine for the diseased. She creates desire, she is the delighter, the charming one, the radiant one, and the remover of disease.
She is the royal swan (*rājahaṃsā*), possessing jewel-like waves that shine with rows of ripples.

She is *ratnāciḥ*, one whose luster is like the brilliance of gems. She is *rudraramaṇī*, the delighter of Rudra. She is *rāgadveṣavināśinī*, the destroyer of passion and hatred. She is *ramā*, because she delights the eyes and the mind. She is *rāmā*, the most excellent woman.
She is the line of loveliness, the destroyer of diseases and anger,
the full moon, the alleviator of the suffering of the wretched, the delightful one, and she who resounds with the humming of bees.
Passionate, she who has colored Śiva with love, a treasure-trove of beauty and grace, the mother of the world, venerated by the world, garlanded with shimmering waves;
Līlāvatī (880), the ground of the world, the moonlight for the eyes of the world.
The stream of her writing is graceful, swift-flowing, and removes all heaviness;
she is indeed delightful, possessing the beauty of lovely lines and currents of water, as described by the experts on the ocean, upon her hands and feet.
She whose hands perform the *taraṅga* gesture of the *lāsya* dance, who moves with graceful rhythm and tempo;
she who is the kinsman of the world, the kinsman of the world, the sustainer of the world, the sustainer of the world, and is adorned with transcendent qualities;
she who brings benefit to the three worlds, the Fortune of the world, marked with all auspicious characteristics.
She is playful, characterized by liberation, and a showerer of the nectar of loveliness.
She is the fire within all, the consort of Indra, the remover of barrenness,
the destroyer of the dust from the feet of Vāsudeva, and the warder-off of Indra’s thunderbolt.

She whose hands are the waves that perform the *lāsya* dance is *Lāsyattaraṅgahastā*; or she is the goddess residing in Kāśī known as Lalitā, who is graceful and captivating, moving with a rhythmic gait characterized by a breaking of tempo.
Śubhāvatī, Śubhaphalā, Śānti, Śāntanuvallabhā, Śūlinī, Śaiśavavayā, Śītalā, Mṛtavāhinī,
Śobhāvatī, Śīlavatī, and Śoṣitāśeṣakilbiṣā. || 155 ||
She who is worthy of refuge, the bestower of auspiciousness, the disciplined one, the mother of Śarajanman, and the auspicious Śivā;
she who is Power (Śakti), pure as the moon, esteemed by the sister of Śamana,
tranquility itself, the possessor of the path to peace, and the great beloved of the blue-throated Lord.
She from whom auspicious things proceed on all sides is Śubhāvatī; she whose fruit is auspicious, or who is herself auspicious, is Śubhā.
She is Śuci (the Pure) and Śucikarī (the Purifier). She is Śeṣā, born from the state of reclining upon Śeṣa.
The scripture concerning Śrīnivāsa (630), faith, the illustrious one, Śrī, and the possessor of auspiciousness. || 158 ||
She is Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā), the Whirlpool of Auspiciousness (Śubhāvartā), the Bliss of Sacred Learning (Śrutānandā), and the Praise of the Vedas (Śrutistuti).

She is the Destroyer of that which is inauspicious (Śivetaraghnī), the Śabara woman (Śabarī), the Assumer of Illusory Forms (Śāmbarīrūpadhāriṇī), the Purifier of the Cremation Ground (Śmaśānaśodhanī), the Peaceful One (Śāntā), and she who is eternally praised by those possessing a hundredfold fortitude (Śaśvacchatadhṛtiṣṭutā). || 156 ||
She is the Śālinī, rich with the splendor of rice, and she bears within her the one whose vehicle is the peacock (Skanda). || 160 ||
Her conduct is praiseworthy and she has eradicated all sins;
she is endowed with the sovereignty of the six qualities and is the embodiment of the Veda with its six limbs. 161.
The river that removes impotence, the best of streams with hundreds of flowing channels, the Surasā, the Suprabhā, and the Suradodhikā;
the celestial Ganges, the destroyer of all suffering, and the great panacea for all diseases.
Success is to be served; the virtuous woman is to be served; and Sarasvatī, who reveals the secrets of Skanda, is to be served. || 163 ||

She who has reached the river of perfection, she whose abode is upon the crest of Śiva, she who bestows steadfastness, she who is auspicious, she who grants happiness, and she who bestows good fortune upon women. 164.

She whose conduct is praiseworthy—that is, worthy of hymns—is Śaṃsanīyacaritrā. She by whom all sins without exception have been cut away or destroyed is Śātitāśeṣapātakā. [She is] endowed with the sixfold sovereign powers (ṣaḍguṇaiśvarya).
[Pt 2 Page 195]
She is the subtle ladder to heaven, whose waters are *svadhā*, *svāhā*, and nectar;
she is embodied as the ocean, celestial, and the enemy of all sins.
Remembered as the remover of evil, Sītā is the raft for crossing the ocean of worldly existence.
Sandhyā is beautiful with good fortune and endowed with the essence of all things. || 166 ||

She who is dear to Hara, the mistress of the senses; she who has the form of a swan, the golden-hued one; she who has removed the multitude of sins, the benefactor, the playful one, who takes away the pride of sin and pride. 167.

She is the ladder to heaven, the sole staircase to the celestial realm. As it is said in the *Kāśīsāra*: "For she is the path to heaven for all beings and for men. She is subtle, beyond the reach of the senses and other such means. She is Svadhā, the wife of the ancestors (*pitṛs*), who exists in the form of sacred mantra.
Bestower of security, washer away of the flood of sins, dispeller of the base, and patient—
O Agastya, born from a jar, by reciting these one thousand names of Gaṅgā correctly, a person shall obtain the full fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. 168.
It pacifies all sins, destroys all obstacles, is superior to the recitation of all hymns of praise, and is the purifier of all that purifies. (166)
O Sage, by reciting this even once with faith, one obtains the fruit of a single *kratu*, which bestows desired results and brings about the prosperity of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*).
It is as if one has bathed in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and been initiated into all sacrifices (*yajña*).
Whatever fruit has been declared for that, it is obtained from reciting it at the three times of day. || 171 ||
O Brāhmaṇa, he who recites this with self-restraint at the three junctions of the day obtains that same fruit which is gained from all vows when they have been correctly performed.
O Sage, at whatever body of water one may recite this at the time of bathing, the Ganges, which flows through the three paths, is surely present there.
One who seeks excellence attains excellence; one who seeks wealth attains wealth;
one who seeks desires obtains desires; and one who seeks liberation shall attain liberation.
By reciting this three times a day for a year with purity and a clean mind, [one gains these fruits].
By approaching his wife during her fertile period, a sonless man shall obtain a son.
O Sage, for one who recites the thousand names of the Gaṅgā with faith, there is no untimely death, nor fear of fire, thieves, or serpents. || 175–176 ||
Having recited the thousand names of Gaṅgā, one should proceed to another village;
one attains the accomplishment of one's purpose and shall enter one's home free from obstacles.
At that time, no defect arising from the lunar day, the weekday, the asterism, or the planetary conjunction shall prevail.
When a man, having recited this hymn, goes to another village, [he attains success]. || 178 ||
The Thousand Names of Gaṅgā produce long life and health, destroy all calamities, and bring about all spiritual accomplishments for men;
whatever sin has been fully accumulated over thousands of previous births [is destroyed by it].
By reciting the thousand names of Gaṅgā, that [sin] shall go to its destruction. || 180 ||

O Sage, the killer of a Brāhmaṇa, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief of gold, the violator of the Guru’s bed, one who associates with such persons, the destroyer of an embryo, and the killer of a mother or a father— [these are the great sinners]. (181)
A betrayer of trust, a poisoner, an ungrateful person, a slayer of friends, an arsonist, a killer of cows, a stealer of the teacher’s property—
even one joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) or associated with minor sins (upapātaka)— [is purified]. || 182 ||

One is liberated by reciting the *Gaṅgānāmasahasra* with faith [from] minor offenses (*upapātaka*) such as the killing of cows; for according to the maxim that words ending in the plural number indicate a class, the plural form here refers to the categories of acts causing loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakaraṇa*), acts of social degradation (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*), acts rendering one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*), and acts causing impurity (*malinīkaraṇa*).
Enveloped by mental and physical ailments and overwhelmed by terrible torments,
one is liberated from all sufferings by reciting this hymn. (184)
One whose self is disciplined, who recites this for a year while devoted to faith,
shall obtain his desired success and be liberated from all sins—
even one whose mind is possessed by doubt and who hates righteousness. || 185 ||
Even the mind of a hypocrite or a violent person may become devoted to righteousness.

Whatever fruit a man of knowledge attains by following the path of the castes and stages of life and being free from desire and anger, he obtains that very fruit by the recitation of this [text]. (186–187)
Whatever fruit is acquired by reciting the Gāyatrī ten thousand times,
one shall obtain that entirely by reciting this [text] properly just once.
Whatever fruit the virtuous man obtains by giving a cow to a knower of the Vedas, [he shall obtain that as well].
That merit is correctly declared to arise from reciting this king of hymns even once.
Sexual intercourse with a *jehmī* woman and with a *maithunī* woman is remembered as causing loss of caste,
as is the killing of donkeys, horses, camels, deer, elephants, goats, and sheep.
The mixing of castes is to be known as occurring through [intercourse with] a fish, a snake, or a buffalo;
taking wealth from those who are censured, trade, service to Śūdras,
and speaking untruths are to be known as acts that render one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa).
"Killing worms, insects, or birds; eating food mixed with intoxicants; stealing fruits, firewood, or flowers; and lack of fortitude—these bring about impurity. (183)

O Sage, the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief of gold, the violator of the Guru’s bed, one who associates with such persons, the destroyer of an embryo, and the slayer of a mother or father— [these are the great sinners]. (181)
A betrayer of trust, a poisoner, an ungrateful person, a murderer of friends, an arsonist, a killer of cows, and a stealer of a teacher’s property—
though joined with these great sins (mahāpātakas) and even associated with secondary sins (upapātakas)— 182.

One is liberated by reciting the *Gaṅgānāmasahasra* with faith [from] minor offenses (*upapātaka*) such as the killing of a cow; for according to the maxim that "words ending in the plural number indicate a class," the plural form here refers to the categories of acts causing loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakaraṇa*), acts making one impure through association (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*), acts rendering one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*), and acts causing defilement (*malinīkaraṇa*).

The Commentary on the *Kathāvatthu* (Sammohavinodanī), Part Two, Pages 1–400 [Main Text from Page 1] **Chapter One: On the Nature of the Aggregates** **Topic 1: That the Aggregate of Form is Permanent** The first topic is: "The aggregate of form is permanent. Herein, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the aggregate of form is permanent. Why? Because they hold that the atoms (*paramāṇu*) are eternal. They argue that since the atoms are eternal, the aggregate of form, being composed of them, must also be permanent. This is not so. Why? Because it is subject to change. For the aggregate of form undergoes transformation through the processes of birth, aging, sickness, and death; it is also affected by heat, cold, and other external conditions. Therefore, it cannot be permanent. Furthermore, if the aggregate of form were permanent, then the arising and passing away of all conditioned phenomena would be impossible. Since we observe that forms arise and cease moment by moment, the claim that the aggregate of form is permanent is untenable. Thus, the aggregate of form is impermanent, being characterized by the nature of conditioned origination and cessation. *** **Topic 2: That the Aggregate of Feeling is Permanent** The second topic is: "The aggregate of feeling is permanent. Herein, some maintain that the aggregate of feeling is permanent because it is the basis for the experience of pleasure and pain, which they claim are eternal states. However, this is not the case. Feeling arises dependent upon contact; since contact is impermanent, its result—feeling—must also be impermanent. If feeling were permanent, there would be no distinction between pleasant, painful, and neutral sensations. Yet, we clearly perceive these variations. Therefore, the aggregate of feeling is impermanent.

*** **Topic 3: That the Aggregate of Perception is Permanent** The third topic is: "The aggregate of perception is permanent. Some argue that perception is permanent because the mental impression (*saññā*) of an object remains constant even after the object has vanished. This is incorrect. While the latent impression may persist, the actual act of perceiving is a conditioned process that arises and ceases. If perception were permanent, one would be constantly perceiving all objects simultaneously, which is contrary to experience. Thus, the aggregate of perception is impermanent. *** **Topic 4: That the Aggregate of Volitional Formations is Permanent** The fourth topic is: "The aggregate of volitional formations is permanent. The proponents of this view suggest that volitional formations are permanent because the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are eternal. However, volitional formations are merely the activities of the mind, body, and speech. As these activities depend on the impermanent aggregates, they themselves are impermanent. To claim they are permanent contradicts the very nature of conditioned existence. *** **Topic 5: That the Aggregate of Consciousness is Permanent** The fifth topic is: "The aggregate of consciousness is permanent. Some maintain that consciousness is permanent because the stream of awareness is unbroken. This is not so. Consciousness arises in dependence upon the sense bases and their corresponding objects. Since these conditions are impermanent, consciousness must also be impermanent. If consciousness were permanent, liberation from suffering would be impossible, as the cycle of rebirth would never cease. Therefore, the aggregate of consciousness is impermanent. *** **Conclusion** In summary, none of the five aggregates are permanent. All are characterized by impermanence, suffering, and non-self. To understand this is to transcend delusion and attain true insight. [End of Main Text from Page 1] ==================================================================================================== # smp_kkh_pt2_p201-400_OCR (Commentary from page 1) ==================================================================================================== **Commentary on Topic 1: The Aggregate of Form** Regarding the statement that the aggregate of form is permanent: the Vaibhāṣika school posits that the ultimate particles (*paramāṇu*) are eternal. They reason that because the atoms are eternal, the composite matter formed by them must also be eternal. However, this position is refuted by the fact of change. The aggregate of form is subject to transformation through the four marks of existence: birth, aging, sickness, and death. It is further altered by external factors such as temperature and humidity. Consequently, it cannot be considered permanent. Moreover, if form were permanent, the fundamental principle of the arising and passing away of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) would be violated. Our direct observation confirms that forms arise and perish momentarily; thus, the doctrine of the permanence of form is logically inconsistent

By means of the three marks— the heart, the touch of faith, and the cause—
[which are] destroyers of the darkness of ignorance and bestowers of the gift of knowledge,
[and] which produce a bliss exceeding the bliss of Umā’s touch for the Sustainer of the Universe; 24.
O Pot-born One, with pitchers possessing a thousand streams, which effect great purification and serve as a grand ceremonial bath (*avabhṛtha*), that Lord,
with a joyful mind, bathed [him] a thousand times. || 25-26 ||

"By those whose nature is to provide primary protection for the lives of living beings tormented by the heat of the form of ignorance— [by those] of curd, milk, ghee, honey, and sugar..."
Because it bestows even greater fruit than the bathing performed with water-jars, it is called "tathā" (thus) by means of those [jars].
In the hearts of those whose nature it is to touch and sip water with faith, there exist the three marks caused by the three marks—[Chapter Thirty-three].
"O Īśāna of noble vows, I am pleased with you because of this great act,

"O you who are devoted to great exertion, there is nothing today that cannot be granted to you.
