O Śaṅkara, let this incomparable holy site be known by your name.
Viśveśvara said:
Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist within the three worlds—whether in Bhūr, Bhuvar, or Svar—all those sacred fords together are inferior to this Śiva-tīrtha. || 31 ||
Those who contemplate the meaning of the word "Śiva" would call it the knowledge of Śiva;
and that knowledge has become liquefied here through the emergence of my own majesty.
Therefore, this sacred ford named Jñānodana is renowned throughout the three worlds;
by the mere touch of it, one is liberated from all sins. || 33 ||
By touching the Jñānoda-tīrtha, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; and by both touching and sipping its water, one gains the fruits of both the Rājasūya and the Aśvamedha sacrifices.

Whatever fruit a man obtains by bathing at Phalgutīrtha and satiating his ancestors with libations, that same fruit he attains here through the performance of the Śrāddha rite. When the Vyatīpāta yoga occurs on the eighth day of the dark fortnight under the Puṣya constellation, it is known as Gurupuṣyāsitāṣṭamī.
Then, by performing a śrāddha here, it shall become ten million times more meritorious than at Gayā. || 36 ||
Whatever fruit one obtains by satiating the ancestors at Puṣkara,
that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold by offering water with sesame seeds at Jñānatīrtha and at Phalgutīrtha within Gayā. (35–37)

A Sunday coinciding with the new moon, or the specific conjunction known as Vyatīpāta; or when the Vyatīpāta conjunction occurs on the eighth day of the dark fortnight under Jupiter and the Puṣya asterism—this constitutes one statement.
At Puṣkara, located near Mount Pāriyātra within the region of Citrakūṭa.

Whatever fruit is obtained by the offering of funeral cakes at Sannihatī in Kurukṣetra when the sun is eclipsed by darkness, that same fruit is attained day after day through the awakening of knowledge.
Those for whom the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) has been performed by their sons at Jñānatīrtha rejoice in the world of Śiva until the dissolution of all beings.
On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, that best of men,
having fasted and bathed in the morning, becomes one with the inner Liṅga after drinking water.
Having fasted here on the eleventh day, he who drinks three mouthfuls of water will undoubtedly have three lingas born within his heart. (41)
Having bathed specifically at the Īśāna-tīrtha on a Monday, and having offered libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors, and having given gifts according to his capacity,
he should then worship the Śrī-liṅga with extensive and grand preparations.
Having given various gifts here as well, a man becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose. || 43 ||
Having performed the twilight devotions at Jñānoda, whatever sin was born from the omission of the proper time is dispelled in an instant, and the twice-born becomes possessed of knowledge. 44.
This is declared to be the Śiva-tīrtha; this is the auspicious Jñāna-tīrtha;
this is the Tīrtha known as Tāraka; this is certainly the Mokṣa-tīrtha. || 45 ||
Even by mere remembrance, the flood of sins of one who possesses knowledge will certainly perish;
through seeing, touching, bathing in, or drinking [of it], there arises merit and other virtues.
Ḍākinīs, śākinīs, bhūtas, pretas, vetālas, and rākṣasas—
The grahas are the Kūṣmāṇḍas, Jhoṭiṅgas, Kālakarṇīs, and Śiśugrahas. || 47 ||
Fever, epilepsy, eruptive boils, quotidian, tertian, and quartan fevers— all these are pacified in an instant by the waters of the Śiva-tīrtha.
The wise man who bathes the Liṅga with the waters of the Jñānoda-tīrtha [attains the highest state].
By him, the waters of all sacred fords have certainly been used to perform his ceremonial bath.
It is called *tāraka* because it delivers [one across]; that is its designation, that is its name. || 45 ||
"Assuming here a liquid form, I myself, who am of the nature of knowledge,
shall effect the destruction of ignorance and provide instruction in wisdom. [50]
Having thus granted these boons, Śambhu vanished right there;
and the wielder of the trident also considered himself to have accomplished his purpose.
The matted-haired Rudra, the Lord, having consumed that supreme water,
attained supreme knowledge by means of which he reached liberation.
Skanda said: "O Pot-born One, listen as I relate this ancient history for the sake of diverse instruction— namely, that which occurred at Jñānavāpī."
In ancient times, there was a twice-born man in Kāśī renowned as Harisvāmī;
to him was born a daughter whose beauty was peerless on earth. (54)
On this earth, there was no one equal to her in the perfection of her virtue;
she surpassed the cuckoo with her voice and was skilled in the entire range of musical arts.
[55] He attained the bliss of Brahman, which is liberation; the meaning is that he became liberated while living. [52]

To show that it is not at all surprising that Īśāna attained his own bliss through the drinking of that water—since even ordinary people are seen to do so—the author introduces a traditional narrative (itihāsa) with the words "O Kalaśodbhava" (53).
She is called *tanayā* because her lineage (*vaṃśa*) is extended by her; he describes her with fifteen verses and a quarter [beginning with] "by her beauty" (54).
There is no woman here like her— not an Apsaras, nor a Kinnarī,
nor a Vidyādharī, nor a Nāgī, nor a Gāndharvī, nor an Asurī. (56)
The abode of all beauty and the true mine of all auspicious marks surely dwells upon the darkness [of her hair], out of fear of the sun [upon her crest]. (57)
I believe that the moon, out of fear of Rāhu, has sought refuge in her face;
terrified of the fierce-rayed sun, it does not leave her even during the day.
Her pair of eyebrows is like a swarm of bees within the creeper-like foliage of her cheeks.
Moving upward, moving downward, rising, and falling—she partakes in these through constant practice.
The word "tādṛk" (such) is to be connected with every [instance]. Regarding the reading "kinnarīti ca," the phrase "iti ca" indicates an alternative view.
She was indicated by the fear of Bradhna—that is, out of fear of the Sun. || 56–57 ||

"Out of fear of being seen" means out of fear of being destroyed; "even by day"—by the use of the word "even," it is implied "even at night"—"from the fierce-rayed one," that is, from the sun. || 58 ||
The line of hair situated above her eyebrows and cheeks— that very leaf which is a particular ornament—

acts as a creeper; within it, in its middle, there is a repetition characterized by similarity to the practice of the "flying motion," a specific movement of a bird consisting of rising upward and descending downward.
And wandering in the field of that beautiful-eyed one, the two wagtails always enjoy the autumnal delight according to their own desire. (50)
On the uneven surfaces of the rows of teeth of that fair-toothed woman, a golden line was drawn by the god of the flowery arrow; what other such digit could there be in the moon?
For it is likely situated within the auspicious jewel of the palace of King Madana.
The two lips of hers possess a luster that surpasses even fresh coral.
Neither in heaven, nor on earth, nor in the netherworld (pātāla) does such a line exist anywhere among women;
thus, under the guise of the three lines upon her neck, the God of Love pronounces a curse.

In that field of her beautiful eyes, O lady with beautiful eyes!— that field being the region near the root of her nose— I suspect there are two shimmering cloth tents belonging to King Citta-bhū (the Mind-born).
Her two breasts were enriched with a treasury of priceless jewels;

and the Creator fashioned the line of hair on the slender-waisted woman’s waist as if it were an upward-pointing staff, appearing by necessity invisible in the middle of that region where Cupid was born.
Having reached her navel and belly, Kandarpa became bodiless;
as if to regain his limbs once more, he performs supreme penance.
By this hip of the Guru, through the initiation of great passion,
and by the paralysis of her thighs— who would not have their mind rendered motionless?
Even the well-rounded gait of that sage was not obstructed by her excellent conduct.
O Sage, whose splendor was not eclipsed by the radiance of the light from the toe-nail of that fawn-eyed woman, which destroys [all else] through its discernment? (58–59)
Bathing day after day in the Jñānavāpī, she performed tasks such as sweeping in the temple of Śiva with an undistracted mind.
In Kāśī, the deer-like minds of young men do not wander to any other forest; grazing upon the blades of grass that are the lines of their footprints reflected in the water, they do not go elsewhere.
A "thigh-stiffness" (ūrustambha) is indeed a paralysis of the thighs, appearing like a plantain tree or similar growth; by means of that, even the mind of some sage whose nature is contemplation—
[at that time]— abandoned his lotus-face and was seized by the garland of the bee-like eyes of the youths.
Nor did he resort to another creeper, even one endowed with fragrance and blossoms.
That girl Sulocanā would not look at the face of anyone; that young woman Suśravā would not listen to the words of anyone;
and though she was of excellent character and endowed with virtue, she was distressed by their absence in private.

Although she was sought after by those endowed with great beauty, she did not fix her desire upon them. Her father, Dharna, though himself much courted by young men, was unable to give away that virtuous girl, whose splendor was augmented by her excellent character.
By resorting to that holy ford of the ocean of knowledge, that virtuous maiden then beheld the entire universe, both within and without, as consisting of the Liṅga.
Chapter Twenty-Seven.
Once, on one occasion, while she was fast asleep in the courtyard of her dwelling,
a certain Vidyadhara, infatuated by the perfection of her beauty, carried her away.
While he was wishing to lead her through the path of the sky as far as the Malaya mountain during that night, Vidyunmālī arrived.
The Rākṣasa had a terrifying body, wore earrings made of skulls, his limbs were smeared with fat and blood, and he was bearded with tawny eyes. || 76 ||
The Rākṣasa said:
"O young Vidyādhara, having come within the range of my vision,
today I shall send you along with her to the abode of Yama."
Having heard these words, she trembled violently with great fear, like a doe scented by a tiger, repeatedly quivering like a plantain leaf.
He struck down that Rākṣasa and that Vidyādhara with his trident;
and the Vidyādhara youth, though possessed of an exceedingly sweet form and great strength,
had his chest split open by that terrifying trident.
He struck him with a blow of his fist that was like the falling of a thunderbolt.
Intoxicated by human flesh and fat, Vidyunmālin was crushed by a blow from [Rāvaṇa’s] fist in the battle;
like a great mountain struck by a thunderbolt, the Rākṣasa fell to the surface of the earth, coming under the power of death.
The Vidyādhara, too, rendered incapacitated by the blow of that spear, spoke with a faltering voice, his eyes rolling, uttering these words:
"O beloved, you have been brought here in vain," as he spoke the half-verse beginning with "suśiti. || 85–86 ||
The hero gave up his life in battle, remembering that beloved woman all around him. Having experienced the pleasure of a touch never before shared by another,
and regarding him alone as her husband, she consumed her body in the fire of grief.
By virtue of the presence of her who possesses the three genders within her body,
that Rākṣasa, having attained a divine form, went to the third heaven.
Even that son of a Vidyadhara, having staked his very life in battle,
finally attained birth from Malayaketu while remembering his beloved.
Meditating upon that Vidyādhara youth, that young woman,
having surrendered her life in the fire of separation, took birth in Karṇāṭa.
In due course, the son of Malayaketu married her.
Mālyaketu, whose beauty was like that of the bodiless god of love, received from his father the hand of a woman skilled in the arts.
She too, due to the influence of her past impressions, remained devoted to the worship of the Liṅga;
having abandoned sandalwood paste from the Malaya mountains, she considered the sacred ash alone to be sufficient for her body.
That pregnant lady considered even the attire of rudrākṣa beads to be unsurpassed compared to pearls, lapis lazuli, rubies, and topazes. [In some versions, it says:
"Because she had never before been touched by another man," and because of the word "and" (ca), she also cast her body into the fire of grief.
Having obtained Mālyaketu as her husband, the devoted wife Kalāvatī,
partaking in the abundance of divine enjoyments, gave birth to three children. (9.5)
Once, a certain man from the north showed a king, Mālyaketu,
a wonderful and variegated painted cloth.
The king, in turn, presented that painted cloth to Kalāvatī.

Then, with the hair on her body standing on end from joy, she gazed again and again in private at the beautiful painted cloth, the deity of her life; like a yoginī absorbed in samādhi, she forgot even herself.
Opening his eyes for a moment and making the cloth his guest, he then raised the tip of his forefinger and awakened himself:
"This confluence is not beautiful here; the sun is shimmering right before me."
This excellent river has "the destruction of the hair of the substrates" as its name.
[Verse 96: He is from the north, born in the northern direction.
The deity of life, Viśvanātha, beholds her as the support of his own liṅga; likewise, he beholds his own body.
She is this very river of heaven (Svargataraṅgiṇī), whose touch is sought after in the celestial realm.
That which the celestial dwellers always desire as the upward-flowing [river] in heaven;
that which is proclaimed in the Vedānta as the imperceptible Fortune of Liberation (mokṣalakṣmī);
that very glorious Maṇikarṇikā exists for the liberation of the virtuous. 101–102.
Where death is auspicious and where life is fruitful, where even heaven is regarded as a mere blade of grass— that is this glorious Maṇikarṇikā.
There, distributing the accumulations of his prosperity with no desire for death,
he remains observing the ascetic vow, subsisting on roots and tubers.

The meaning of the phrase "whose touch is sought after even in heaven" is as follows: nevertheless, because the river flowing northward (udagvahā) based in Kāśī is so preeminent that it is difficult to attain elsewhere, it is said that "her touch is sought after even in heaven. *Udagvahā* means flowing toward the north.
[Pt 2 Page 334]
Where Śaṅkara, seeking the earth where the triple-pathed Gaṅgā flows, leads even the dead to liberation by pointing out the path of release with the young moon upon his crest;
there, Śaṅkara ferries across the difficult-to-cross cycle of worldly existence.
For by means of the helmsman and others, even those who have died act as if they were immortal.

The path to the essence of *saṃsāra* is not far off for those men who, through abundant merits accumulated over many births, [seek it] from Maheśāna— the abode of compassion— who whispers [the truth] into their ears. (107)
Where they obtain the whispered instruction (karṇejapa) from Bhava, which removes worldly existence (bhavāpaha).

The ellipsis is: where Hara remains, showing the path to liberation to those who have died there. Of what nature is he? Seeking the Gaṅgā together with the young moon upon his own crest. [He does this] for the sake of granting liberation in the form of *sārūpya* (likeness in form) according to the distinction of qualified recipients, [seeking her] from his own head—

It deceives and destroys one who is difficult to restrain and imperishable except through the knowledge of reality. Having accepted the renunciation of the field (*kṣetrasaṃnyāsa*) by whose power the great-minded ones bring about auspiciousness (*śam*), [it acts]. [Pt 2 Page 335]
They consider even Death to be as insignificant as a blade of grass; such is this glorious Maṇikarṇikā.
It is here that Hariścandra, the best of royal sages, having treated his own body as a mere straw, sold it along with his wife for the sake of wealth—this indeed is she.
This is that Śrī Maṇikarṇikā, whose soft sandy bed even the residents of Vaikuṇṭha desire.
This is that glorious Maṇikarṇikā, where those who have been liberated, having cast off the constraints of the cords of karma produced over many births, may dwell;
even those beings in the world of Satyaloka constantly long for this place.
This is that glorious Maṇikarṇikā, which Yama has assigned as a long sleep.
For this is the pillar of the Śakula family, where the illustrious Kālabhairava chastises those who commit offenses against the sacred field (kṣetrapāpa), demonstrating his fierce torments. (114)
Sin committed elsewhere may perish by the mere sight of Kāśī; however, this is the terrible torment for sins committed within Kāśī itself. This Kapālamocana Tīrtha is also purifying.
Where the skull fell from the hand of Vidhibhairava. || 116 ||
That sacred ford which generates purity, where the best of men, having bathed, are liberated from the three debts— that is this Ṛṇamocana.
This wonderful Oṃkāreśa is endowed with five abodes (pañcāyatana), wherein the supreme Brahman known as the Praṇava shines eternally.
For those men who have committed sins within the sacred field (kṣetra) or who have performed evil deeds outside it, [this is the place for] the entry into the field of their sins...

"Because [the sin] is exhausted by that very [attainment], surely [it is so]. One might object: "How can this be consistent with the statement in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*: 'No sinful man whatsoever goes to hell in Avimukta; for all those favored by the Lord go to the supreme goal'? Anticipating this doubt himself, he says:
The letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, the resonance (*nāda*), and the fifth, the point (*bindu*)—
the Supreme Brahman consisting of these five shines eternally therein. (11.9)
This is the beautiful Matsyodara; it is certain that the best of men who bathes here shall not again enter the cavity of his mother’s womb.
This Lord Trilocana will surely make him three-eyed.
Endowed with compassion, this Lord Kāmeśvara fulfills the desires of the virtuous even when they reside in another land;
he is the one by whom even Durvāsas attained the great success of his own desires.
Maheśa himself is merged here for the sake of fulfilling the desires of his devotees;
therefore, this is known as Svalana of the trident-bearing God of gods.
The Lord Mahādeva who is celebrated in the Purāṇas as the presiding deity of this sacred field— this is his wonderful temple.
By beholding this god Skandeśvara with faith,
a human being obtains the fruit of lifelong celibacy.
And this Vināyakeśvara is the bestower of all spiritual perfections.
By serving whom all obstacles of men are destroyed. (126)
This auspicious goddess Vārāṇasī is present here in personified form;
by beholding her, men shall never again undergo birth from a womb.
This, indeed, is the great sanctuary of the Pārvatīśvara Liṅga.
Where Maheśāna, together with Gaurī, eternally bestows liberation. || 128 ||
This is the glorious Bhṛṅgeśvara, the destroyer of great sins; by the service of this Liṅga, Bhṛṅgī became liberated while yet alive. (12.9) Vināyakas are the causes of obstacles. (12.6)
This Lord of the Four Vedas is the Ordainer who upholds the four Vedas;
by beholding him, a Brahmin obtains the fruit born of the study of the Vedas. (130)
This Liṅga, named Yajñeśvara, was established as a sacrifice;
by worshipping it, a mortal may obtain the great fruit of all sacrifices.
This Liṅga named Purāṇeśvara measures eighteen finger-breadths;
by its sight, it becomes the support for the eighteen branches of knowledge (vidyās).
And this Dharmaśāstreśvara is established by the Smṛtis.

The merit born from mindfulness and Vedic study that arises from beholding this [Liṅga]—this is the Sārasvata Liṅga, which destroys all dullness of intellect. This is the Lord of all holy places (Tīrtheśvara), a Liṅga that bestows immediate purification. || 133-134 ||
"He who upholds the four Vedas" is thus [described]; in some places he is called "the bearer of four faces. He is called "Vidhi" because he ordains (vidadhāti).
"Eighteen finger-breadths" means measured at eighteen finger-breadths across and upwards. He states its utility with the words "eighteen... (verse 132).
This most wonderful pavilion belongs to the Śaileśvara Liṅga;
it possesses the supreme splendor of every kind of jewel. (135)
This charming Liṅga is indeed known as Saptasāgara;
by beholding it, a mortal obtains the fruit born of bathing in the seven oceans.
This glorious Mantreśvara bestows the fruit of the recitation of mantras.
It was established in a former age by means of seven crores of great mantras. || 137 ||
In front of the Liṅga of Tripureśa is this great pool, formerly excavated by the Tripuras; it is supremely dear to the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva).
This is the Bāṇeśvara Liṅga, worshipped by the Thousand-Armed One (Kārttikeya).
Even for Bāṇa, who has two arms, this [manifestation] is the cause of his thousand arms.
This is Vairocanīśvara, situated before Prahlādakeśava; this one is named Balikeśava, and this is Nāradakeśava.
He bears and sustains. || 135 ||
"Formerly" (purā) means in the Satya-yuga. "Of Tripureśa" means of the Lord residing in Tripura. "By the Tripuras" means by those residing in Tripura.
To the east of Ādikeśava is this Ādityakeśava;
that one named Bhīṣmakeśava is indeed Dattātreyeśvara. (141)
To the east of Dattātreyeśvara is this Ādigadādhara;
he is named Bhṛgukeśava and is indeed Vāmanakeśava.
These two are Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and [this is] Yajñavārāha Keśava.
This is the lion who tears asunder; this indeed is Gopīgovinda.
This is the temple of Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha, adorned with jeweled banners,
by whose grace Prahlāda attained the station of Indra.
This dwarf Vināyaka bestows upon men no small measure of spiritual perfection.
This one named Śeṣamādhava was established here in ancient times by Śeṣa;
his devotees are not consumed even by the fire of universal destruction (saṃvarta-vahni).
This one named Śaṅkhamādhava remained here after slaying Śaṅkha.
"Ha" signifies what is well-known; even when the reading is "ho," the meaning is the same. || 143 ||
Kharvavināyaka is the lord of the Gaṇas named Kharva. One might then ask: "Since he is called 'Kharva' (dwarf/stunted), does he not bestow only stunted results? To this, he says:
"This is the Sarasvatī stream, the elixir of the supreme Brahman."
Where the great river Sarasvatī meets the Gaṅgā,
there men who have bathed are never born again upon the earth.
This very place is Śrī Bindumādhava, the supreme Lord of Lakṣmī in person.
By bowing with faith to him, a mortal shall not dwell in the abode of the womb;
he does not encounter poverty, nor is he overcome by diseases. (146)
Even Yama bows down to him who is a devotee of Bindumādhava;
he who is the one essence of the *praṇava*, bearing the nature of *nāda* and *bindu*.
That which is the supreme, unmanifest Brahman is indeed Bindumādhava himself.
This is the Pañcanada Tīrtha, known as the essence of the five Brahmas.
Having bathed there, one shall no longer assume a body composed of the five elements;
this is that Maṅgalāgaurī in Kāśī, the supreme auspiciousness,
by whose grace a person attains [liberation] both in this world and the next.
This one known as Mayūkhāditya is garlanded with rays and dispels darkness;
he is Gabhastīśa, this divine Mahāliṅga that bestows splendor.
In ancient times, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu also performed great penance here after installing a supreme liṅga in his own name that bestows longevity. This liṅga,
known by the name Kiraṇeśvara, is renowned throughout the three worlds.
This Liṅga, Dhautapāpeśvara, which washes away sins, would lead this world to the state of being most pure, just as the rays of the sun lead the world to such a state. || 156 ||
This is the Man-Lion of Nirvāṇa, the cause of liberation for his devotees;
this is the Serpent of the Jewel-Lamp, adorned with the great jewel.
By worshipping him, a person is never again overcome by serpents.
This Liṅga, Kapileśa, was installed by Kapila;
even monkeys are liberated by the sight of it, so what need be said of human beings?
This great Liṅga, Priyavrateśvara, shines forth brilliantly. || 158-159 ||
By worshipping Him, a seeker may attain the state of being beloved by all living beings.

This supreme sanctuary, constructed of jewels and rubies, is known as Gabhastīśa—the term *puṃstvam* (masculine gender) is an archaic Vedic usage. It bestows that divine day, the self-luminous light; [it was established by] Mṛkaṇḍu—
By his son Mārkaṇḍeya,
[this was told] of the glorious Kālarāja, who removes the excessive suffering of the Kali age.
He who protects his own devotees from sin is the devourer of sins.
Striking down those wicked ones who create obstacles to the sacred field with hundreds of torments,
this beautiful Mandākinī has come here to perform penance.
Having attained the happiness of dwelling in Kāśī, a person does not long even for heaven;
for by bathing here, satiating the ancestors, and performing the śrāddha rite according to the rules,
a man— even if he has committed evil deeds— shall not behold hell.
Whatever thousands of lingas exist in Kāśī,
among them this linga named Ratneśvara is like a jewel itself.
By the grace of Ratneśvara, having enjoyed manifold jewels, || 164–165 ||
Viśveśvara and Avimukta are these two right hands;
Dharmeśa and Maṇikarṇeśa are the two left hands. (166)
Kāleśvara and Kapardīśa are his two exceedingly pure feet;
Jyeṣṭheśvara is his hips, and Madhyameśvara is indeed his navel.
Mahādeva is his topknot (kaparda), and Śrutīśvara is the ornament of his head.
Candreśa is his heart; Vīreśvara is his supreme self.
His *liṅga* is Kedāra, and they know his semen to be Śukreśvara; as for the other *liṅgas*, there are more than hundreds of millions of them.
The nails and hair of his body should be known as ornaments;
for these two right hands are indeed the perpetual bestowers of nirvāṇa. Having granted fearlessness to living beings falling into the ocean of delusion, [he protects them].

That desirable power, brilliance, or exertion of the divine Savitṛ, and that which impels our intellects—that we meditate upon. And he is like Savitṛ; or rather, the construction may be made by changing the gender: "We meditate upon that desirable splendor (bhargas) of the divine Savitṛ. [And] that splendor which impels our intellects. [The mantra begins with] *āpo hi ṣṭhā*.

The remainder of the phrase is "with three *kaṇḍikās*. In that context, the remainder of the mantra is: "O waters, be our source of joy; grant us strength for great delight; and may the purifying ones release us from that sin. Its meaning is as follows: O Waters, this [is for the] immolation of the animal—

Carry away, remove the evil omen! Whatever is blameworthy or censurable, whatever impurity such as a curse and the like, and whatever impurity adheres to the body—namely the well-known excrement, urine, and so forth—carry that away, remove it! And whatever malice or falsehood—I use the root *druh* in the sense of "desire to harm"—whatever I have harbored malice toward, whatever untrue word I have uttered, and whatever I have sworn... carry that away, remove it!

Regarding *abhīruṇam*: the root *śap* means to curse or revile. Thus, *yacchapitavān asmi abhīruṇam* means that which I have cursed—the one who is fearless—referring to one who does not fear [the consequences] despite being an offender, or rather, that which, when uttered, cuts through the vital points (*marmāṇi*) like a fearless one. And that which is fearless: may the Waters, the purifying Soma, or Vāyu, release me—that is, separate me—from that sin or evil. Regarding *haviṣmatīḥ*.
"May these waters, possessing the oblation, invite him; may the divine sacrifice possess the oblation; may Sūrya possess the oblation"—thus [it is said]. Also:
"The divine waters, the goddesses, [grant] us bliss; the goddesses, the waters, [grant] us their essence."
"May they purify me"— thus the nine Pāvamānī verses are proclaimed.
Then, having recited the Aghamarṣaṇa, one should thereafter recite the Drupadā.
Or else, one should perform breath control according to the rules, or recite the mantra while submerged within water.

This [verb] contains the sense of the causative (*ṇij*): "you purify" means "you cause to go. Furthermore, *āsuva*—grant us *ūrj* (strength) and *iṣ* (food); that is, grant us *iṣ*, such as rice and other grains, and *ūrj*, such as curd, milk, and other condiments. *Āre* means situated far away;
*duḥśunām* refers to misfortune, calamity, and diseases. By this, wicked people and the like are indicated; the meaning is: "drive them away."

"May the divine beings purify me; may they purify me with mind and intellect; may all beings purify me; O Jātavedas, purify me"—this is the fourth mantra. Its meaning is as follows: the *anuṣṭubh* meter, with the "divine beings" (*devajanāḥ*)—the beings who follow the gods—as its indicative mark, [expresses: "May the divine beings purify me. "With mind and intellect" (*manasā dhiyā*): by means of a mind endowed with discernment (*viveka*), [and] the intellects (*dhīḥ*) produced by that mind, [namely] the deities.
May the cognitions of objects or my actions purify me; may all beings purify me. O Śrījātavedas, the wise man should either mutter the Praṇava three times or meditate upon Viṣṇu.
Having bathed in this manner and wrung out his garment, he should put on two washed cloths.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should perform the morning twilight devotion (prātaḥ-sandhyā) with kuśa grass.
For a Brāhmaṇa, especially, must not fail to attend upon the twilight devotion.
While still alive, such a Śūdra is indeed reborn as a dog after death;
he who constantly neglects the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) remains impure and unfit for all ritual acts.
Whatever other work he performs, he shall not partake in its fruit.
Having first meditated upon the Praṇava in the eastern direction and then offered a seat of Kuśa grass,
one should recite this four-cornered mantra with a mind focused on nothing else. || 112-113 ||
Facing either the east or the north, with his topknot tied, he should sit down,
sprinkle himself in a clockwise direction, and perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).

One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its head (śiras) preceded by the seven vyāhṛtis three times, along with ten oṃkāras; this is called prāṇāyāma. A Brahmin performing these prāṇāyāmas, with his senses and mind restrained, [attains purity].
One is instantly liberated from the sins committed during the day and night. || 116 ||
If ten or twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) are performed while restraining the mind, then a great austerity has been practiced thereby. || 17 || [Pt 2 Page 400]
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), performed daily with the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava for a month, purify even the killer of a learned Brahmin.
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burnt away by blowing [with a bellows], so too are the taints of the body destroyed.
In the same way, the defects produced by the senses are burned away through the restraint of the vital breaths.
Whatever fruit one may obtain by duly feeding a single Brāhmaṇa, that same fruit is attained through twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) performed with faith.
Since the entire body of speech, beginning with the Vedas, is established in the Praṇava; [therefore, it is the supreme means].

Then, one who recites the Vedas should practice the Praṇava, which is the beginning of the Vedas. For one who is constantly disciplined in the Praṇava, as well as in the seven Vyāhṛtis and the three-footed Gāyatrī, no fear arises anywhere.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity.
O Pot-born One (Agastya), there is nothing more purifying than the Gāyatrī.
[Even] a killer of a fetus, a destroyer of an embryo, or a slayer of an eminent Brāhmaṇa—118–123.

"They are burned"—the ellipsis implies "by those who perform the burning. "From fanning" means from contact with fire. "They are inflamed" means they are destroyed; [this refers to] the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Whatever sin one commits at night by deed, mind, or speech—
Rising at the morning twilight, one should purify oneself with breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
Whatever sin one commits during the day through the actions of mind, speech, and body, one may remove that by performing breath control (prāṇāyāma) while seated during the evening twilight.
One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun appears; but one should remain seated during the evening twilight until the stars are clearly visible.
By standing and reciting during the morning twilight, one dispels the sin committed at night.
Sitting facing the west, however, one destroys the impurity created during the day. || 127 ||
He who does not attend upon the morning [prayer] and he who does not worship at the evening [prayer] should be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra. (128)
Having approached the vicinity of water, one should perform the daily rites;
having gone to the forest, one should recite the Gāyatrī with a concentrated mind.
Since the twilight devotion performed outside the home possesses many virtues,
even a Brahmin who has conquered his senses is better off if he performs merely the recitation of the Gāyatrī outside.
Even one who knows the three Vedas must honor her; she may eat anything and sell anything.
She whose deity is Savitṛ, whose mouth is Agni, and who has three feet—[that is the Gāyatrī].
The seer is Viśvāmitra; the meter is Gāyatrī, which is preeminent.
At dawn, one should meditate upon Gāyatrī, who is red in color, has Brahman as her deity, is mounted upon a swan, is sixteen years of age, and is adorned with red birds and unguents. (132)
She whose nature is the Ṛgveda, the bestower of fearlessness, and who holds a rosary of beads.
Praised by Vyāsa with verses in the Anuṣṭubh meter,
this meditation upon the Goddess Uṣas dispels the sin of the night.
The supreme sipping of water (ācamana) should be performed with the mantra beginning "sūryaśca";
thereafter, one should perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā".
[He should be] devoted solely to the repetition of the Gāyatrī, having the Gāyatrī as his sole essence, with his senses conquered and well-restrained. And so Manu says:
"A Brahmin who is well-restrained, even if he knows only the essence of the Gāyatrī, is better than this Trita, who, though learned in the three Vedas, eats all things and sells all things. (130)
Of the goddess Uṣas, who is to be worshipped at the time of dawn, [namely] Gāyatrī. || 134 ||
One should cast it ninefold: on the ground, on the head, and in the sky; in the sky, on the ground, and on the head; and likewise on the head, in the sky, and on the ground. (136)
By the word *bhūmi*, the feet, the sky, and the heart are remembered;
the word *śiras* is declared by those who know the ritual purification (*mārjana*) to refer specifically to the head.
[This applies] even from the waters of Varuṇa, from Agni, from Vāyu, and from Indra.
This Brāhma-bath is even superior to the mantra-bath;
he who has bathed with the Brāhma-bath is pure both externally and internally.
In all matters, such as rites of worship to the gods, he attains the status of an Arhat. Are fishermen pure simply by immersing themselves in water day and night?
Likewise, even if they bathe hundreds of times, those whose inner disposition is corrupted are not purified.
May my divine power purify those whose internal organs are pure;
for why are donkeys proclaimed as sanctifiers simply because they are grey with dust?
He who has bathed in all sacred fords is he who is freed from all impurity.
He whose mind here is stainless has performed hundreds of sacrifices.
Listen, O Sage, to how that very mind may become stainless:
it shall be so only if Viśveśa is pleased, and never otherwise. (142–143)

In this context, "earthly" (*bhauma*) refers to having clay as its object, meaning the application of *tilaka* and so forth; "divine" (*divya*) refers to that pertaining to Indra; and "mental" (*mānasa*) refers to the contemplation of Hari and Hara according to the distinction between the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa*). Thus, it is shown that mental bathing is superior even to bathing performed with water from the Brahma-tirtha. Alternatively, the two verses beginning with "on the earth" (*bhūmau*) are intended to specify a particular form of cleansing (*mārjana*); in that case, [the sequence begins] with the Vāruṇa [bathing], etc.
Therefore, for the sake of purifying the mind, one should take refuge in the Lord of Kāśī; by taking refuge in Him, the impurities of the mind are certainly destroyed. (144)
With the impurities of the mind diminished through the supreme grace of the Lord of the Universe,
one casts off this body and attains the Supreme Brahman. (145) Good conduct is considered by men to be the cause for the grace of the Lord of the Universe.
Therefore, one should take refuge in that which is declared by both Śruti and Smṛti.
Then, having recited the Drupada mantra and taking water in his hand,
one who knows the ritual procedure should perform the Aghamarṣaṇa rite with the mantra beginning with "ṛtam."
Furthermore, for that wise man who, having immersed himself in the waters, recites the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times,
it is certain that his merit shall be exactly like that of the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice.
Whether in water or on land, whoever performs the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite,
his flood of sins shall perish, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Then, having recited this mantra, the twice-born should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Some teachers maintain this, while others do so according to the specific Vedic branch (śākhā).
"You move within all beings, dwelling in the secret cave of every creature, facing in all directions."
"You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, you are the waters, the lights, the essence, and the nectar.
(151) Standing, while reciting the *Gāyatrī* preceded by the *Mahāvyāhṛtis* and beginning with the *Praṇava*, accompanied by its head (*śiras*), one should cast three handfuls of water. (152)
By that adamantine water (vajrodaka), the Rākṣasas known as Mandehas,
who are enemies of the sun, are swiftly dissolved like mountains struck by a thunderbolt.
That twice-born man who does not offer three handfuls [of water] for the sake of assisting Vivasvat—
One should cast it for the destruction of the Mandehas; that [offering] shall likewise attain the state of a Mandeha.
In the morning, one should stand reciting [the mantra] until the sun is seen;
in the evening, one should sit and recite until the stars appear.
"This very one, O Varuṇa"—this is the mantra. Regarding the word "teachers" (*ācāryāḥ*): some other teachers [belonging to other] Vedic schools—

The phrase "you move within through differentiation" is the remainder of the sentence; it means they desire this mantra for sipping water (ācamana). Having recited this mantra which is about to be described, a twice-born man desiring his own welfare must not neglect the proper time for sipping water. [Pt 2 Page 407]
Therefore, at the time of half-rise or half-set, one should pour vajra-water.
Even if the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā) is performed according to the rules, it becomes fruitless if the proper time has passed;
for this is indeed like the sexual union of a barren woman.

That twilight which is performed by twice-born men while holding water in the left hand should be known as a *vṛṣalī* (a low-caste woman), which brings forth hosts of Rākṣasas. [The mantras] *udvayantam*, *udutyam*, and thereafter *citram devānām*— Please note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete, as it ends abruptly after the third mantra citation. The mantra "taccakṣur" is an upasthāna-mantra that grants success to the Sun (Braghna).
In the phrase "udvayantam," the anusvāra is an archaic (ārṣa) usage, or it is intended as a representative portion (pratīka) of the verse. [They behold the light] from all sides.
One should perform the ritual attendance (upasthiti) to the Sun-goddess with the Gāyatrī mantra one thousand times, or again one hundred times, or even ten times;
[reciting] the Goddess who has a thousand as her maximum, a hundred as her middle, and ten as her minimum.
The Brahmin who mutters the Gāyatrī is not defiled by sins.
Alternatively, he should mutter the *Vibhrāṭ* section, or any hymn (*sūkta*), or the Puruṣa-sūkta;
or else the Śivasaṃkalpa, the Brāhmaṇa, or the Maṇḍala hymn.
These services bring delight to the Sun;
they are performed with water mixed with red sandalwood, unbroken grains, flowers, and *kuśa* grass. (163)
One should cause the removal of sin by means of mantras declared in the Vedas or the Āgamas;
for by him by whom the Sun is worshipped, the three worlds are worshipped. (164)
When worshipped, Savitṛ procreates sons, cattle, and wealth;
he removes diseases, bestows long life, and fulfills even one's desires.
For this Rudra is the Āditya, and this Divākara is Hari.
He is the sun, the Golden Germ (Hiraṇyagarbha), this Āryaman who is the embodiment of the three Vedas. || 166 ||
By pleasing you, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are satisfied, as are all the gods beginning with Indra and the great sages beginning with Marīci. (167)
Having thus performed the ritual for the Sun, one should then begin the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the *mānavas*, the chief *manus*, the *somapās*, and the *pitāmahas*.
One should either recite this *maṇḍala* hymn of the Brāhmaṇa, beginning with "This is the *maṇḍala*," which consists of twenty-three sections, or [recite] these [verses].
Taking nine, seven, or five blades of *darbha* grass—
possessing tips, with roots, and uncut— the twice-born man should hold them in his right hand. (166)
With the left hand held in the *anvārabdha* position, one should offer libations to the six Vināyakas,
to all the gods beginning with Brahmā, and likewise to the sages beginning with Marīci,
using flowers fragrant with sandalwood, agallochum, and musk.
He should offer libations with pure waters while reciting, "May they be satisfied. Then,

wearing the sacred thread around his neck (nivītī), the twice-born man should satisfy Sanaka and the other sages, as well as human beings, with barley grains, placing straight darbha blades between his two thumbs.

One should also satisfy the divine ancestors, such as Kavyavāḍ, Anala, and the others, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and using double-folded darbha grass mixed with sesame seeds. (173)
A Brāhmaṇa seeking spiritual welfare should never perform the libation of sesame seeds on a Sunday, on a Friday, on the thirteenth or seventh lunar days, at night, or during the two twilights.
With the left hand held behind [the right], that is, with the left hand joined to the right hand— [one should offer] to the Vināyakas.
To Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Dharma, Vināyaka, Vighnarāja, and Mahāgaṇapati;
(170) [he is] *nivītī*, with the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) resting on the neck;
(172) [he is] *prācīnāvītī*, having the sacrificial thread over the right shoulder; (173)
If he should perform it, then the successful practitioner should do so with white sesame seeds;
afterwards, he should gratify the fourteen Yamas while uttering their names.

Then, having pronounced his own lineage, he should joyfully offer libations to his ancestors with the right knee lowered, using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors), while remaining silent. He should offer one handful (*añjali*) for each of the gods, and two for each of the [sages] beginning with Sanaka.
The ancestors desire three [handfuls], while women desire one handful each.

That which is at the tips of the fingers belongs to the gods; that which reaches the base of the fingers belongs to the sages (ṛṣis); that at the base of the thumb belongs to Brahmā; and that in the middle of the palm belongs to Prajāpati.
Between the thumb and the forefinger, they declare the ancestral (pitrya) tīrtha;
reciting the nine verses, the wise man should perform the libation for the ancestors.
One should recite "May the Aṅgirases rise up; may they come to us," and thereafter recite "Bringing nourishment for the Svadhā-offering ancestors. (180)

In that regard, he states an exception for those who act by chance: "If," and so forth. Regarding the fourteen: "To Yama, to Dharmarāja, to Mṛtyu, and to Antaka; to Vaivasvata, to Kāla, to Sarvabhūtakṣaya, and to Audumbara, to Dadhna.
[Pt 2, Page 412]
And for those ancestors here, he should recite the three-verse hymn beginning with "madhuvātā," say "namo vaḥ pitaraḥ," and while reciting, sprinkle water upon the ground.
[He should offer this] to all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass— gods, sages, ancestors, and humans.
May all the ancestors— the mother, maternal grandfather, and others— be satisfied.
May this water mixed with sesame seeds reach those who have passed away from ten million lineages, those dwelling in the seven continents, and all the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā.
And those who were born in our family, who died childless and without heirs—may they all attain satisfaction through the water squeezed from this cloth. (184)

Then, having performed the fire-ritual (agnikārya), one should engage in the study of the Vedas. The study of the Śruti is fivefold: formal acceptance, investigation of the meaning, repeated practice, recitation (japa), and instruction to disciples. (185)
For the sake of preserving what has been obtained and for the sake of obtaining what has not yet been obtained,
one should indeed approach a donor and increase one's own status as a guru.
O best of the twice-born, this is declared to be the morning duty of the twice-born.

Having recited nine verses—namely, the five beginning with *svadhāyibhyaḥ*, the six beginning with *ye ceha*, and the three sections beginning with *madhuvātā*—one should perform the libation for the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*); this is to be construed with the preceding [text]. (180) Having performed the libation for the mothers with their respective mantras, he states the libation for the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) as follows: "Obeisance to you... (181)
Reciting the three mantras beginning with "ā brahma," one should sprinkle water upon the ground; this is the syntactical connection of the three and a quarter verses.
Alternatively, having risen in the morning and performed the necessary duties... [Pt 2 Page 413]... [and so forth].
Having performed purification and ritual sipping of water, he should chew the tooth-stick;
having cleansed all his limbs, he should perform the morning twilight devotion (prātaḥsandhyā) and study the meanings of the Vedas as well as various other scriptures. || 188–189 ||
He should teach pure disciples who are well-disposed and endowed with intelligence;
he should also approach the Lord for the sake of attaining security and prosperity.
Then, for the purpose of accomplishing the midday rites, he should perform the previously mentioned bath.
Having bathed, the wise man should perform the midday *saṃdhyā* worship.
[He should meditate upon] Sāvitrī, whose limbs are blossoming with fresh youth, who is as pure as clear crystal,
who is associated with the *triṣṭubh* meter, and whose presiding deity is Rudra.
Having worshipped the supreme deity— who is associated with the sage Kaśyapa, who embodies the Yajurveda,
who consists of three syllables, who is mounted upon a bull, and who bestows fearlessness upon her devotees—
one should then perform the daily ritual.

Having kindled the fire for cooking, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite. (1.9.4) Regarding those who are unable to perform the morning bath, he says "Alternatively" (atha vā). (1.188) The three-syllabled [mantra] whose essence is the Praṇava. (1.9.3)
The cooking fire is the fire for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. || 1.9.4 ||
One should avoid niṣpāva, kodrava, māṣa, kalāya, and caṇaka; one should also avoid food cooked in oil, cooked food in general, and anything mixed with salt. 1.95.
One should avoid pigeon pea, lentils, round beans, and likewise *varaṭa* beans; as well as the remnants of a meal and anything that has become stale, during the Vaiśvadeva rite.
Having sipped water for purification with *darbha* grass in hand and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), [one should proceed].

Then, having sprinkled water around the fire while reciting the mantra "pṛṣṭho devī," one should perform the circumambulation. Having sprinkled water around it clockwise and having spread the *kuśa* grass three times,
one should face the east with the mantra "eṣo ha deva."

Then, having worshipped Vaiśvānara with flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and clarified butter (ājya), the Brahmin should likewise offer three oblations beginning with the syllable Om and ending with Svāhā, starting with "Bhūḥ" and so forth:
"Oṃ Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Svāhā. Thus he should give the oblation.
Likewise, one should offer six oblations for that which was done by the gods;
[these include] *niṣpāva* (flat beans), *śimbī*, and *vallā*—the latter being well-known in Gauḍa as *vallahā*; and *kodrava*, which are *koradūṣaka* grains.
[Pt 2 Page 415]
One should offer one [portion] silently to Yama, and likewise two for the Sviṣṭakṛt;
then one should give the bali offering on the ground to the Viśvedevas,
and to all beings (bhūtas), one should offer salutation to the north of that.
To the south of that, one who wears the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) should offer [oblations] to the ancestors.
One should offer the water for rinsing and the food to Yakṣman in the northeast;

then, to the north of that, one should pay homage to Brahmā and the other gods. Wearing the sacred thread around the neck (nivītī), one should offer it to Sanaka and the others, and wearing it over the right shoulder (apasavyavān) to the ancestors.
Sixteen morsels are known as a handful (hanta), and four handfuls are considered a puṣkala.
Alms consisting of a single mouthful bring merit to the householder;
these six are the righteous mendicants: the traveler, the one whose livelihood is exhausted, the student, the one who supports his teacher, the ascetic, and the celibate student. (205)
A guest should be understood as a traveler, one who is learned in the Vedas and has mastered the sacred scriptures. || 206 ||
These two are worthy of honor by householders who desire the world of Brahmā;
even when given to an outcaste or a dog, food never goes to waste. (207)
Two [offerings] for the Sviṣṭakṛt: two oblations with the formula "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
|| 201 || An *anūcāna* is one who has studied the Veda together with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*). || 206 ||
When one seeking food arrives, one should not consider whether they are a worthy recipient or not—
whether they be dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers, or those afflicted with loathsome diseases. (208)
One should scatter food on the ground for the crows and the worms.
May those who belong to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma,
and Nirṛti accept this ball of rice (piṇḍa) offered by me upon the earth for the crows.

"Two dogs, one dark and one brindled, born of the lineage of Vaivasvata—(210) to these two I shall offer the funeral cake; may they both be harmless. Gods, humans, animals, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and birds—(211)"
The Daityas, Siddhas, Piśācas, Pretas, Bhūtas, and Dānavas—
even the grasses and trees— have no desire for the food given by me.
Even worms, insects, moths, and the like, though bound by their karma and hungry, [do not seek it].

"Indeed, this food has been given by me for the sake of satisfaction; may it truly be for their delight. Having thus offered the *bhūtabali*, he should wait for the duration of a cow’s milking for a guest who might arrive, and then enter the dining room.

In that case, should food not be given to others, setting aside the eight types of travelers and so forth? To the question "By whom was this said?", he replies: "To those seeking food," but specifically "to dogs.
Or, O Vāyasabala, one should perform the daily *śrāddha* even without giving [food].

At the daily *śrāddha*, according to one's own capacity, one should feed three, two, or even one for the sake of the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*); however, one who is weak should give after setting aside [a portion] from his meal.
The daily śrāddha is devoid of deities and is free from [specific] observances and the like.
Having thus performed the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) without a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), devoid of giver or enjoyer, and abandoned by vows,
one who is healthy-minded and free from affliction should sit upon an unobjectionable seat and eat together with his children. (217)

Fragrant, cheerful, wearing a garland and clean garments, endowed with these two [qualities], facing either the east or the north, he should eat that which has been partaken of by the ancestors. || 218 || 219 ||
Having made the food "not naked" by placing water above and below it, and having performed the ritual of *āpośana*, the wise twice-born man should eat. (220)
Having uttered "Svāhā to the Lord of the Earth, likewise to the Lord of the World, and to the Lord of Beings," one should offer three oblations on the ground. Having set aside [a portion],
the weak and the poor person, having set aside something from all their own food that is fit for consumption, should give it.

The meaning is that one should give a single morsel to all. Having ensured that the food is neither below nor above the level of the navel, and having touched water once, one should offer the five oblations beginning with *prāṇa*. [Pt 2 Page 418]
One should offer [the food] into the stomach; one should offer it into the fire of the stomach-pit with darbha grass in hand and a tranquil mind.

As long as one who is eating does not speak of the merits or defects [of the food], the ancestors partake of it; they continue to do so until the merits and defects have been mentioned.

Therefore, he who eats in silence eats nothing but pure nectar. Then, having drunk either milk, curd, or water, he should sip water once with the mantra: "Thou art the covering of nectar" (amṛtāpidhānam asi). || 225 ||

"May the water of the remnants remain inexhaustible for those who desire it.
