Hirsute eyebrows are said to indicate widowhood, while flattened ones signify misfortune;
a gap in the middle portends great suffering, and coarse skin indicates poverty.
The hips of deer-eyed women are praised when they measure twenty-four finger-breadths, are elevated, well-proportioned, and square.
He describes the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the hair arising from the pores: "A single hair" refers to one hair per pore; this applies to all three [types of pores].
A waist that is sunken, flat, long, fleshless, or narrow [is inauspicious].
These short, hairy lines do not indicate suffering or widowhood.
The buttocks of women that are elevated, fleshy, and broad are said to lead to great enjoyment; any other kind is considered to lead to unhappiness.
Those that are rounded like a wood-apple fruit, soft, fleshy, and firm—
The buttocks are free from folds and increase the pleasure of sexual delight. || 36 ||
The vulva is auspicious when it resembles the back of a tortoise or the shoulder of an elephant;
if the left side is elevated, it indicates the birth of a daughter, while if the right side is elevated, it indicates the birth of a son.
One that is high, resembling a lotus leaf, auspicious, and shaped like an *aśvattha* leaf;
one that has the form of a deer's hoof, or resembles the interior of a hearth—[these are auspicious]. (38)
One who has a hairy vulva, an open mouth, and a visible nose is extremely unfortunate.
She whose vulva has a whorl like a conch-shell does not desire pregnancy here.
A vulva that is flat and shaped like a shallow bowl brings the status of a servant.
Resembling a bamboo or a reed leaf, with a trunk as thick as an elephant's hair and a prominent nose, he was misshapen, crooked in form, with hanging cheeks, and thus inauspicious. || 41 ||

One whose body hairs are tawny like those of *ākhu* or mice is such; one whose specific middle portion (*madhyabhāga*) is like a hidden gem (*maṇi*) due to the excellence of his private parts is such; "well-knit" means very compact; "compact" means firm; "broad"—[Page 450].
The forehead of Bhaga is broad, the hips are wide, high, and fleshy;
they are soft, rich with delicate hair, and auspiciously curled to the right. || 42 ||
A hip that spirals to the left, is fleshless, and bent indicates widowhood; one that is narrow, uneven, and rough always brings misery.
A bladder-like region (the lower abdomen) that is broad, soft, and slightly elevated is praised.
A navel that is hairy, veiny, or marked with lines is not auspicious.
A navel that is deep and turns to the right brings about happiness and prosperity;
one that turns to the left, is flat, or has a prominent knot is not auspicious.

One who has such hair, a high nose— that is, a long nose— and is deformed, meaning contemptible and of crooked appearance, shall, with a belly resembling that of a frog, beget a son who is a lord of the earth. || 46 ||
By means of a belly that is protruding, wrinkled, or even marked with a clockwise curl, a woman will respectively become barren, a female ascetic, or a slave in this world. (47)
With sides that are even, fleshy, soft, auspicious, and with bones well-sunken, there will undoubtedly be a treasury of good fortune and happiness. (48)
She whose visible temples are elevated and covered with hair will be childless, ill-behaved, and a treasury of suffering. || 46 ||
A woman whose belly is very small, devoid of veins, and soft-skinned becomes rich in enjoyments and always partakes of sweet food. (50)
The belly of a woman becomes like that of a poor potter, resembling a gourd or a barley grain;
she is difficult to satisfy, possesses a very large abdomen, is childless, and is unfortunate. (51)
A woman with a protruding belly destroys her father-in-law and her husband's younger brother.
One who is slender at the waist is fortunate and rich in enjoyments; she who possesses all three folds [of skin] and whose line of hair is straight and thin is the source of happiness and sport.
A line of body hair that is crooked, thick, or broken brings about theft, widowhood, and misfortune for women in this world. (54)
Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the belly, he says with three [verses] beginning with "by the belly": the meaning is "excessively small" and "excessively thin. || 50 ||
A brother-in-law is the husband’s brother.
|| 52 || [Pt 2 Page 453] She whose heart is hairless, being level and devoid of depressions or elevations.
She shall obtain sovereignty, freedom from widowhood, and the love of her beloved.
A woman with a broad chest, one who is unchaste, or likewise one who is merciless,
and one whose chest is covered in excessive hair, certainly kills her husband.
The chest, eighteen finger-breadths in width, plump and elevated, leads to happiness; if it is hairy, uneven, or broad, it leads to suffering.
The breasts are praised when they are dense, round, firm, full, and symmetrical.
If the tips of the thighs are thick, sparse, or withered, they do not bring happiness to women with beautiful thighs.
A woman whose right breast is elevated is considered foremost among those who have sons;
one whose left breast is elevated gives birth to a daughter who is beautiful and fortunate.
[He now describes] the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the heart with two verses beginning with "nirlomā."
He describes the auspicious and inauspicious marks of the chest with the verse beginning "eighteen" (verse 57).
He describes the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the breasts with four verses beginning with "ghanau. The term "śastī" means praiseworthy.
The two breasts, resembling the buckets of a waterwheel, indicate immoral conduct;
being large at the base, separated by a wide space, and broad at the edges, they are not auspicious. (60)
The breasts that are thick at the base, gradually tapering toward the tips,
and sharp-pointed are givers of happiness in the early period, but later they become sources of extreme suffering.
A pair of nipples that are very firm, dark, and well-rounded is auspicious.
A neck that is sunken, long, and thin leads to suffering.
A bride with thick collarbones is a treasury of wealth and grain;
one with loose, depressed, and uneven collarbones will be poor.
Shoulders that are not bound together, nor drooping, nor long, nor thin, but beautiful,
broad, thick, and covered with abundant hair, indicate servitude and widowhood.

An *araghaṭṭa* is a water-wheel, known in the Gujarati region as a *rahaṭṭa*. Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the nipple, he speaks of it being like the bucket situated therein; [this is expressed] by the single word "very firm" (*sudṛḍham*). In some places, the reading is "of those with good eyes" (*sudṛśām*). || 62 ||
When these two are conjoined at the beginning of widowhood and so forth, they are fleshless and cause extreme suffering.
The armpits are auspicious when they have very fine hair, are elevated, smooth, and fleshy;
they are inauspicious if they are deep, veiny, or moist with sweat.

The two thighs of gazelle-eyed women should be flawless, free from blemishes, with hidden bone-joints and soft, hairless, and smooth, devoid of veins and body hair; they should be straight. If they have thick hair and are short, they indicate widowhood and misfortune.
The arms of women, with their heads visible, lead to great affliction. 68.
The two hands of a deer-eyed woman, joined together with the thumbs and fingers facing each other in the shape of a lotus bud, lead to great enjoyment.
(66) Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the shoulders, he says in one verse beginning with "nigūḍha": "samuccāgrī" means having raised tips. (65)

Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious marks on the armpits, he says in one [verse]: "In the armpits" (*kakṣe*). "Veiny" (*śirāle*) means possessed of veins; "sweaty and oily" (*svedamedure*) means moist with sweat. || 66 ||
Regarding the characteristics of the auspicious and inauspicious, he speaks with two verses beginning with "sthātām" (66). Those whose bone-joints are hidden are "gūḍhāsthigranthī";
those who are both such and soft are described as "gūḍhāsthigranthikomalo.
(67) He describes the auspicious characteristic of the hand up to the wrist with one verse beginning with "ambhoja": the thumb and the fingers.
That whose face is perfectly straight is thus described.
[Pt 2,
Page 456] The palms of the hands should be soft, with the middle portion elevated, red, and without cracks.
It is praiseworthy, rich with auspicious lines, possessing few lines, and endowed with the splendor of good fortune.
A woman with a palm marked by many lines becomes a widow, one with few lines becomes poor,
and one with prominent veins becomes a beggar.
A palm that is hairless, without visible veins, and well-elevated is praised.
One should avoid a woman who has excessive body hair as a cause for widowhood, and one who is fleshless and sinewy. || 72 ||
The lines on a woman's hand— red, distinct, deep, glossy, full, and circular— are auspicious according to her fortune.
A woman with a fish-shaped line is fortunate, while one with a svastika brings wealth.
By means of the Padma [mudrā], the wife of a king shall give birth to a son who is a lord of the earth. || 74 ||
Disregarding the sequence, he speaks of the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the palm with the two [verses] beginning "soft, middling, and raised. (70)
He describes the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the back of the hand with one verse (72).
He describes the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the lines on the hand with eight and a half verses beginning with "rakta" (73).
[The term] *svastika* refers to a specific type of line marked by a triangle (74).
The conch, the lotus leaf, and the tortoise are indicators of the status of being a king’s mother.
[Pt 2 Page 458]
Cranes, jackals, frogs, crows, scorpions, and serpents, as well as donkeys, camels, and cats, when held in the hand, bring suffering to women. (80)
The thumb that bestows auspiciousness is straight, rounded, with rounded nails, and soft. || 81 ||
The fingers have well-jointed, long, rounded, and gradually tapering nails; those that are flattened, uneven, rough, or covered with hair on the back are inauspicious. (82)
The fingers of women that are excessively short, thin, crooked, sparse, or possessed of many joints are causes of disease and lead to suffering. (83)
Coppery-red, possessing tufts, lofty, and beautiful to behold, the nails of the virtuous are auspicious;
those that are sunken, discolored, resembling oyster shells, or yellow bring about poverty.
Men also are born miserable if their nails are flower-like (curved).
A back with bones deeply sunk within and covered with flesh is auspicious;
however, by a back covered in hair, one certainly attains widowhood.
Even if bent, drooping, or veiny, [the neck] is for those who are suffering;
however, a straight nape is best when it is fleshy and well-elevated.
A neck that is withered, veiny, hairy, broad, or crooked is not auspicious.
A neck that is fleshy, round, and four finger-breadths in circumference is praised. || 88 ||
A neck marked with three lines is praised; it should have unmanifest bones, be well-knit, fleshy, not flat, long, and without depressions, for such a neck bestows auspiciousness.
A thick neck indicates a widow, and a crooked neck indicates a servant-woman.
For she who has a flat neck or a short neck is indeed barren and childless.

In this context, he describes the inauspicious characteristics of the nails of men as well, with the half-verse beginning "rough" (paruṣāḥ). "Blooming" (puṣpitaiḥ) means having the color of white flowers.

|| 85 || He describes the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the backs [of the hands] with the verse and a half beginning "inside" (antar). "Sunk inside" (antarnimagnam) refers to that which has the shape of a horizontal bamboo joint (tiryagvaṃśākāra)—
One whose backbone is submerged within the shoulders has bone [in the nape].
Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the *kṛkāṭikā* (the nape of the neck), he says: "Straight" by means of one [verse] (87).
Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the neck, he says in two and a half verses beginning with "māṃsala":
A chin measuring two finger-breadths is praised when it is round, full, and very soft.
One should discard that which is thick, divided into two parts, elongated, or hairy. || 9.1 ||
The jaw that is joined to the chin, hairless, and very dense is auspicious;
one that is crooked, thick, thin, short, or hairy does not bestow good fortune.
The cheeks of a woman with beautiful eyes are praised when they are plump, rounded, and well-elevated.
One should avoid those that are hairy, rough, sunken, or devoid of flesh. || 9.3 ||
A face that is symmetrical, fleshy, very smooth, fragrant, and round,
possessing the luster of its mother’s face, is born here for those who are fortunate.
A face that is pale-red, round, smooth, and with a center adorned by lines—
A woman whose lower lip is like that of the Lord of the Earth (the Moon) shall be beloved by her husband.
Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the chin, he says in one verse: "One should avoid a woman who possesses a chin that is too thick," and so forth.
[Pt 2 Page 461]
A lower lip that is dark-brown and thick brings widowhood and strife.
The upper lip of a passionate woman should be smooth and grants great enjoyment;
it should be slightly elevated in the middle and hairless, for the opposite characteristics bring adversity.
The thirty-two teeth are auspicious when they resemble cow’s milk in color, are glossy,
and are even above and below, slightly elevated.
Teeth that are yellowish-brown, dark, thick, long, or arranged in two rows are inauspicious.
Those with teeth shaped like mother-of-pearl shells are rare and are a cause of suffering and misfortune.
(99) One with teeth that protrude excessively below will clearly devour one's mother;
one with large, gaping teeth will be deprived of her husband, while one with sparse teeth will become unchaste. (100)
Śyāva means brownish-tawny. (9.6) Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the number of teeth on the upper lip, he says: "smooth" by one [verse].
That which is the opposite is contemptible, or else the opposite of what was stated previously. Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the teeth, he says: "like cow's milk."

A tongue that is red, soft, and dark is desirable for one who eats delicacies; a tongue that is medium-sized, variegated, and broad leads to suffering and is characteristic of one who is forward-looking.
With a white tongue, she dies by water; with a dark-blue tongue, she is fond of quarreling; with a fleshy tongue, she is poor; with a pendulous tongue, she eats what should not be eaten;
and with a broad tongue, a woman indulges in extreme intoxication.
The palate that is glossy, resembling the color of a red lotus, soft, and excellent is praised. (103)
If it is pale at the palate, there will be widowhood;
if yellow, she will become a female ascetic; if black, she will suffer the pain of separation from her offspring; and if rough, she will have a very large family.

[Regarding the tongue: "Thick at the throat, well-rounded, gradually tapering to a sharp point, and very red; not hanging down, such a bell [of a tongue] is auspicious; thick and black, it brings suffering. (105) He describes the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the tongue in two and a half verses beginning with "jihvā" (the tongue). "Śoṇā" means red in color. (101)

Disregarding the sequence, he describes the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the palate with the verse beginning "smooth" (snigdham). [He describes] the appearance resembling a red lotus (*kokanada*), which has a slightly reddish complexion.
He describes the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the uvula (*ghaṇṭikā*) with one verse beginning "the throat" (*kaṇṭhe*). [It is] sharp and subtle.
A smile is praised for those of beautiful vision when the eyes are not closed. (106)
A nose with symmetrical nostrils and small openings brings good fortune;
one that is thick at the tip and thin in the middle is not praiseworthy, nor is one that is overly elevated.
One that is curved and has reddish tips bestows widowhood and suffering.

One who is flat-nosed, short, tall, or fond of strife is a servant to others. Long eyes are auspicious for women when they are slightly curved, long, joined together in two or three places, red at the corners, and with black pupils. 106–108.
One with eyes that are as white as cow’s milk, very glossy, and with black eyelashes is long-lived;
one with protruding eyes is not long-lived, while one with round eyes will be unchaste.
One with eyes like a ram's, one with eyes like a buffalo's, and one with squinting eyes are not auspicious;
one who is utterly seized by lust, one with tawny eyes like a cow's, and one of very wicked conduct are likewise inauspicious. (111)
A woman with eyes like a pigeon's is ill-behaved; one with red eyes is a killer of her husband;
one with sunken eyes is wicked; and one with eyes like an elephant's is not auspicious.
A woman who is left-eyed is unchaste, while one who is right-eyed is barren.
The beautiful woman with honey-brown eyes shall possess an abundance of wealth and grain. || 113 ||
A woman possessing eyelashes that are thick, glossy, black, and fine partakes in good fortune;
however, one whose lashes are tawny, sparse, and coarse becomes censurable.
The eyebrows of the slender woman are well-rounded, glossy, black, and not joined together;
they are praised as having soft hairs and, for one with beautiful brows, being shaped like a bow.
|| 115 || Having grasped [them], she is greedy. || 111 ||
*Koṭarānayanā* means one whose eyes are like hollows (*koṭara*), that is, like the cavities in a tree; she is thus described as having sunken eyes. || 112 ||
Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the eyelashes, he says [the following] with the single verse beginning "With the eyelashes" (pakṣmabhiḥ). || 114 ||
Eyebrows that are joined together, long-haired, or tawny are not praised. (116)
Long ears that are auspicious in form grant happiness and bestow good fortune;
however, those lacking the earlobe, or which are veiny, crooked, or thin, are to be censured. (117)
A woman’s forehead that is free of visible veins, hairless, resembling a crescent moon, and measuring three finger-breadths without being sunken, is a cause of good fortune and health. (118)
A forehead marked with a clearly visible svastika brings about the attainment of sovereignty;
however, she whose head is excessively long certainly kills her husband's younger brother.
A woman with hair that is excessively hairy, veiny, or long is considered to be sickly. A straight parting of the hair is auspicious, and a well-elevated head is auspicious;
one shaped like the frontal globe of an elephant and rounded indicates good fortune and prosperity.
He describes the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the ears with one verse (117).
He describes the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the forehead with two and a half verses (118).
A widow has a thick head, and an unchaste woman has a long head;
even with a broad head, one becomes a vessel for misfortune.
The hair has the luster of a swarm of bees; it is fine, glossy, very soft, with slightly curled tips, wavy, and exceedingly beautiful. (123)
Hair that is coarse, with split ends, thin, reddish-brown, scanty, and dry brings about suffering, poverty, and bondage. (124)
A mole between the eyebrows or on the forehead indicates sovereignty;
a red mole on the left cheek bestows sweet food upon a woman.
Furthermore, a birthmark or a mole on the heart is a cause of good fortune.

Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the hair on her head, he speaks in two verses beginning with "The hair": "The hair has the luster of a swarm of bees, dark like a cluster of black bees. (123) [And] "On whose right breast, marked by a red mole... (126).
The light ones are short. || 124 ||
She gives birth to four daughters and three sons;
she on whose left breast there is a red tilaka mark. (127)
If a woman has a *tilaka* on the right side of her private parts, she will first give birth to one son and thereafter become a widow. (128)
At that time, the king’s wife either gives birth to a son who is a ruler of the earth, or a red fly appears on the tip of the nose of the queen herself. (126)
That very black mark is proclaimed to belong to a woman who kills her husband or one who is unchaste.
A mole, a freckle, or a birthmark below the navel is auspicious.
However, a mole, a freckle, or a mark on the region of the ankle causes poverty.
If it should appear on the hand, the ear, the cheek, or the left neck—
any one of these three appearing during the first pregnancy shall grant a son.
It was fashioned by Svayambhū with a trident-marked forehead.
A woman who, while asleep, grinds her teeth against one another (*kiṭikiṭāyate*) shall attain the lordship over thousands of broad-hipped women;
she becomes a consecrated queen (*mahiṣī*), a sovereign lady. (133) [12.9]

He states that even one endowed with all auspicious marks must be rejected due to a specific defect, using the single word "suptā" (sleeping). The meaning is that she "kiṭikiṭāyate," which is to say, she makes a sound produced by the grinding of her teeth.
[Pt 2 Page 468]
Even if she possesses auspicious marks, she is not praised if she prattles incoherently;
a clockwise whorl on the hand is desirable, whereas a counter-clockwise one is not auspicious. (134)
A clockwise curl (dakṣiṇāvarta) praised when located at the navel, the ear, or the chest brings happiness;
likewise, one on the right side of the spine [is auspicious].
A curl situated internally along the spine, equal to that at the navel, increases longevity and progeny.
If a clockwise mark should appear on the crown of the vulva of the king’s wife, it is auspicious;
however, if it is shaped like a broken cart, it bestows many children and happiness.
A mark located on the hips, by piercing the secret parts, brings about the downfall of both husband and offspring.
If the two [lines] curve toward the back by piercing the belly, they are not auspicious;
by one of them, she kills her husband, and by the other, she becomes unchaste.

Having described the auspicious and inauspicious marks of the body, he now speaks of the *āvarta* (whorls), which follows in the sequence, with the portion of the text beginning from "on the hand" (*pāṇau*) up to "an auspicious mark" (*sulakṣaṇa*). The phrase "a clockwise whorl of the hairs" (*pradakṣiṇāvarto romṇām*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. "Dharya" means worthy of dharma. "Vāma" means a counter-clockwise whorl. || 134 ||
A clockwise curl reaching the throat is a cause of suffering and widowhood;
whether it appears on the parting of the hair or on the forehead, it should be avoided from afar with great effort. (136)
She whose hair-whorl at the nape of the neck is clockwise or counterclockwise kills her husband within a year. (140)
If one [crane] is on the head or two are on the left, moving to the left, they both kill the husband; for ten days they must be avoided from afar by one of sound intellect.
One with a whorl on the hip is unchaste; one with a whorl at the navel is devoted to her husband;
and one with a whorl on the back becomes either a slayer of her husband or an unchaste woman.
Skanda said:

Though possessing auspicious marks, she was ill-behaved and the crest-jewel of those with inauspicious traits; though lacking auspicious marks, she was a virtuous woman and the very ground of all auspicious characteristics. (143)
"Between the nape of the neck" means in the middle of the nape of the neck.

|| 140 || The auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the six [types of women], beginning with the *gandhinī*, should be observed in the treatises on erotics (*ratiśāstra*). And so it is said: "The *padminī* has the fragrance of a lotus, and the *citriṇī* has the fragrance of fish."
Śaṅkhinī, Kṣāragandhā, Madagandhā, and Hastinī.
A woman endowed with auspicious marks, virtuous conduct, self-control, and devotion to her husband as a deity is obtained in the home only through the grace of the Lord of the Universe. (144)

Indeed, those women who in their previous birth were adorned with various kinds of ornaments while living as wives in their own homes, become embodiments of those very ornaments themselves. Those by whom the body was emaciated or cast away at sacred fords (sutīrtha), [attain that state].
They become rivers of loveliness here, endowed with auspicious marks. || 146 ||
A woman who has the complexion of a swan or a punnāga flower and red eyes gives birth to eight sons and attains supreme happiness.
One should avoid that girl who has the voice of a crow, whose shanks resemble those of a crow, who likewise has an upward-pointing voice, who has hanging lips, and who has a pendulous face.
A woman whose gait is like that of a swan shall become a queen;
by her mere arrival, an earthquake is produced.
That woman should be known as bringing misery, according to the words of the Sāmudrika-śāstra: "O whirlpool!
She in whose birth-canal there is a clockwise rotation in the middle."

"She shall give birth to one son, a king who is the lord of the earth," and so forth. [Verse 143] Now, one might ask: "Why then is such a virtuous woman, distinguished by qualities such as auspicious marks, not found? To this he replies: "Auspicious marks... [Verse 144]
He states the cause for women attaining beauty, charm, virtuous conduct, and a husband who is under their own control: "Adorned by them,
the Mother of the Worlds is like the consort of Mṛḍa (Śiva)."
Those women whose husbands are under their own control become virtuous in conduct; such is the case for those whose husbands are subject to their will. || 147 ||
And [the sight] of deer-eyed women of virtuous character;
for that indeed is the fruit of auspicious marks, resulting in both heaven and liberation right here. 148.
By means of auspicious marks and virtuous conduct, women— who are the very abode of joy— transform even a short-lived husband into one who possesses long life.

Therefore, a woman with auspicious marks should be married by the wise, after first examining her characteristics and rejecting those who possess inauspicious ones. In the phrase "like the wife of Mṛḍa," the particle *iva* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Alternatively, there is a reading "iha" (here). [She should possess] excellent conduct.

Those women whose conduct is virtuous, characterized by devotion to their husbands and other such qualities; those whose husbands are "self-subdued"—meaning brought under control and satisfied through service and the like, and not ones who are "enslaved by women"—are described as such.
"I have described the characteristics for the welfare of householders;
I shall now speak of the forms of marriage as well—learn them from me, O Pot-born One (Agastya).
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Women," in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
Having introduced the subject matter of the subsequent chapter by way of restating what has been said, he says: "The characteristics... (151).
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the commentary on the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa* composed by Śrī Rāmānanda. 37.
[Pt 2,
Page 473] Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter.
Skanda said:
The forms of marriage are the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Prājāpatya, Asura,
Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, and the eighth is said to be the Paiśāca.
Now, in the thirty-eighth chapter on Dharma, which is exceedingly beautiful—
The praise of the true Dharma is performed through its actual practice. || 1 ||

The statement, "The *brāhma*, *daiva*, and *ārṣa* marriages are called [such], and the *prājāpatya* and *āsura* marriages are called [such]," is explained by transposing the word "are called" so that the verb "is called" is attached to each term. Among these, the *brāhma* marriage consists of giving [the girl] after inviting the groom; the *daiva* marriage consists of giving her to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).
[Pt 2 Page 474]

Having invited a distinguished Brāhmaṇa, when a well-adorned maiden is given to him, his son shall sanctify twenty-one generations. When [the bride] is given to an officiating priest at a sacrifice, it is the Daiva rite; his son protects fourteen [generations].
Having received a pair of cows as a boon, the son born of that [union] purifies six generations through the rite of the seers (ārṣa).
Having said, "May both of you practice dharma together," the gift is given to the seeker;
where the daughter is thus given, that Prājāpatya rite purifies six generations of the lineage.
These four are recorded as the lawful forms of marriage for Brahmins:

the Āsura, through the purchase of goods; the Gāndharva, through mutual affection; the Rākṣasa, through the forcible abduction of the maiden; and [the Brāhma], which is not mentioned here but is traditionally the first. The Rākṣasa is censured by the virtuous.
The eighth, the Paiśāca [form], is censured because of the abduction of a maiden by force.

Explaining these very [forms] according to their characteristics, [the author] uses the section beginning with "For which caste this marriage is appropriate" and "Of which marriage this is appropriate," and so forth, up until the point before the word "savarṇam. (2–3)
But this eighth [type] is the most wicked, and it may arise among the most wicked.
The hand should be grasped by a woman of the same caste, and the arrow should be held by a Kṣatriya woman.
A goad should be held by a Vaiśya wife, and likewise a hem of the garment by a Śūdra wife.
This rule is recorded and observed for marriage with women of a different caste;

Through marriages performed according to dharma, children who are themselves righteous and live for a hundred years are born; through those contrary to dharma, children are born devoid of righteousness, possessing meager fortune, wealth, and lifespan.
Approaching one's wife during her fertile period is the supreme duty of a householder; however, it may also be according to her desire, keeping in mind the excellence of women. (11)
Approaching a woman during the day is considered extremely detrimental to the lifespan of men.
A wise man should diligently avoid all festival days and the day of a Śrāddha ceremony;
for by approaching a woman on such occasions out of delusion, he falls away from the supreme Dharma. (12-13)
He who approaches his wife only during her fertile period and is devoted solely to his own wife should be known as one who is always a celibate student and a true householder. 14.
Among them, those born in pairs were sons, while those born in odd numbers were daughters.
Having abandoned the ill-situated Moon (Candramas), as well as Maghā and Revatī (Pauṣṇa),
one who is pure should approach his wife, especially under a male asterism;
thus she shall give birth to a pure son who accomplishes the goals of human existence.
The pair of cattle mentioned in the case of the Ārṣa marriage is not commended;
even a tiny fee for a maiden is a cause of the sin of selling a daughter. (17)
A seller of his offspring shall dwell for a kalpa in the hell Viṭkṛmibhojana;
therefore, a father must not live off even the slightest wealth derived from his daughter. (18) [The daughters] are those from whom offspring are born; such are they. (15)
[The asterism] occupied by Rāhu is afflicted; the asterisms named Puṣya, Śravaṇa, Hasta, Punarvasu, Mūla, Puṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, and Āśleṣā are likewise. 16.
[Pt 2 Page 478] Those kinsmen who, out of delusion, live off the wealth of women in this world—

Not only do they go to hell, but their ancestors as well. Wherever a woman is satisfied with her husband and wherever a husband is satisfied with his wife, there Mahālakṣmī, the enemy of the Dānavas, shall dwell in satisfaction.
Trade, service to the king, teaching the Vedas,
improper marriage, and the omission of sacred rites are the causes of downfall for a family.
A householder should perform the domestic rituals daily in the nuptial fire.
He also performed the five great sacrifices and the daily cooking.
For those in the householder stage of life, there are five "sacrificial implements" (sunākarma) day after day:
the mortar, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and the broom.
And for the purpose of eliminating those five slaughter-houses,
five sacrifices have been prescribed which increase the welfare of the householder. (24)

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña), and libation (tarpaṇa) is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛkratu). The fire-oblation (homa) is the sacrifice to the gods (daivayajña), the food offering (bali) is the sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña), and the honoring of guests (atithyarcā) is the sacrifice to men (nṛkratu), in that order.
Seeking to please his ancestors,
the householder should perform the Śrāddha rite every day with food, water, milk, roots, or even fruits.
And whatever merit is gained by giving a gift of a cow to a worthy recipient according to the prescribed rite, one shall obtain that same fruit by respectfully giving alms to a mendicant. || 27 ||
Offered into the sacrificial fire of the Brahmin’s mouth, which is kindled by the fuel of austerity and knowledge,
it shall deliver one from the multitude of obstacles and even from the ocean of sin so difficult to cross.
If a guest departs from someone's house with his hopes frustrated because he was not honored, that person is instantly cast out from the merit accumulated since birth. (26)
Sentences preceded by "sānvat" are for the purpose of a bed; earth, grass, and water—these also should always be given for the satisfaction of a guest. (30)
A householder who eats the food of others will, after death, become the animal of that person;
for the giver of food shall receive the merit of one who is nourished by another's food.
A guest who arrives with the setting sun must be honored with great effort in the evening;
if he departs elsewhere unhonored, he bestows a vast amount of his own misdeeds [upon the host]. (32)
One who eats the food remaining after the guests has become a partaker of long life and wealth in this world;
whereas one who eats food while having turned away a guest is a sinner and a failure in the householder's stage of life.
One who arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite, or one brought by the setting sun, is known as a guest (atithi);
he has not arrived during the previous time, nor has he been seen before anywhere.
One whose habit is to eat food cooked by others is a *parapākāda*—that is, one who eats (*ada*) or consumes (*adana*) the food of another’s cooking.
The phrase "the state of being a beast for him" means that he becomes a beast for the person whose food he eats. || 31 ||
"Having driven away," meaning having abandoned or cast far away.
[Pt 2 Page 481] Without giving that food to him, one should offer food to the child according to one's ability. || 35 ||
Young boys, daughters living in their parents' homes, pregnant women, and those afflicted by severe illness—these should be fed even before the guest; there is no doubt about this.
Having offered [food] to the ancestors, the gods, and men, the householder eats the nectar (amṛta).
Cooking for his own sake, he eats only sin; he is merely one who fills his own belly.
The householder himself should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite at midday;
his wife should offer the evening bali with cooked food, omitting the mantras.
This is known as the Sāyantana Vaiśvadeva in the householder's stage of life;
thus, one should diligently perform the Vaiśvadeva both in the evening and in the morning.
Those who are devoid of the Vaiśvadeva and destitute of hospitality [fall into misfortune].
All those twice-born men, even if they have acquired the Vedas, should be known as outcasts (vṛṣala).
The unmarried daughters living in their own homes are called *ciriṇṭyaḥ*. || 36 ||
Those lowest of the twice-born who eat without having performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice shall be destitute of food in this world and thereafter enter the womb of a crow. (41)

One should constantly perform one’s own duty as ordained by the Vedas without indolence; for by performing that according to one's ability, one shall attain the supreme goal. Sin resides in oil on the sixth lunar day and in meat always on the eighth.
On the fifteenth day and likewise on the fourteenth day, [one should perform the rite] upon the vulva and the razor.

One should not look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting, nor when it is at the meridian; nor should one look at the sun when it is eclipsed by Rāhu, nor when it is reflected in water.
One should not look at one's own reflection; one should run quickly when it rains; one should not step over a cow’s tethering rope; and one should not enter water naked. 45.
A temple, a Brahmin, a cow, honey, earth, clarified butter, one advanced by birth, one advanced by age, one advanced by learning, and an ascetic—[if these are seen]...

In the *bhaga* is the vulva (*yoni*). [43] That which is approached is that which is seized.

While walking, one should keep the following to one's right: the holy fig tree (aśvattha), a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), a teacher, a jar filled with water, prepared food, curd, and white mustard seeds.
One should not approach a woman during her menses, nor eat together with one's wife;
one should not eat wearing only a single garment, nor eat while seated on a high seat.
A twice-born man desiring spiritual luster should not look at a woman while she is eating;
nor should he ever eat fresh food without first having gratified the ancestors and the gods.
One who desires to live for a long time should not eat cooked food nor meat;
one should not void urine in a cow-pen, nor on an anthill, nor in ashes.
One should not void urine in pits containing living beings, nor while standing or walking;
nor should one do so toward cows, Brahmins, the sun, wind, fire, the moon, the stars, water, or elders.

A *caityavṛkṣa* is a tree that is to be resorted to during times of heat and so forth, or a worshipful tree—that is, a tree beneath which worship is performed—or a *siddhārtha*, meaning mustard seed. || 47 ||
The seat within the *pīṭha* and other [locations] is the *utkaṭāsana*; [one should sit] upon that. || 48 ||
Eating, that is, performing the act of eating. || 4.9 ||

Regarding the reading "paviṣṭa ca vinā," it means that one who desires to live for a long time should not eat meat—whether he has gratified the gods and ancestors or not—without the sacrifice involving the immolation of an animal (*paśvālambhana-yāga*).
While looking ahead, one should not discharge feces or urine;
having covered the ground with clods of earth, wood, leaves, grass, and so forth. [52]
Having covered his head with a cloth, he should void excrement and urine in silence;

In times of fear or when one's life is threatened, one may discharge excrement. One should not blow on a fire with the mouth, nor look at a naked woman.
One should not warm one's intestines over a fire, nor cast any impure substance into it.
One should not commit violence against living beings, nor should one eat during the two twilights (55).
One should not lie down during the twilight, even with the head facing south or east;
nor should one who desires a long life void excrement, urine, or saliva into water (56).
One should not point out a rainbow to a cow suckling her calf.
One should never sleep alone in a deserted place, nor should one awaken someone who is sleeping. 57.
One should not travel alone on a road, nor drink water from one's cupped hands; nor should one eat curd from which the essence has been extracted during the day, nor at night.

One should not greet a woman during her menses, nor eat to satiety on the nights [of the dark fortnight]; one should not be devoted to water-pipes, nor should one wash one's feet in a vessel of bell-metal.
If one who lacks knowledge should eat at another's śrāddha after having already performed his own śrāddha,

One should not eat from a vessel that is not shared with others, nor sit on ground defiled by fire or other such things;

One who desires to live a long life should avoid mounting the backs of cows, the smoke from a funeral pyre, crossing a river, the morning sun, and sleeping during the day. (62)
Having bathed, one should not wipe the limbs, nor should one loosen the topknot on the road;
one should not shake the hands or the head, nor should one drag a seat with the foot.
One should never pluck out hair or nails with the teeth.
One should avoid cutting one's nails with the fingernails and should avoid cutting grass.
One should diligently abandon that action which does not lead to future welfare;
one should not enter one's own house or the house of another by any way other than the door.

One should never sleep naked, nor should one ever eat from the hand.

nor should he perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while wearing shoes, nor should he drink from a continuous stream while standing.
One who desires well-being should not consume food made of sesame seeds in the evening.
One should not look at feces or urine, nor, while still impure from food remnants, should one touch the head.

During the two twilights, at the death of a Śūdra, and during the birth-impurity of a king or Rāhu; || 76 ||

Even after having studied the Āraṇyaka, as well as the Bāṇa and Sāman hymns.

One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak an unpleasant truth, nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood. This is the dharma, O Pot-born One (Agastya). 83.
One should always speak what is auspicious and always contemplate what is auspicious; one should associate here with those who are auspicious and never with those who are inauspicious.
A wise person should not revile men who are deficient in beauty, wealth, or lineage.

One should not offer praise to men, nor should one disparage oneself; one should not repel one who approaches for help, nor should one utter the secret vulnerabilities of others. Through unrighteousness one prospers at first, but even those who were once enemies will be won over.
Even if one performs the *sarvatobhadra* rite, he shall nevertheless perish along with his lineage.
Having extracted five lumps of earth, one should bathe in another reservoir;

Whatever wealth is given with faith, having approached a worthy recipient at the proper place and time according to the prescribed rule, that conduces to infinity.
The giver of land becomes a sovereign of a realm; the givers of food are happy everywhere;
the giver of water is always satisfied; the giver of silver becomes possessed of beauty;
the giver of lamps gains clear vision; and the giver of cows attains the world of Aryaman.
The giver of gold shall be long-lived, and the giver of sesame seeds shall have excellent offspring.
The giver of a house dwells in a lofty mansion; the giver of clothing partakes in the realm of the Moon;
the giver of a horse possesses a divine vehicle; and the giver of a bull becomes possessed of fortune.
One who gives a wife obtains a good wife; one who gives a palanquin becomes a giver of excellent seats;

One who gives the Veda is honored in the world of Brahmā; the giver of the Veda is considered the giver of everything.

Even he who causes another to give Brahman through skillful means is equal to him. He who receives with faith and he who gives with faith—both of them shall go to heaven; those who act without faith fall to a very low state.
One with good offspring is one who has excellent sons.

"Therefore, you shall obtain the name Divodāsa, renowned throughout the world;
and by my power, O King, may divine capability be yours. (36)
Having heard the words of Parameṣṭhin, that best of kings then praised the Creator many times and spoke these words.
The king said:
"O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, on this earth crowded with people, why are there no other kings, and why is it that you speak thus to me? (41)
Brahmā said:
"While you are exercising sovereignty, the god will provide rain;
but when the king is devoted to sin, the god will not rain again."
He indicates Ripuñjaya’s future change of name along with his lineage by means of the verse beginning with "divo 'pi" (even from heaven).
[Pt 2, p. 504] The King said:
"O Grandfather, O highly venerable one, capable of creating the three worlds!
'Great favor'—thus I have received your command upon my head. (43)
If you will grant me the fulfillment of a certain desire I wish to express,
then I shall rule the earth as one who has no rival.
Brahmā said:
"O King, speak that without delay; consider it already accomplished.
O mighty-armed one, there is nothing whatsoever that should not be given to you."
The king said:
"O Grandfather of all the worlds, if I am the lord of the earth, then let the gods, the inhabitants of heaven, remain in heaven and not on the earth."
"While the gods remain in heaven and I remain upon the earth, the subjects shall obtain happiness through a kingdom free of rivals.
(47) The epithet "diviṣadaḥ" (those who dwell in heaven) is used with specific intention; therefore, there is no tautology. (46)
The king spoke again:
"O Grandfather, capable of creating the three worlds! O highly venerable one! This is a great favor from you."
He caused the drum to be sounded, saying: "Let the gods go to heaven;
let the nāgas not come here; let men remain in their own places.
While I rule the earth, let the gods be at ease. || 48-49 ||
In the meantime, as Brahmā was about to prostrate before Viśveśa and make his request, the Lord spoke to the Creator.
"O Lord of the World, come, come! There is a mountain named Mandara;
having come here from Kuśadvīpa, he shall perform difficult austerities.
While he performs penance for a long time in order to receive a boon from you," [51]
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Pārvatī, preceded by Nandin and Bhṛṅgin, mounted his bull and went to where Mandara stood.
And the God of gods, whose banner is the bull, spoke with a gracious soul: || 52-53 ||
"Arise, arise! May it be well with you; choose a boon, O best of mountains.
Then he, having heard the Great Lord, the God of gods, the Three-eyed One— [Pt 2 Page 506] —54.
Having prostrated many times upon the ground, he addressed him thus:
"O Śambhu, who assumes a playful form, sole treasure of compassion for those who bow before you!
How is it that even you, the omniscient one, do not know my desire? (55)
O protector of those who have come for refuge, O you who are skilled in all matters!
O Śarva, the joy of the hearts of all, omnipresent, and the creator of all!
If a boon is to be granted to me, even though by my very nature I am as hard as stone— || 56–57 ||
O Destroyer of the distress of those who bow before You, O most pitiable of supplicants,
I therefore truly desire equality with the sacred field of Avimukta.
O Lord, today in Kuśadvīpa, may You, together with Umā and Your retinue, [be present].

"May this bridegroom, who assumes a playful form—that is, one who takes on a body for sport—come to dwell upon my head. (Verse 56) [The suffix *kṛt* is used here in the sense of "one who performs an action," as seen in some instances. (Verse 55)
[Pt 2 Page 507] Having recognized the opportune moment, Brahmā,
having become the foremost and bowing with both hands joined upon his head, addressed Śambhu.
Brahmā said: O Lord of the Universe, O Master of the worlds, I have been appointed by my husband, the Gracious One, O All-pervading Lord,
to perform the fourfold creation.
"By my effort, that creation was brought forth with your permission;
yet, due to a drought lasting sixty years, the subjects on earth were destroyed therein."
The world was then without a king and fell into a state of great distress.
Consequently, a royal sage named Ripuñjaya, born of the lineage of Manu,
was consecrated by me as the lord of men to protect the subjects.
He too, of great heroism and great austerity, made a solemn agreement.
He made this request; he informed [the Lord]:
"If, by your command, all the inhabitants of heaven shall remain in the celestial realm... [Pt 2, p. 508]
Likewise, the Nāgas in the world of the Nāgas; from that, I shall exercise sovereignty.
"I said, 'So be it,' and let that be made authoritative.
O Treasure of Compassion, let this boon be granted to Mandara;
let this be his heart's desire so that he may protect the subjects of that king. (66)
"The two channels are my kingdom, as is that of Śatakratu. What account can there be here for mortals, who blink but half a moment?
Even the god, considering Mandara with its beautiful caves to be pure," || 67-68 ||
Hara likewise honored the dignity of the injunction,
[saying] that just as Kāśī always bestows the state of liberation in Jambūdvīpa, so shall it be there.

Likewise, for a very long time, that Mandara mountain was an island; yet, by the god who desired to go to Mandara with its variegated caves—the god [who measures] two nāḍīs, which is two ghaṭikās—[it became so]. 67–70.
"Of those who blink at half a moment" means those whose nature it is to blink for half a *nimeṣa*; of them.
(68) "Even of Vidhi" means even of Brahmā.
This linga, consisting of his own form and unknown even to Brahmā,
was established in order to be offered to those who had installed it, as the source of all supernatural powers.
And to bestow the supreme good upon beings who have fallen away.
[He was appointed] for the sake of Śrī, and to protect the field of all the settlements here. || 72 ||
Even though the wielder of the Pināka bow has gone to Mount Mandara, this sacred field has not been abandoned by him in the form of a Liṅga; therefore, it is remembered as Avimukta (the Unabandoned).
Formerly this sacred field was celebrated by the name Nandavana;
from that time onwards, its name has been renowned throughout the world as Avimukta.
The name Avimukta belonged to both the field and the liṅga.
Having attained these two, one shall not again be subject to birth in a womb.
Having beheld the Avimukteśvara Liṅga in the sacred field of Avimuktaka, one becomes truly liberated from all bondage of karma. || 76 ||
All worship the Lord of All; the Creator of All, the Lord of All, worships the Liṅga of Avimukteśvara, which bestows liberation upon the earth. (77)
Formerly, no *liṅga* had been established by anyone for anyone anywhere;
nor did anyone know what the form of this *liṅga* might be.
Having seen the form of Avimukta, Brahmā, Acyuta, and the others [realized it].
Vasiṣṭha and the other sages likewise installed a liṅga.
This great liṅga is proclaimed as Ādiliṅga, the Lord of Avimukta;
from it, other liṅgas subsequently arose here upon the circle of the earth.
Even by hearing the name of Avimukteśa, a mortal may be liberated from the [sins] accumulated over lifetimes; he becomes free in an instant—no deliberation is required here. (81)
Even if one has gone far away, by remembering the Avimukteśvara Liṅga,
one is liberated in an instant from the sins committed in two lifetimes;
and by beholding the Unliberated One in the great sacred field of Avimukta.
Having abandoned the sins produced in three lifetimes, one shall become composed of merit. || 83 ||
Whatever sin has been committed during five lifetimes through the loss of knowledge is destroyed simply by touching the Lord of Avimukta; it cannot be otherwise.
Having worshipped the great Liṅga Avimukteśvara, a person here becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose; he shall not be subject to birth again—how could that be?
Having praised, bowed to, and worshipped [the Lord] according to one's capacity and according to one's intelligence.
In Avimukta, the Lord of Liberation is praised, praised, bowed to, and worshipped.
This beginningless Linga, personally worshipped by Viśveśvara, is Avimukta; it should be served with great effort in Kāśī for the sake of liberation. || 86-87 ||
There are many *liṅgas* in sacred shrines;
they all come forth when the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha arrives.
By keeping a vigil at Avimukteśa on the dark fourteenth day of Māgha, [one attains the fruit].
For the yogin who is ever free from sleep, there shall be the attainment of the supreme goal.
The various shrines and lingas grant even the fourfold aims of human existence.
If on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha one worships Avimukta,
what fear can that wise man have of the mountain-like heap of sins,
provided he wields the thunderbolt of devotion to the Liṅga of Avimukteśa? 9.1.
Where is the great *liṅga* of Avimukta, which yields the fruit of the four aims of life?
And where is the insignificant mountain of sins of the wicked, which arises from destruction?
[It is] in the great field of Avimukta, presided over by Viśveśa.
Those by whom this supreme Liṅga of Avimukta has not been seen are utterly deluded.
Having seen the beholder of Avimukta, Yama, the wielder of the staff,
bows from afar with his palms joined in reverence.

Blessed is that creation of the eyes, and fulfilled indeed are those two hands, by which one may behold or touch Avimukteśvara. He who is known by the name Pāpipāparaula was manifested for destruction; once targeted, he shall bring about the ruin of his enemies.
"He should go"—this is the meaning of "where? In the reading *anādipāpa*, the single word *kva* (where) should be construed with both [phrases].
Regarding the phrase *nāmasambhṛtaḥ*, there is a variant reading in some places: *nāmni saṃsmṛtaḥ*. || 9.2 ||
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter in the commentary on the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa* composed by Śrī Rāmānanda.
Even one who has perished in a distant land shall obtain the fruit of dying in Kāśī.
Having beheld the great Liṅga of Avimukta, one should proceed to another village;
having swiftly attained the successful accomplishment of his purpose, he shall enter his home in safety.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Avimukteśa," in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
Now begins the fortieth chapter.
Skanda said:
"The greatness of Avimukteśa has been described by me before you."
"Furthermore, since you are desirous of hearing, I shall tell it to you once more.
Agastya said:
"My ears, having repeatedly heard the majesty of Avimukteśa..."
"Even though Suśruta has been born most excellently, I am still not satisfied.
O Ṣaṇmukha, tell me how the attainment of the Avimukteśvara Liṅga and the sacred field of Avimuktaka may come to pass."
In these forty extensive chapters, the auspicious duties of a householder, which bring delight to the Lord and fall within the scope of prohibitions and injunctions, are described. (1)
Having first repeated what was said, he urges Agastya toward further hearing with the words, "O Lord of Avimukta" (1).
Having first repeated what was heard, he asks [a question] while making known his own lack of satiety, using two verses beginning with "O Lord of Avimukta.

*Śrāvaṃ śrāvaṃ* means having heard again and again. *Suśrute* means in the excellent organ of hearing. *Na dhinomi* means I am not satisfied; I do not have enough. *Pratyayaṃ* [is used here in the sense of] conviction or fulfillment.
"I do not go. Skanda said: [Pt 2, p. 515] Skanda said:
Listen, O Pot-born one, I shall explain how attainment may be achieved here in this Avimukta,
which bestows its own welfare, O high-minded one.
The accomplishment of all desired aims is obtained through the weight of merit.
And that merit, O Brahmin, arises from honoring the path of the Vedas;
for even the Kali age and Time itself, ever seeking a flaw to strike down the man who dwells upon the path of the Vedas, perish through his mere touch, O Sage.
Indeed, by the performance of what is forbidden and the non-performance of what is prescribed, even the fruits of the Kali age are destroyed;
likewise, one destroys a Brahmin by looking for his faults.
Therefore, I shall describe before you the practice of what is forbidden;
by abandoning that from afar, a person shall not become a denizen of hell.
Onion, village-pig, śelu, garlic,
gṛñjana, cow's colostrum, taṇḍulīya, and mushrooms should always be avoided.
One should also avoid trees that have been cut down, exudations from trees, milk-rice, cakes, and fried pastries.
One should abandon meat that has not been offered to the gods or ancestors, as well as milk from a cow whose calf is absent.
Milk from one-hoofed animals is to be avoided, as is that of camels and sheep;
curd should not be eaten at night, nor should fresh butter be consumed during the day. (11)

One should avoid the onion (*palāṇḍu*), which is a variety of red garlic well-known as *pyāja*; the village pig (*viḍvarāha*), which feeds on excrement; all meat-eaters; the crane (*sārasa*); the domestic cock (*kukkuṭa*); and the parrot (*śuka*). [Pt 2, p. 517] 12.
Having avoided the web-footed *khañjarīṭa* birds that dive and feed on fish, one who eats fish is a consumer of all kinds of meat; therefore, one should avoid those fish entirely.
The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish are fit to be eaten when employed for offerings to the gods (*havya*) or the ancestors (*kavya*).
Furthermore, by those who eat meat, these may be consumed: the hare, the porcupine, and the tortoise. (14)
The porcupine and the monitor lizard are praiseworthy, as are known deer and birds;
those desiring long life and those desiring heaven should diligently avoid meat. (15)
The slaughter of animals for the sake of sacrifice leads to heaven, but never any other kind;
one should discard all food that is stale, provided it is not devoid of its unbroken oiliness.
In cases of life-threatening danger, during a funeral rite (*śrāddha*), for medicinal purposes, or at the desire of a Brahmin,
one who eats meat without greed incurs no fault.
Such sin would not accrue even to one who seeks hunting as a livelihood.
Such is the state that awaits after death the one who, out of greed, habitually consumes meat.
(18) Animals, trees, deer, and medicinal herbs were created by Brahmā for the purpose of sacrifice; therefore, even for a Brahmin who slays them as a sacrificer, there is a fortunate destiny. (16)

For the sake of sacrifices to the ancestors and gods, and specifically for the purpose of the honey-mixture (madhuparka), there is non-violence even in that violence; otherwise, violence is most difficult to overcome.

"Free from broken oil" (akhaṇḍasnehavarjita) means devoid of all oil; according to another reading, it means that which is not made with broken or [ordinary] oil, but is instead made with unbroken oil (akhaṇḍasnehanirmita). || 16 ||
One who is weak in wisdom destroys living beings for the sake of his own nourishment;
for such a person of evil conduct, there is no happiness anywhere, neither in this world nor in the next. || 21 ||

The enjoyer, the consenter, the preparer, the buyer, the seller, the one who harms, the one who causes slaughter, and the one who permits slaughter—these are remembered as the eight types of killers. || 22 ||
He who might perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years,
and he who abstains from eating meat— of these two, the latter is distinguished as superior.
Just as one's own self, so too should another be regarded by one who desires happiness.
Pleasures and pains are equal; as they are toward oneself, so they are toward others. (24)
Whatever is done for another, whether it be for their happiness or anything else, all that which was performed will later accrue back to oneself.
Without hardship there is no wealth; and for one devoid of wealth, how can there be any purposeful action?
Where there is no action, how can there be dharma? Where there is no dharma, how can there be happiness? (26)
For happiness is desired by all, and that arises from dharma;
therefore, dharma must be practiced here with effort by the four varṇas.
[The word] "is remembered" by the learned is the ellipsis. Alternatively, there is a reading: "the lowest is eightfold. (22)
The fourfold caste system (cāturvarṇya) consists of exactly those four castes; by that [system]. || 27 ||
With wealth acquired through righteous means, one should perform deeds for the sake of the next world;
and gifts should be given according to the prescribed rule, at the proper time, to a worthy recipient, and with sincere devotion.
If one gives a gift to an unworthy recipient in a manner contrary to the prescribed rules, not only does that gift go to waste,
but his remaining merit is also destroyed.
That which is given for the sake of calamity, for the sake of the family, or for the sake of debt [is likewise lost].
That shall become inexhaustible both in this world and the next; of this there is no doubt.

He who, by means of his own wealth, performs the purificatory rites—such as the investiture of the sacred thread and marriage—for one who is bereft of mother and father, attains infinite spiritual merit.
Neither by Agnihotra sacrifices nor by rites such as the Agniṣṭoma is that supreme good attained which is obtained when a single twice-born man is established in his station among mortals—
that virtuous man who takes the hand of a protectorless Brahmin woman.
In this world he attains happiness and shall reach the imperishable heaven; [this is done] with sincerity and devotion. Whatever other merit remains, [it too is attained].
The meaning is that its fruit becomes inexhaustible and long-lasting.
(30) *Śreyaḥ* means merit (*puṇya*). (31) *Pāṇiṃ grāhayate* means he causes [her] to take his hand, i.e., he performs the marriage ceremony. (33)
If an unmarried maiden should see her menses while still in her father’s house,
her father should be known as a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahā), and that maiden is likewise a vṛṣalī.
He who, through delusion, should marry her would become the husband of a *vṛṣalī*;
one must always avoid conversation with him, for he is forever excluded from the company at meals.
Having understood the faults of both the girl and the groom, one should subsequently arrange the alliance; otherwise, the father incurs blame.
Women are eternally pure; they cannot be defiled by anyone. Month after month, their menstrual flow washes away their misdeeds. (37)
In former times, women were enjoyed by the gods—by Soma, Gandharva, and Agni;
men enjoy them afterwards, yet they are not defiled by anyone. (38)
Soma bestowed purity upon women, and Pāvaka (Fire) bestowed the state of being entirely pure;

the Gandharvas bestowed auspicious speech. Therefore, women are always pure. A *bhrūṇahā* is a killer of an excellent Brāhmaṇa, or alternatively, a killer of a Brāhmaṇa fetus or a child. A *vṛṣalī* is a Śūdra woman.
"Subsequent to the appearance of the menses" means before [the third period]; that is the meaning.
Regarding "previously, the women": they were enjoyed in sequence over three days immediately following the marriage. And thus says the Śruti:
"Soma first obtained her; Gandharva obtained her next."
"Agni is your third husband; the fourth is born of man," and so forth. || 38 ||
Fire consumes a maiden during her period; the Moon, upon the appearance of body hair;
and the Gandharvas, at the budding of her breasts. Therefore, she should be given away even before that. (40)

One with visible body hair destroys her offspring; one whose youth has fully emerged destroys the family; and one who has manifested menses destroys her father; therefore, one should avoid such women.
Therefore, one who desires the fruit of giving a maiden in marriage should give her while she is still unmarried;
otherwise, there is no fruit for the giver, and the recipient falls downward.
By giving away a maiden who has not been enjoyed by the Moon and other [deities], one obtains the full fruit of the gift.
A donor who gives land already enjoyed by a deity does not attain heaven.
Beds, seats, vehicles, a corpse, the face of a woman, kusha grass, and all sacrificial vessels—wise men are never defiled by these at any time. 44.
"A calf is pure at the watering place; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall;
women are pure during sexual union; and a dog is pure in the seizing of game"—as it has been stated previously [in verse 42].
A "corpse" (kuṇapa) refers by that term to a sword, a vessel, and so forth; a "woman's face" refers to it at the time of enjoyment. And thus Manu says:
"The mouth of women is always pure. They do not become defiled, nor do they cause defilement; the meaning is that they do not look upon them with a corrupted mind. || 44 ||
Brahmins are pure from their feet; women are pure in every respect.
Even if she has been enjoyed by force or has fallen into the hands of a thief, [she remains pure].

A beloved wife must not be abandoned; her abandonment is not ordained. Just as copper is purified by sour gruel and bell-metal by ashes, women are purified by their menses, and a river is pure through its current.
For even if one should here contemplate another man with the mind,
she enjoys pleasures together with him, and she too shares in this merit a crore-fold.

The father, the grandfather, the brother, a paternal relative, and likewise the mother—each subsequent one among these, provided he is of sound mind, is the giver of the daughter in the absence of the preceding one. (50)
By not giving her away during her fertile season (*ṛtu*), one incurs the sin of killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*).
However, in the absence of givers, the maiden herself may choose a husband (*svayaṃvara*).
Abandonment is not prescribed; the sense is that she must perform nourishment and supervision [of herself]. This is so when the literal meaning is accepted.
For it was impossible for Viṣṇu to abandon Lakṣmī, who had fallen into the hands of Rāvaṇa and feared being enjoyed by him through force. || 47 ||

The meaning is that purification by menstrual blood occurs only when there is mental transgression; it is not as the literal text suggests—that women are liberated by it—because that would contradict the statement of Yājñavalkya: "A woman's mind is not defiled by her menses. *Śuciḥ* means purity. Or, [the word] *taṭinī* [may be used here].
[Page 524]
One should cause an unfaithful wife to live deprived of her authority, soiled, subsisting on mere alms, humiliated, and sleeping on the ground. || 52 ||
Purification is prescribed after her menstrual period if there has been infidelity; purification occurs upon conception, and abandonment is ordained upon conception.
This applies even in the case of great sins such as the killing of a fetus or the husband.
A Śūdra woman alone is declared to be the wife of a Śūdra, while she and a woman of his own caste are both considered the wives of a Vaiśya.
They belong to him alone, and they belong to the king; they belong to him alone, and they belong to the one born of the first caste.
By mounting a Śūdra woman upon his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by procreating a son upon a Śūdra woman, he falls away from Brāhmaṇahood itself. (55)
But he for whom rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests are not primarily focused— him the gods and others do not eat from, and he does not go to heaven. (56) [Pt 2 Page 525]
Those households which female relatives, when unhonored, curse, will undoubtedly perish as if struck down by magical spells (kṛtyā). || 57 ||
Therefore, those women who have not yet borne children should always be honored with ornaments, clothing, and food by men desiring prosperity, both at formal ceremonies and during festivals. (58)
Where women are delighted with ornaments, clothing, and food, there the gods reside; there all ritual acts become fruitful.
But where the wife is satisfied by her husband and the husband is satisfied by his wife, [there the gods dwell].
In that house, prosperity shall be attained at every step.
The unoffered sacrifice (ahuta), the offered sacrifice (huta), the poured offering (prahuta), the consumed offering (prāśita),
and the fifth, the sacrifice to Brahman (brāhmahuta)— these are the five auspicious sacrifices.

Regarding the word "jāmayaḥ": those houses in which female relatives—namely sisters-in-law, brothers' wives, sisters, wives, daughters, daughters-in-law, and so forth—are not honored and instead utter curses, saying, "May this undesirable thing happen to them," perish along with their wealth, cattle, and other possessions, as if struck by malevolent magic (abhicāra). Thus it is said. || 57 ||

Recitation is the *huta* sacrifice; the fire-oblation is the *prahuta*; the offering to the spirits is the *bhautika bali*; the consumption of food is the satisfaction of the ancestors (*pitṛsantṛpti*); and the worship of the twice-born is the *brāhma* sacrifice. (62)
A Brāhmaṇa who performs these five sacrifices does not come to grief;
by failing to perform them, he incurs the five slaughtering grounds. One should ask a Brāhmaṇa about his welfare (*kuśala*) and a member of the Kṣatriya caste about his health (*anāmaya*).
Having approached a Vaiśya, one attains happiness, and a Śūdra, contentment alone. || 64 ||
A child is considered [to be under restraint] only from birth until eight years have passed;
he is not tainted by [the consumption of] things fit or unfit for food as long as he has not been initiated.
The maintenance of those who are to be supported brings about both visible and invisible rewards;
for there is indeed transgression in failing to support them. Therefore, they must be supported with diligent effort.
"Mother, father, teacher, wife, children, dependents, the guest, the traveler, and the fire—these are the nine classes of those to be supported.
He explains the verse beginning with "ahutam": "Japa is ahuta"; by the word *ahuta*, he means the silent recitation (*japa*) known as the *brahmayajña*.
Furthermore, a man who merely fills his own belly should be known as one who is dead while yet alive. (68)
One who desires prosperity should give to the poor, the helpless, and the distinguished;
those who do not give gifts are born to live upon the fortune of others.
One who is endowed with the virtue of discernment, compassionate, possessed of forbearance, and devoted to the deities and guests is remembered as a righteous householder. (70)
A Brāhmaṇa who sleeps during the two middle watches of the night and eats only the remnants of the oblation does not come to grief. Indeed,
those [duties] are never to be performed by a householder when a guest has arrived.
That gentle speech, eye, mind, and face which are an inexhaustible store of nectar—72.
One who fills his own belly is one who satisfies only his own stomach.
(68) Vibhāga means distribution; śīla means good conduct or a virtuous nature; he is endowed with both of these.
(70) "Sudhāvyayāni" means auspicious things that are imperishable like nectar (*sudhā*); this constitutes a single [term]. "Yatsaumyam" refers to the statement—
This is a qualification of the miserable. || 72 ||
Rising to greet them upon their arrival here, speaking with affection first, attending to them, and following them as they depart— these are for the sake of the exaltation of the householder. (73)
Likewise, these nine tasks, joined with effort and expenditure, are indeed to be performed: providing a seat, washing the feet, food according to one's ability, and a place on the ground. (74)
A bed, grass, water, anointing oil, and a lamp grant success in the householder’s life;
likewise, these nine improper acts must be abandoned by householders:
backbiting, another’s wife, malice, anger, falsehood, and what is unpleasant.
Hatred, hypocrisy, and deceit are indeed the bolts barring the path to heaven.
Nine essential duties must be performed every day:
bathing, the twilight prayers, recitation, fire-offerings, self-study of the scriptures, and worship of the deity.
"Come here, come," speaking thus with affection—this is the first [mark]. "Attendance" refers to massaging the feet and so forth.
It is for the sake of the elevation and prosperity of householders. || 73 ||
O Sage, listen now to those nine things that must be kept secret here:
one's birth sign, sexual intercourse, a mantra, the secrets of one's house, and deception.
One's lifespan, wealth, disgrace, and wife should never be disclosed under any circumstances. || 76 ||

These nine matters are to be disclosed in private: a sin that is not blameworthy, a loan, the clearing of a debt, a purchase or sale along with its lineage, the giving away of a daughter, and excellence of merit; none of these should be discussed by anyone with anyone else. (80)
O Pātramitra, this crane has been given as an inexhaustible gift to those who are disciplined, to the poor and the helpless, to benefactors, and to mothers, fathers, and teachers. (81)
The birth asterism is the asterism of one's birth. "Wealth" (dhana) and "honor" (māna)—this is a singular compound formed from a copulative (dvandva) [of the two]. || 7 9 ||

"Unreproachable" means consistent. "Fit for application" means related to the performance [of the rite]. "Purification of debt" means the discharge of what is owed by the debtor; this is the meaning. || 80 ||
That which is bestowed nine times upon a rogue, a bard, a thief, a quack physician, a gambler, a cheat, a scoundrel, a wrestler, or a panegyrist is fruitless.
Even in times of calamity, nine things must never be given away under any circumstances: one's entire estate when there is progeny remaining, one's wife, and those who have sought refuge. (83)

Having thus sequentially attended to the four stages of life, the wise man,
free from dualities and having abandoned all attachments, becomes fit for union with Brahman.
The self of those with wicked intellects, when unrestrained, leads to bondage; yet that same self, when restrained by the wise, may grant the state free from affliction.
Having understood the recitation of the Vedas, as well as the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, the sciences, the Upaniṣads,

This very point is clarified by means of an illustration: "to be known by oneself" (*svasaṃvedya*). Therefore, one should restrain the vital air for the sake of achieving steadiness of mind;

Posture, restraint of the breath, withdrawal of the senses,
concentration, meditation, and absorption— these are the six limbs of yoga.
As for postures, there are as many as there are sources of life.
This is declared to be the Siddhāsana, which bestows the perfection of yoga upon the yogi.

Furthermore, since even the immovable Brahmā possesses instability that is dependent upon the mind, one should therefore steady the breath for the sake of steadying the mind; and for the sake of steadying that [breath], one should thoroughly practice that yoga which has six limbs, beginning with the postures (āsanas).
One should perform this repeatedly;
by constant practice of this, one shall attain firmness in armor. || 58 || 61 ||
Placing the right foot upon the left thigh and the left foot upon the right thigh, the knower of yoga knows this as the lotus posture (padmāsana).
One should then hold the two thumbs with both hands using a firm grip;
from this practice of Padmāsana, one's body becomes firm.
Alternatively, the knower of yoga, having sat upon whatever seat—such as the Svastika posture—in which comfort arises for him, should practice yoga. 64.
Nor in a place swarming with gadflies and mosquitoes, nor in a shrine, nor at a crossroads.
One should not practice in a place defiled by hair, ashes, husks, charcoal, bones, and the like, nor in a foul-smelling place, nor in a crowded area of people. (65–66)
Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs,
sitting with the body straight— this they call the Svastika posture.
One should place the right ankle on the left side,
and likewise the left on the right, so that it forms the "cow's mouth" (gomukha) posture.
One should place one foot upon one thigh and likewise the other thigh upon the other [foot]; this is declared to be the vīrāsana posture.
Restraining the anus with the two heels in reverse order while remaining composed—
this, those who know yoga understand, is the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana).

Having joined the lotus posture (padmāsana) by placing the hands between the knees and the thighs, and having established them on the ground, one should place [the hands] facing upward; this is the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana).

For one bound in the cock-posture (*kukkuṭāsana*), having clasped the neck with both arms, one should lie face upward like a tortoise; this is the *uttānakūrma* [posture]. Having grasped the two big toes with the hands up to the ears...
Having performed the drawing of the bow, it is called the bow posture (dhanurāsana).

Placing the right knee upon the root of the left thigh and grasping it with the right arm wrapped both inside and outside, one should remain standing with the body turned; this is the seat proclaimed as the glorious Matsyendra-āsana.
And so forth. || 64 ||

He indicates the locus of yoga by way of negation with the two verses beginning "not water. A "sting" (daṃśa) is of the form of a fly; from that comes "bone" (kīkasa), which means a bone; by the word "etcetera" (ādi), blood and other such things are included. || 66 ||
Free from all affliction, bringing pleasure to all the senses, generating clarity of mind, and gladdened by the fragrance of garlands and incense. (67)
One who knows yoga should practice yoga when he is neither over-satiated nor afflicted by hunger, nor oppressed by excrement or urine, nor exhausted by travel, nor distressed by anxiety.
(68) With his feet placed upward upon his thighs and his right hand resting on the left, [he should sit].
Lifting the face slightly upward and bracing the chest,
with eyes closed, established in *sattva*, one should not let the teeth touch the teeth;
the tongue should rest motionless against the palate, the mouth closed, and remaining perfectly still.
Having restrained the collection of the senses and sitting on a seat that is neither too low nor too high,
one should then undertake the middle and the highest forms of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having spoken by way of negation, he also speaks by way of affirmation with the single verse beginning "sarva" (all).
In response to the question, "With what specific qualification should one practice yoga?", he points out the yogin: "One who is neither over-satiated," etc. (68).
Having thus defined the qualifications of the person established in the posture, he states that being in such a state, one should perform *prāṇāyāma*.

Everything moving becomes motionless therein;
by restraining the vital breath, the yogi attains the state of a pillar as long as he remains in the body. || 72 ||

It produces perspiration, trembling, and despondency in succession;

Indeed, by the third [stage], the vital breath (prāṇa) becomes perfected for the yogi;

Being cultivated in this sequence, it leads him wherever he desires. (78)
If this prāṇa, forcibly restrained, should escape through the pores of the skin,

And one should not bypass that;
