Once grasped, however, when cultivated, it attains a state of trust.
The *haṃsa* (the breath) moves thirty-six finger-breadths outside;
because it moves by way of the left and right paths, it is called *prāṇa*.
When everything attains purity.
Seated firmly, one should fill the breath with the moon (the left nostril) according to one's capacity, and then exhale it through the sun (the right nostril); this is called *prāṇāyāma*. (84)
Meditating upon the moon accompanied by a flowing torrent of nectar,
the lord of yogis attains bliss in that very instant through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having drawn the vital breath (prāṇa) with the sun [through the right nostril], one should fill the cavern of the belly.
Having performed *kumbhaka* (retention), the yogi should then exhale through the moon (*candra*).

By reciting [the mantra] thirty-two times, he should expel the external air. Then, having visualized the fire-seed syllable *raṃ*, which is red in color, as the wind that has entered through the right nostril, he should [exhale] through the right nostril by reciting this very fire-seed syllable *raṃ* sixteen times.

Having filled [the left nostril] with air and burned the entire body with the fire arising from the seed-syllable *raṃ*, one should exhale the external air through the left nostril along with the ashes by reciting the seed-syllable *raṃ* thirty-two times. Then, having visualized the lunar seed-syllable *vaṃ*, white in color, within the left nostril-passage, one should lead the moon in the form of the seed-syllable *vaṃ*— the moon of the forehead— to that location by reciting *vaṃ* sixteen times.

Therefore, by reciting "vaṃ" sixty-four times from the moon on the forehead through the practice of *kuṃbhaka* (breath retention), one should produce a rain of nectar consisting of the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa'. Having visualized the entire body as regenerated by that nectar and having flooded it with that very water, one should contemplate the entire body as firm by means of the yellow-colored earth-seed syllable "laṃ". || 83 ||
One should contemplate within the heart that which possesses the heat of moral conduct (*śīla*) and has the brilliance of a blazing mass of fire;
by this practice of southern extension (*yāmyāyāma*), the lord of yogis shall become a partaker of bliss. (87)

Thus, through three months of practice and by means of employing both types of *āyāma*, the yogi whose network of channels is perfected is called one who has mastered the vital breath (*siddhaprāṇa*).
From the purification of the channels (nāḍī), there arises the ability to hold the breath as desired, the kindling of the internal fire, the manifestation of the inner sound (nāda), and good health.
One should meditate upon Śrī Viśveśvara or Nārāyaṇa, who is presided over by the Sun and possesses a heat resembling a mass of blazing fire.
The heart, the senses, the vital breath, the wind, fire, water, earth,
the sun, the moon, and austerity— these indeed are the eleven locations.

"Always to be meditated upon is Nārāyaṇa, situated in the center of the solar disc, seated upon a lotus throne, adorned with armlets, crocodile-shaped earrings, and a crown, wearing a necklace, possessing a golden body, and holding the conch and the discus"—according to this statement. The lord of yogis, practicing and contemplating [the Lord] while He resides within the solar disc in the heart, [controls the senses] by means of this [meditation] just described; thus they are restrained (*yamyante*).
The meaning is: "by the extension of those vital breaths (prāṇas) belonging to Yama. The meaning is: "one shall partake of bliss" means one shall partake of the bliss of Brahman.
[Pt 2 Page 568] Prāṇa is the air residing in the body; āyāma is that which is bound to it.
A single breath constitutes one *mātrā*, and this is defined as *prāṇāyāma*.
In inferior *prāṇāyāma* there is heat; in middling, trembling occurs;

One should burn away defects through breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and sin through withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra); one attains steadiness of mind through concentration (dhāraṇā), and the vision of the Lord through meditation (dhyāna). 9.2.
One may attain liberation through *samādhi* by abandoning both auspicious and inauspicious phenomena;
through *āsana*, one gains firmness of body—this is proclaimed as the sixfold [system].
(9.3) He explains the etymology of the term *prāṇāyāma* in another way: "Prāṇa... [and] its basis is that which is composed of *prāṇa*.
Withdrawal has been explained;
by means of twelve withdrawals, concentration is proclaimed.
This may lead to union with Īśvara. || 9.4 ||
Dhyāna consists of twelve dhāraṇās;
by means of these twelve dhyānas alone, samādhi is designated.
Beyond samādhi lies the infinite light, which is self-luminous.
When that is seen, the ritualistic path of coming and going ceases.
When the wind reaches the ether, a great sound arises from bells and other such instruments; from that, accomplishment is not far off.
Through properly applied *prāṇāyāma*, there shall be the destruction of all diseases;
through improperly practiced yoga, there arises the emergence of all diseases. (9.8)
Hiccups, dyspnea, cough, and pains in the head, ears, and eyes—
various disorders arise from the derangement of the vital air (vāyu).
One should exhale the air little by little and fill it in little by little.
One who knows yoga succeeds in this way by binding [the mind] again and again as it becomes engaged.
For when the senses wander at will among their objects, the skillful withdrawal of them is called *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal). 100–101.
He withdraws his own [faculties] from all sides, just as a tortoise draws in its limbs.
By means of the practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), he shall become free from all impurity.
The sun resides in the region of the navel, and the moon in the region of the palate.
When the moon rains while facing downward and the sun devours while facing upward, that specific astronomical calculation (karaṇa) must be performed by which [the result is determined]. || 103 ||
That nectar is obtained.
The navel is above and the palate is below; the sun is above and the moon is below.
This process, known as "reversal," arises only through practice. (104)
With a mouth like the beak of a crow, the yogi who knows the method of vital breath should drink it very, very slowly; thus he becomes ageless. 105.
Placing the tongue in the cavity of the palate and facing upwards, one who drinks the nectar for six months will undoubtedly attain immortality.
He who, with the tongue turned upwards and remaining steady, performs the drinking of the soma, [attains the same].

Within half a month, without a doubt, the knower of yoga conquers death. By pressing the great cavity of the *rājadanta* with the tip of the tongue and meditating upon the goddess consisting of nectar, one becomes a poet within six months.
For the yogi whose body is filled with nectar, after two or three years,
semen begins to flow upward, resulting in the manifestation of powers such as *aṇimā*.
For that yogi whose body is eternally filled with the digits of the moon, [the same occurs].

Even if bitten by Takṣaka, the poison does not spread within him—this follows from the preceding text. With a face like the beak of a crow, that is, with a mouth resembling the bill of a crow, he is cool.

Endowed with *prāṇāyāma* and joined with *pratyāhāra*, he should then practice *dhāraṇā*. He who performs the *dhāraṇā* of the five elements individually within the heart— || 111 ||
That which is called *dhāraṇā* is defined as the steadiness of the mind.

One should meditate within the heart upon the earth, resembling yellow orpiment, marked with the letter *La*, adorned with the letter *La*, and possessing the Creator; it is four-cornered—this is the *kṣitidhāraṇā*.
Meditating on the water-principle (ambutattva) at the throat, resembling a half-moon and accompanied by Viṣṇu—
the seed-syllable *va* which has the luster of a kunda flower— one shall conquer water.

Having meditated upon the fire-element situated in the palate, triangular in shape, resembling an indragopa insect, joined with the letter 'ra', and presided over by Rudra, one should thus conquer the fire. || 115 ||
The wind element is in the middle of the eyebrows, circular and resembling collyrium;
meditating upon the seed-syllable *Yaṃ*, whose presiding deity is Īśa, one should conquer the wind. || 116 ||
Space, which resembles a mirage or water, situated at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
accompanied by the Lord Sadāśiva, is the peaceful syllable *Ha*.
Having fixed the vital breath there for five ghaṭikās, one should maintain it together with the mind.
This is declared to be the concentration on space (nabho-dhāraṇā), which is skillful in shattering the door-panel of liberation.
The five concentrations (dhāraṇās) of living beings are: the paralyzing, the flooding, the burning, the wandering, and likewise the pacifying.
The verbal root *dhyai* is remembered in the sense of "thinking"; thus, the reality of thought is perfectly immovable.
This meditation is declared here to be of two kinds: with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa). || 116 ||
That which possesses qualities is considered to be differentiated by color, while that which is devoid of qualities is held to be absolute.
Know that which is accompanied by mantra to be with qualities, and that which is devoid of mantra to be without qualities.
Having established a comfortable posture with the mind directed inward and the gaze fixed outward,
and maintaining equilibrium of the body, this meditation-mudrā bestows supreme accomplishment.
That merit which a yogi of steady posture obtains through a single moment of meditation is not attained by means of the horse sacrifice, nor indeed by the Rājasūya sacrifice.
And as long as the subtle elements of sound and the rest remain within the ears and other sense organs—
At that very moment, mindfulness becomes meditation; thereafter, one is devoted to concentration.
Dhāraṇā consists of five nāḍīs; dhyāna would consist of sixty nāḍīs;
and samādhi is said here to occur after twelve days.
Just as the identity of water and salt occurs through their union, so too is the unification of the self and the mind here designated as *samādhi*. (125)
When the vital breath is completely dissolved and the mind is absorbed, that state of equanimity which arises is here called samādhi.
That equality which exists here between the two— the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)— is it.
With all conceptual constructions destroyed, that state is designated as *samādhi*.
The lord of yogis, when joined with *samādhi*, knows neither self nor other, neither cold nor heat, neither pleasure nor that which is other than pleasure. (127–128)

The yogi who is disciplined in samādhi is not measured by time, nor is he stained by karma; he is not pierced by weapons or missiles. Having thus explained, as the occasion arose, the classification of dhāraṇā and the other [limbs] as effected by time, there may now follow the discussion on samādhi.

Just as salt and water, through their appropriate mixing, attain equilibrium and oneness (*aikya*), so too the oneness and equilibrium of the self (*ātman*) and the mind (*manas*) occurs when the well-disposed mind, having abandoned external objects, remains fixed upon the self alone; this is what is called "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*) here.
Alternatively, it is the oneness of the supreme self and the mind, where the mind is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*). 125.
The yogi who is moderate in diet and conduct, disciplined in his activities, and balanced in sleep and wakefulness, perceives reality. (130)
The knowers of Brahman know Reality to be consciousness and bliss, Brahman, which is devoid of cause and illustration, and is beyond the reach of speech and mind. (131)
Therein, by means of the six-limbed yoga practice, the yogi merges into the supreme Brahman, which is without support, without fear, and free from affliction.
Just as when ghee is poured into ghee, it indeed becomes ghee alone.
Just as milk [merges] with milk, so too the yogi attains identity with that.
One should perform massage with water that has not been boiled; one should avoid lukewarm water and salt, and should always subsist on a diet of milk. (134)
A celibate practitioner who has conquered anger, conquered greed, and is free from envy— by constant practice in this manner for a year, he is called a yogi.
[He masters] Mahāmudrā, Nabhomudrā, Uḍḍīyāna, and Jālandhara.
The yogi who knows the *mūlabandha* possesses the perfection of yoga.
The thorough purification of the network of channels, the union of the moon and the sun,
and the complete drying up of the fluids— this is designated as *mahāmudrā*.

With substances such as *vibhūti* (sacred ash) and others in which water has not been mixed— that is, those in which water has not been added— one should massage the body while pressing the perineum with the left foot. 52.9 [Pt 2 Page 579]
Having placed the chin upon the chest,
one should hold the extended right foot with both hands for a long time while retaining the breath.
Having filled the abdomen, one should slowly release it for a long time;
this is called Mahāmudrā, which destroys the flood of great sins when practiced during the phase of the moon. (136)
Having practiced [the breath] with the sun, one should practice again until the count becomes equal; then one should release the mudrā. || 140 ||
For indeed, whether wholesome or unwholesome, all tastes are not devoid of flavor;
even dreadful poison, when drunk, is digested like nectar.

Consumption, leprosy, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, indigestion, and other such ailments— the bodily humors of one who practices Mahāmudrā go to their destruction.
When the tongue enters the cavity of the skull and moves in reverse, [it is Mahāmudrā].
The gaze directed between the two ladles (sruva) becomes the Khecarī mudrā.
He who knows the Khecarī mudrā is not afflicted by a shower of arrows, nor is he stained by karma; he is not oppressed by time. (144)
She moves through the sky;
therefore, this mudrā, practiced by the Siddhas, is named Khecarī. || 145 ||
As long as the drop remains in the body, whence can there be fear of death?
As long as the sky-seal (nabhomudrā) is bound, the drop does not depart. (146)
Because the great bird flies (*uḍḍīyana*) day and night, it is therefore called *Uḍḍīyāna*; therein the *bandha* is prescribed. (147)
One should maintain the posterior contraction in the abdomen above the navel;
this is indeed the Uḍḍīyāna Bandha, by which one may abandon even the fear of death.

He provides the etymological derivation for *khecarī*, which is indeed [a form of] *nabhomudrā*: "the mind moves (*carati*) in the sky (*khe*). He further explains this very point in that same [text]:
"For it binds the network of channels (*śirājāla*) that flow downward; [it is] the water of the sky."
This is the Jālandhara-bandha, which destroys the flood of suffering in the throat. || 146 ||
When the Jālandhara bandha, characterized by the constriction of the throat, is performed,
the nectar does not fall into the fire, nor does the breath rush upward.
Pressing the perineum with the heel of the hand, one should contract the anus.
Drawing the apāna upward, the mūlabandha is prescribed.
Through the union of apāna and prāṇa, there is the cessation of urine and feces;
even an old man becomes young through the constant practice of mūlabandha. || 151-152 ||

He describes the Jālandhara-bandha preceded by its etymological derivation: "It binds. It binds, that is, it holds fast. The network of channels (śirājāla) through which the vital breath (jīva) runs upward and downward is bound.
Moving through the left and right channels, it is restless and finds no stability.
Just as a bird,
though it has flown away, is drawn back again by being bound with a string,
so too the individual soul (jīva), bound by the qualities (guṇas), is drawn [upward] by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The apāna draws up the prāṇa, and the prāṇa draws up the apāna;
the knower of yoga unites these two which are situated above and below.
Pressing the perineum with the heel of the foot, one should contract the anus.
Drawing the apāna upward is called this mūlabandha.
By means of contraction, one forcibly causes the downward-moving apāna to move upward;
yogis call this the mūlabandha.
Pressing the anus with the heels, one should forcefully contract the wind;
by doing so repeatedly, the vital air (samīraṇa) rises upward.
When the prāṇa and apāna, along with nāda and bindu, attain oneness through the mūlabandha, one attains the perfect accomplishment of yoga; of this there is no doubt.
"The unification of the downward and upward breaths, and the cessation of urine and feces—by means of the constant *mūlabandha*, even an old man becomes young. (152)
Now, one might ask: since the Self is immutable and devoid of modification, what is accomplished by yoga? To this, he says:
By the sound *pra*, the breath goes out; by the sound *sa*, it enters again.
The individual soul (jīva) constantly mutters the mantra "haṃsa, haṃsa" from this [source]. (156)
Twenty-one thousand six hundred times—endowed with this number—the individual soul constantly recites the mantra day and night. (157)
The Gāyatrī known as Ajapā bestows liberation upon yogis;
by the mere resolve toward her, a person is released from sins. 158.

News from afar is heard, and that which is far away is seen before one's eyes.
One would have the power to travel a hundred yojanas in half a moment;
indeed, scriptures never before considered would become committed to memory by rote.
One’s capacity for retention becomes exceedingly intense, and even a great burden becomes light.
At one moment he is emaciated, at another stout; at one moment small, at another great.
He enters the bodies of others and understands the speech of animals.
He bears a divine fragrance upon his body and utters divine speech.
He is solicited by celestial maidens, and he maintains a divine body;
such obstacles as these may arise as indicators of the perfection of yoga.
If his mind is not distracted here by these obstacles—
At the end of that, he attains that state which is difficult even for Brahmā and others to reach.
(164) As the yogin practices yoga, supernatural powers (*siddhis*) appear in the form of obstacles; disregarding them, the mind must be fixed solely upon Brahman.
This is stated in the section beginning with "The obstacles" (*antarāyāḥ*) and ending with "having attained which" (*yat prāpya*). [The author] now briefly describes those very obstacles.
"O Pot-born One, that which, once attained, one does not return from, and having attained which one does not grieve— that is obtained through yoga consisting of six limbs. (165)
How can such a mastery of yoga be accomplished in a single lifetime?
And without the perfection of yoga, how can liberation be attained even here? (166)
"O Pot-born One, both are indeed paths to Nirvana;
for what is the casting off of the body at Kāśī, and what is this kind of yoga?
[Both are equal] because of the restless movement of the senses and the expansion of the impurities of the Kali age. (167)
Likewise, for men of short lifespan, where in this world is the great success of yoga? (168)
For this very reason, Viśveśvara, the ocean of compassion, who bestows the state of great exaltation upon all living beings, remains eternally in Kāśī;
so that creatures may easily attain absolute liberation (kaivalya) in Kāśī.
Nor can such [liberation] be attained anywhere else through means such as the application of yoga;
for in Kāśī, union with one's own body is declared to be the perfect yoga.
One is not liberated here so swiftly by any other yoga whatsoever.
Showing that very state, he concludes with the fruit of yoga: "That which, having attained... (165).
[He is] one whose speech is compassion, an ocean of mercy (169).
The glorious Duṇḍi, who holds a staff in his hand— this indeed is the six-limbed Yoga.
He who constantly practices this six-limbed yoga in Kāśī, having attained the long yogic sleep, partakes of immortality. (173)
Oṃkāra, Kṛttivāsas, Kedāra, Triviṣṭapa, Vīreśvara, and Viśveśa—this is another set of six limbs here. Pādodaka, Asi-sambheda, Jñāna, Uda, Maṇikarṇikā, [and]... [174]
This great yoga consists of six limbs, even within the heart of the Brahman-dharma.
O best of men, by practicing these six limbs here in Vārāṇasī,
a living being is never again born in a mother’s womb.

Now, one might object: "One should cast off the body at the end through yoga"; for yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, and based on such statements as "having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place," they consider liberation (kaivalya) to result from yoga alone. To the question, "How then can liberation come merely by casting off the body in Kāśī?", [the author replies] according to the maxim, "Let the wicked man be satisfied," [by describing] another form of yoga consisting of six limbs (ṣaḍaṅgayoga), which is easily accomplished.
The bath in the Gaṅgā is the Mahāmudrā, which destroys great sins; by practicing this mudrā, even one who has committed such acts shall attain immortality. (177)
Movement within the streets of Kāśī becomes the khecarī mudrā;
by means of this khecarī mudrā, one truly becomes a khecarī.

Flying up from all regions toward Vārāṇasī— this is the great Uḍḍiyāna-bandha, which leads to liberation. The retention of water, arising from bathing in Viśveśvara at the crown of the head, is the retention (dhāraṇa) at the top of the head.
This is the Jālandhara-bandha, difficult for all the gods to attain.
Even when surrounded by hundreds of obstacles, the wise man does not abandon Kāśī;
indeed, this is known as the Mūla-bandha, which cuts away the root of suffering. (180-181)
"Thus, O Sage, this twofold yoga has been fully explained by me to you—the one with its six limbs and the 'sky-farer' (khecarī), as spoken by Śambhu for the sake of liberation.
[The term] *khecaro* refers to one who moves in the sky, that is, in Brahman; he is established in Brahman. [For] *kaṃ* is Brahman..."
"Space is Brahman," according to the sacred scripture (śruti). || 178 ||
He summarizes the two-fold yoga: "Thus is yoga. The ocean is accompanied by the mudrās. (182) As long as there is delay in time, for that long one should remain devoted to yoga. (183)
Between these two yogas, this Kāśī-yoga is the most excellent.
By practicing the Kāśī-yoga, one shall attain the supreme yoga.
[One is liberated] by means of old age, which accompanies mental and physical ailments and bears the very signs of death.
Knowing that death is near, one should take refuge in the Lord of Kāśī. Having taken refuge in the Lord of Kāśī, how can there be any fear of time for men?
Even though Time is enraged and is the snatcher of life, that [Time] is most auspicious in Kāśī.

[Main Text from Page 86] The following is the section concerning the *samanubhāsanīya-kamma* (formal act of admonition): When a monk, having been formally admonished by the Saṅgha regarding a matter that ought to be confessed, does not confess it, and furthermore, being questioned by the monks, denies it, saying, "I do not know this," or "I have forgotten this," and thus repeatedly commits an offense; when he has reached the third time of being questioned and still does not confess, the Saṅgha should perform the *samanubhāsanīya-kamma* against him. This formal act of admonition is to be carried out by a quorum of at least four monks. It is performed by means of a motion (*ñatti*) and a single proclamation (*ekavācikā kammavācā*). Once the *samanubhāsanīya-kamma* has been performed, the monk must confess his offense. If he does not confess, he incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense for every step he takes toward a village or monastery. If he does not confess after being admonished, he incurs a *pācittiya* offense. If a monk is subject to this *samanubhāsanīya-kamma*, he is prohibited from:

1. Participating in the Uposatha ceremony; 2. Participating in the Pavāraṇā ceremony; 3. Being appointed as a *kammavācaka* (the one who recites the formal act); 4. Being appointed as a *cārika-bhikkhu* (a monk on a journey); 5. Being appointed as a *vassa-vuttha-bhikkhu* (a monk who has completed the rains retreat); 6. Being appointed as a *cīvara-bhājaka* (distributor of robes); 7. Being appointed as a *cīvara-paṭiggāhaka* (receiver of robes); 8. Being appointed as a *phala-bhājaka* (distributor of fruit); 9. Being appointed as a *khajjaka-bhājaka* (distributor of solid food); 10. Being appointed as a *yāgu-bhājaka* (distributor of rice gruel); 11. Being appointed as a *bhattuddesaka* (designator of meals); 12. Being appointed as a *senāsana-paññāpaka* (assigner of lodgings); 13. Being appointed as a *gāmantara-gāmūpacāra-gantā* (one who goes to another village or its vicinity); 14. Being appointed as a *dūta* (messenger); 15. Being appointed as a *sīmā-sammuti-kāraka* (one who establishes the boundaries); 16. Being appointed as a *sīmā-samūhana-kāraka* (one who removes the boundaries); 17. Being appointed as a *sīmā-sandhi-samūhana-kāraka* (one who removes the connection between boundaries); 18. Being appointed as a *sīmā-sandhi-sammuti-kāraka* (one who establishes the connection between boundaries); 19. The Analysis of the Aggregates (Khandha-vibhaṅga)** **The Exposition of the Aggregate of Form (Rūpa-kkhandha-niddesa)** **The Section on the Investigation of the Elements (Dhātu-paccaya-parivīmaṃsā)** Now, regarding the phrase "the aggregate of form": form is that which has the nature of being affected by change. It is called "form" because it undergoes transformation (*ruppati*). What is this transformation? It is the state of being broken down, the state of being afflicted, and the state of being disturbed. Therein, "being broken down" refers to the breaking up of the body at the time of death; "being afflicted" refers to the affliction caused by contact with cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and so forth; and "being disturbed" refers to the disturbance caused by the impact of weapons, fire, water, and the like. Alternatively, "form" is so called because it is the basis for the manifestation of the mind and mental factors. For it is said: "Bhikkhus, form is the basis for the manifestation of the mind and mental factors. Furthermore, "form" is that which is characterized by the four great elements and the form derived from them. It is classified as twenty-eightfold: the four great elements, the ten bases of form, the seven objects of form, and the seven types of non-manifesting form. Among these, the four great elements are earth, water, fire, and air. These are defined respectively by their characteristics of hardness, cohesion, heat, and motion. The ten bases of form are: the eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, the visible-form-base, the sound-base, the odor-base, the flavor-base, and the tangible-object-base. The seven objects of form are: the visible-form-base, the sound-base, the odor-base, the flavor-base, the tangible-object-base, the space-element, and the lightness, malleability, and wieldiness of form. The seven types of non-manifesting form are: restraint born of concentration, restraint born of the path, restraint born of the precepts, non-restraint, the intermediate state between restraint and non-restraint, the sign of the training, and the signless attainment. Thus, all these forms, whether internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, distant or near, are collectively termed the "aggregate of form. This is the first aggregate. [End of Page 1] **The Section on the Investigation of the Bases (Āyatana-paccaya-parivīmaṃsā)** Next, regarding the phrase "the aggregate of feeling": feeling is that which experiences the object. It is called "feeling" because it feels (*vedayati*). What does it feel? It feels pleasure, pain, and neither-pleasure-nor-pain. Therein, "pleasure" is that which is experienced as agreeable; "pain" is that which is experienced as disagreeable; and "neither-pleasure-nor-pain" is that which is experienced as neutral. Feeling is further classified as sixfold: feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact. These feelings, whether internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, distant or near, are collectively termed the "aggregate of feeling. This is the second aggregate. [End of Page 2] **The Section on the Investigation of the Faculties (Indriya-paccaya-parivīmaṃsā)** Next, regarding the phrase "the aggregate of perception": perception is that which perceives the signs of an object. It is called "perception" because it perceives (*sañjānāti*). What does it perceive? It perceives blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, and so forth. Perception is further classified as sixfold: perception born of eye-contact, perception born of ear-contact, perception born of nose-contact, perception born of tongue-contact, perception born of body-contact, and perception born of mind-contact. These perceptions, whether internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, distant or near, are collectively termed the "aggregate of perception. This is the third aggregate.

The Compendium of Abhidhamma (Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha), Part Three: The Chapter on the Investigation of Consciousness (Citta-vibhāga), Section One.
**Investigation of Consciousness** **The Eighteen Mental Factors (Cetasikas)** There are eighteen mental factors that arise together with consciousness.

They are as follows: 1. Contact (phassa) 2. Volition (cetanā) 3. One-pointedness (ekaggatā) 4. Mental life-faculty (jīvitindriya) 5. Attention (manasikāra) 6. Initial application (vitakka) 7. Sustained application (vicāra) 8. Decision (adhimokkha) 9. Energy (viriya) 10. Zest (pīti) 11. Joy (somanassa) 12. Equanimity (upekkhā) 13. Faith (saddhā) 14. Mindfulness (sati) 15. Shame (hiri) 16. Fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) 17. Greed (lobha) 18. Delusion (moha) These eighteen mental factors arise in all classes of consciousness. Among them, the first five—contact, volition, one-pointedness, mental life-faculty, and attention—are called the "universal" (sabba-citta-sādhāraṇa) factors because they arise in every state of consciousness. The next five—initial application, sustained application, decision, energy, and zest—are called the "particular" (pakinnaka) factors because they arise in some states of consciousness but not in others. The remaining eight—joy, equanimity, faith, mindfulness, shame, fear of wrongdoing, greed, and delusion—are called the "occasional" (kaṣāyika) factors because they arise only occasionally in specific types of consciousness. **The Classification of Consciousness** Consciousness is classified according to its moral quality into four categories: wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), resultant (vipāka), and functional (kiriya). **Unwholesome Consciousness** There are twelve types of unwholesome consciousness. These arise through the roots of greed, hatred, and delusion. 1. **Greed-rooted consciousness:** There are eight types of consciousness rooted in greed. These include: - Consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with wrong view. - Consciousness accompanied by joy and dissociated from wrong view. - Consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with wrong view. - Consciousness accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from wrong view. - Consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with restlessness. - Consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with restlessness. - Consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with doubt. - Consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt. 2. **Hatred-rooted consciousness:** There are two types of consciousness rooted in hatred. # Samantapāsādikā, Part 3, Pages 601–658 (Main Text from Page 1) [Page 601] Now, regarding the section on the *pārivāsika* (one undergoing probation): The Buddha, the Blessed One, having stayed at Sāvatthī as long as he desired, set out on tour toward the Southern Country (*Dakkhiṇāpatha*). While traveling along the road, he arrived at a certain village. There, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go to the village and announce to the lay followers: 'Friends, the Blessed One has arrived at this village. Let those who wish to see the Tathāgata come. "Very well, Lord," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Having received his instruction, he went to that village and announced to the lay followers: "Friends, the Blessed One has arrived at this village. Let those who wish to see the Tathāgata come. Then the lay followers of that village, having heard the Venerable Ānanda’s announcement, prepared various kinds of food and drink and set out for the village where the Blessed One was staying. On the way, they encountered the Venerable Ānanda. Seeing him, they asked: "Venerable Ānanda, where is the Blessed One? "Friends, the Blessed One is staying right here in this village," he replied. "Venerable Ānanda, we have already set out from our own village with the intention of seeing the Blessed One. May the Venerable Ānanda inform the Blessed One of this. "Very well, friends," the Venerable Ānanda said, and he informed the Blessed One accordingly. Then the Blessed One, having understood the situation, addressed the monks: "Monks, let those who have completed their probation (*parivuttha-pārivāsika*) and are fit to be integrated (*mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha*) be brought before me. "Very well, Lord," the monks replied to the Blessed One. They then brought before the Blessed One those monks who had completed their probation and were fit to be integrated. The Blessed One addressed them: "Monks, I allow you to integrate those who have completed their probation and are fit to be integrated by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation (*ñattidutiya-kamma*). Having been thus instructed, the monks performed the integration ceremony for those monks using a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation. However, the Blessed One declared that this was not in accordance with the Dhamma and not in accordance with the Vinaya. He said: "Monks, one should not integrate a monk who has completed his probation and is fit to be integrated by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation. Whoever should do so commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). The Blessed One further instructed: "Monks, I allow you to integrate a monk who has completed his probation and is fit to be integrated by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*). Having been thus instructed, the monks performed the integration ceremony for those monks using a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations. The Blessed One declared that this was in accordance with the Dhamma and in accordance with the Vinaya. **The Commentary on the Summary of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha-ṭīkā)** **Part IV: The Section on the Analysis of the Path and Fruition (Maggaphala-vibhaṅga)** [Page 1] **The Exposition of the Path and Fruition** Now, following the analysis of the aggregates, elements, and bases, the analysis of the path and fruition is undertaken. Regarding this, the path is that which leads to the cessation of suffering; it is the noble eightfold path consisting of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Fruition is the state of having attained the fruit of the path; it is the realization of the cessation of suffering, which is the result of the path. In this context, the path is explained first because it is the cause of fruition. It should be understood that the path is of four types: the path of stream-entry, the path of once-returning, the path of non-returning, and the path of arhatship. Each of these is further divided into two: the path of seeing and the path of development. The path of seeing is the direct penetration of the Four Noble Truths. The path of development is the repeated cultivation of that same penetration for the purpose of abandoning the defilements. As for fruition: the fruition of stream-entry is the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry; likewise for the others. These fruits are characterized by the destruction of specific fetters and the possession of certain qualities. Now, to explain the path and fruition in detail: **I. The Path of Seeing** The path of seeing consists of the fifteen moments of consciousness that arise upon the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths. These are as follows: 1. **The Knowledge of Suffering:** This is the direct knowledge of the truth of suffering as it truly is. 2. **The Knowledge of Origination:** This is the direct knowledge of the truth of origination as it truly is. 3. **The Knowledge of Cessation:** This is the direct knowledge of the truth of cessation as it truly is. 4. **The Knowledge of the Path:** This is the direct knowledge of the truth of the path as it truly is. Each of these four truths is contemplated through four aspects: suffering, origination, cessation, and the path. Thus, there are sixteen moments of knowledge in total. However, the first moment of each truth is called "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*), while the subsequent moments are called "patience" (*khanti*). Therefore, there are eight moments of patience and eight moments of knowledge, totaling sixteen moments. These sixteen moments constitute the path of seeing. During these moments, the practitioner abandons the ten fetters: the three lower fetters (personality-belief, doubt, and attachment to rites and rituals) and the seven higher fetters (sensual desire, ill-will, restlessness, conceit, ignorance, envy, and avarice). **II. The Path of Development** Following the path of seeing, the path of development arises. This path is the repeated cultivation of the same truths to eradicate the remaining defilements. It is of four stages: 1. **The Path of Once-Returning:** By weakening the fetters of sensual desire and ill-will, one becomes a once-returner. 2. **The Path of Non-Returning:** By completely abandoning the five lower fetters, one becomes a non-returner. 3. **The Path of Arhatship:** By abandoning all remaining defilements, one attains the state of an arhat. Each of these paths is further distinguished as either "with-pursuit" (*sasaṅkhārika*) or "without-pursuit" (*asaṅkhārika*), depending on whether they arise with effort or spontaneously. **III. The Fruits** The fruits correspond to the respective paths. The fruit of stream-entry is the attainment of the state of a stream-enterer, characterized by the destruction of the three lower fetters. The fruit of once-returning is the state of a once-returner, characterized by the weakening of sensual desire and ill-will. The fruit of non-returning is the state of a non-returner, characterized by the total abandonment of the five lower fetters. The fruit of arhatship is the state of an arhat, characterized by the complete destruction of all defilements. In these fruits, the practitioner experiences the bliss of liberation, the peace of Nibbāna, and the cessation of the round of rebirth. Thus ends the detailed exposition of the path and fruition.

Then, the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the monks: "Friends, let us go to Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One. "But, friend, what is the purpose of going there? "Friends, it is for the sake of seeing the Blessed One, and also because we have heard that the Blessed One has said: 'Monks, when five qualities are present in a monk, he is one who is not to be followed, and his instruction is not to be accepted. What five? Here, friends, a monk is one who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, yet he does not speak in accordance with the Vinaya; he speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, yet he speaks with a mind of enmity, not with a mind of loving-kindness; he speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, yet he speaks out of desire, not out of non-desire; he speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, yet he speaks with a mind of delusion, not with a mind of wisdom; and he speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, yet he speaks while being subject to the influence of another, not independently. Friends, when these five qualities are present in a monk, he is one who is not to be followed, and his instruction is not to be accepted. We shall go, friends, so that we may see the Blessed One and refute this teaching. "It is well, friend," they replied. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa set out for Sāvatthī together with a large company of monks. Traveling by stages, he eventually arrived at Sāvatthī. There, the Venerable Mahākassapa approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Mahākassapa said to the Blessed One: "Bhante, I have heard that the Blessed One has said: 'Monks, when five qualities are present in a monk, he is one who is not to be followed, and his instruction is not to be accepted... Therefore, Kassapa, when a monk speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, yet does not speak in accordance with the Vinaya, he is one who is not to be followed, and his instruction is not to be accepted. By beholding Bhadreśvara on the western shore of Lake Hṛda, one shall attain Goloka through that merit; of this there is no doubt. O Sage, Upaśāntaśiva is located at Yātudhānī, starting from Bhadreśvara.
By touching that *liṅga*, one attains supreme peace;
by beholding the *liṅga* of Śiva in his state of quiescence (*upaśānta*), one casts off the heap of misfortunes accumulated over hundreds of births and finds a heap of auspiciousness.
And above that is the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa), the warder-off of the womb-wheel. || 50 ||
The two lords Āśvineya were installed by the two Aśvinīkumāras.

To the north of that is the Cakrahada lake, which increases great merit;

One attains the world of Śiva with a purified inner self;

Having bathed at that sacred ford (tīrtha), a person becomes liberated from sin.
Right there is the Aṅgāraka-tīrtha, and each pool (kuṇḍa) is as stainless as glowing charcoal.
Having bathed at the Aṅgāraka-tīrtha, one shall not enter a womb again;

One shall not be overcome by diseases, nor shall one ever be miserable.
To the north of that is the Viśvakarmeśvara Liṅga, which bestows knowledge;

Because it is exceedingly terrifying like a cremation ground, the "cremation-ground pillar" (śmaśānastambha) is well known as the "family pillar" (kulastambha).
It truly comes to be, indeed it does come to be. From debt—that is, from the three debts. It is stainless charcoal, blazing and radiant like glowing coals.
The well named Śubhoda is certainly to be bathed in;

Then the goddess Mahāmuṇḍā, the remover of sins, emerged;

Then, to the south of Bhuvaneśa, there is the Bhuvaneśvara pool.

Having worshipped that [Liṅga] according to the prescribed rites, one shall attain the abode of Śiva.

There, the sage Kapila, a Pāśupata perfected in asceticism and possessed of great penance, attained success.

This very syllable Oṃ is that [reality], consisting of the primordial phoneme;

Instruction is not the supreme Brahman; instruction is not the supreme goal;

To the west of that, and further to the west,

By practicing [there], the seeker may obtain supreme knowledge even today.
Aghoreśa is at the entrance of the cave, and to its north is an auspicious well;

There are two auspicious Liṅgas there, Gargeśa and Damaneśa,

by worshipping those two Liṅgas, one's desired perfection is achieved.
To the south of that is the great pool known as Rudrāvāsa;

Aghoroda is so called because its water (uda) brings joy (odam) that is non-terrible (aghora) and turns back the cycle of worldly existence.
The fruit of reciting the Rudra-sūkta one hundred thousand times is equal to the fruit of ten million recitations of the Rudra-mantra.
O Aparṇā, when the fourteenth lunar day (Caturdaśī) is conjoined with the asterism of Rudra (Ārdrā), [the merit is manifold].
Then that time is most meritorious; at that pool, it yields great fruit.
Having bathed in the Rudra-kuṇḍa and beheld the omnipresent Lord Rudreśvara,
a person shall attain the world of Rudra, even if they die anywhere at all.
In the south-western quarter of Rudra is the Mahālaya Liṅga;
in front of it is the Pitṛkūpa (Well of the Ancestors), the supreme abode of the ancestors.
Having performed a Śrāddha ceremony there, a man should cast the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) into the well.
Endowed with twenty-one generations of his lineage, one who performs ancestral rites (śrāddha) attains the world of Rudra.
There, O Goddess, is a long pond named Vaitaraṇī, facing the west; a man who bathes in it never goes to hell.
To the west of Rudrakuṇḍa is the Bṛhaspatīśvara Liṅga;
having beheld it during the conjunction of Jupiter and Puṣya, one shall obtain divine speech.
To the south of Rudrāvāsa is the supreme Kāmeśa Liṅga;
to its south is the great Kuṇḍa, which grants all desired objects through bathing.
[Verse 9.6] Rudra’s asterism is Ārdrā. [Verse 9.0]
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, a pilgrimage there bestows all desires;
and to the east of Kāmeśvara is the auspicious Nalakūbara-liṅga.
In front of that is a purifying well which bestows abundance of wealth and grain;
to the east of Nalakūbara are the lords Sūrya and Candramas, who,
when duly worshipped, remove the thick veil of the darkness of ignorance.
To the south of that, Adhvakeśa is seen, the destroyer of delusion.
There is the Siddhīśvara Liṅga, which bestows great supernatural powers (siddhis);
and in that very place is Maṇḍaleśa, who grants the station of the Lord of the Mandala.
To the east of Kāmakuṇḍa is Cyavaneśa, who bestows prosperity;
right there is also Sanakeśa, who grants the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
And to the west of that is the Liṅga of Sanatkumāra, which effects success in Yoga.
To the north of that is Sanandeśa, who empowers great knowledge.
To the south of that is Āhutīśa, who, when beheld, bestows the fruit of the fire-oblation. To the south of that is the Liṅga Pañcaśikheśvara, which generates merit.
To the west of that is the Mārkaṇḍeya lake, which increases merit;
having bathed in that lake, what more would a man have to grieve for? (104)
There, bathing and giving gifts shall yield inexhaustible merit.
To the north of that is Kuṇḍeśa, who is saluted by all the Siddhas.
Having received the Pāśupata initiation, one obtains that fruit which is attained in twelve years [elsewhere].
O Brahmin, a mortal obtains that fruit from the sight of Kuṇḍeśa.
To the east of Mārkaṇḍeya-hrada is Śāṇḍilyeśa, who bestows great merit;
and to its west is Caṇḍeśa, who removes the sins of solar eclipses.
To the south of Kapāleśa is the pool known as Śrīkaṇṭha;
by bathing in that pool, a man becomes a donor through the power of Śrī.

Having bathed in the waters of that pool after duly worshipping Mahālakṣmī,
one is fanned by divine women with chowries in their hands when the inhabitants of heaven depart from the celestial realm for the Matsyodarī.
Then, surrounded by women, they proceed happily by that very same path.
(110) The "Aghahṛt" (the remover of sins) removes as much sin as the "Caṇḍāṃśugrahaṇa" (the eclipse of the sun); it is called Aghahṛt because it destroys sin.
Therefore, O best of sages, that place is renowned as Svargadvāra;
on the southern side of that pool is a Liṅga that bestows the state of Brahmā.
Gāyatrīśvara and Sāvitrīśvara should be worshipped with great effort;
and on the beautiful bank of the Matsyodarī is the Liṅga Satyavatīśvara.
Of these two, the former is to be worshipped; it is austerity that increases one’s fortune.
The great Liṅga Ugreśvara is situated in the eastern direction from Lakṣmīśa. By worshipping that Liṅga, a mortal becomes a rememberer of past births.
To the south of that is Ugrakuṇḍa, which is superior to Kanakhala because of its bath.
To the west of that pool is the Karavīreśvara Liṅga;
by the sight of it, the destruction of diseases occurs for men.
To its northwest is Marīcīśa and a pool that destroys the multitude of sins.

The former [is] by means of the former. || 113 ||
Kanakhala, Haridvāra, Gayā, or any other specific internal holy site (tīrtha);

One attains sovereignty over the Nāgas; of this there is no doubt.

To its south is the great sacrificial pit (mahākuṇḍa), which bestows the fruit of the world of Rudra;

Near Bālacandra is a well dear to the hosts of ancestors;

To the east of that [Liṅga] is the meritorious Liṅga named Viśveśvara;

Those women and men who drink the water there according to their own past actions— for them there is no rebirth here even in hundreds of millions of kalpas;

Those men who perform the restoration of what is broken or dilapidated there—
Having reached the world of Rudra, they rejoice there, ever happy.
To the south of Kāleśa is Mṛttvīśa, who removes untimely death;

To the west of that well is Sukeśa, the bestower of success in yoga.

A man goes to the heavenly world and becomes dear to Pañcacūḍā.

O Sage, she is meritorious even in the heavenly world—how much more so in the human realm!
To the north of that lies Madhyameśa; oh, he sleeps in the Middle Field (Madhyakṣetra).

Mayūkhārka and Gabhastīśa are indeed there in Pañcanada.

bathing in it is difficult to attain, and beholding it is likewise difficult to attain.
To the north of Gabhastīśa is Hara, the Lord of the Dadhikalpa;
having beheld him quickly, a man shall dwell for a kalpa in the city of the Three-eyed One.
To the south of Gabhastīśa, however, is Maṅgalā, the abode of auspiciousness.
One should feed a Brahmin couple, having honored Maṅgalā-Gaurī according to one's means;
the merit of that act is never-ending.
A single circumambulation of Maṅgalā yields the same fruit as circumambulating the entire earth.
Vadanaprekṣaṇādevī is located north of Mukhaprekṣeśvara; near Maṅgalā is the auspicious Sarvasiddhikarī. 188.

At Liṅga, Tvaṣṭrīśa, Vṛtteśa, Mukhaprekṣa, and Uttara are auspicious; by the sight of these two, one obtains the fruit of a gift of land together with gold. To the north of that, the sight of the goddess Carcikā is auspicious.
The Revateśvara Liṅga, located in front of Carcikā, bestows peace;
for great auspiciousness, there is the Pañcanadeśvara Liṅga in front of it.
To the west of Maṅgalā is the auspicious Maṅgaloda great well.

To the west of Maṅgalā is the auspicious Mahāliṅga of Upamanyu; behind that is the Vyāghrapādeśvara Liṅga, which removes the fear of tigers. And to the southwest of Gabhastīśa is Śaśāṅkeśa, the destroyer of the multitude of sins.
To the west of that is the Caitraratha Liṅga, which bestows a divine state.
To the west of Revateśa is Jaiminīśa, the great destroyer of sins;
there, O best of sages, are many Liṅgas belonging to the ṛṣis.
The ninety-seventh chapter:
To the northwest of Jaimineśa is indeed the Liṅga known as Rāvaṇeśvara.
Upon seeing him, no great fear arose in the rākṣasas.
To the south of that is Varāheśa; then Māṇḍavyeśa at Yama;
to the south of that is Pracaṇḍeśa, and then Yogeśa to the south.
To the south of that is Dhāteśa, and Someśa is in front of it;
to its southwest is Kanakeśa, who bestows great gold upon the virtuous.
To the north of that are the five liṅgas of the Pāṇḍavas for the delight of the good.
Saṃvarteśa is at its front, and Śveteśa is to its west.
After that is Kalaśeśa, the Liṅga that bestows fearlessness from Time (Kāla).
O Sage! when Śveta was bound by Kāla, it emerged from a water-pot (kumbha). 1.99.
To the north of that is the Citragupteśvara Liṅga, which destroys sins;

and to the west of Citragupteśvara is Dṛḍheśa, who yields great fruit. The phrase "to the north of that" is stated according to the broad direction; otherwise, it refers to another [Liṅga] called Citragupteśvara.
To the south of Kalaśeśa is the supreme Liṅga Graheśa;
beholding that Liṅga pacifies the afflictions caused by the planets. 201.
To the west of Citragupteśvara is Yadṛccheśa, which yields great fruit;
to the south of Graheśvara is the Utathyavāmadeveśa Liṅga;
and to its south, O auspicious lady, are Kambaleśa and Aśvatereśa.
In that very place is the stainless Liṅga worshipped by Nalakūbara.
To the south of that is Maṇikarṇīśa, and to its north is Paliteśvara;
right there is Jarāhara, and behind it is Pāpanāśana.
To the southwest of those two is Nirjareśa, and there is Pitāmaha;
at Pitāmahasrotikā, a śrāddha ceremony yields great fruit.
To the south of that is Varuṇeśa, and Bāṇeśa is to its south.
In the Pitāmahamnotikā, the Lord Kūśmāṇḍeśa is the bestower of success. || 206 ||
To the east of that is Rākṣaseśa; to its south is Gaṅgeśa; and to its north are the Nimnageśas, where there are numerous liṅgas. [The remaining portion is:
"the liṅga known as Jarāhara. 204–207.
There is Vaivasvateśvara, who wards off the world of Yama;
behind him is Aditīśa, and Cakreśa is in front of him. (208)
In front of that is the supreme [liṅga] named Kālakeśa, which produces direct realization;
there a shadow is clearly seen, and by beholding it, one becomes free from sin.
In front of that is Tārakeśa, and in front of that is Svarṇabhārada.
To the north of that is Marutteśa, and Śakreśa is in front of it;
to its south is Rambheśa, and in that very place is Śaśīśvara.
To the north of that are the Lokapeśas, and there are numerous liṅgas there as well.
It brings about various supernatural powers for the Nāgas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, Apsarases, and the multitudes of divine sages;
and Phālguneśa, who removes great sins, is located to the south of Śakreśa.
And to the south of that is Mahāpāśupateśa, the supreme performer of auspicious deeds;
to its west is Samudreśa; to its north is Īśāneśa;
and to its east is Lāṅgalīśa, who bestows all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 213–214 ||
Those worshippers who are completely free from passion and hatred attain perfection;
their liberation has been declared by me, but they, O Goddess, are not mere human beings.
Madhupiṅga and Śvetaketu, as well as Lāṅgalīśa and Tapasvin,
attained supreme perfection with this very body.
In that very place are Nakulīśa and Kapileśa;
both are my devotees who observe my vows, and they possess the supreme secret.
O beloved, Prītikeśa is there in their presence, and there I find my delight.
In that regard, the fruit from a single fast is more than a hundred years' worth.
Having performed a single vigil while fasting for Prītikeśa on my festival day, his attainment of the rank of a Gaṇa is certain.
To the south of the Lord, there is a pond of auspicious water;
the drinking of that water by men leads to the cause of non-rebirth.
To the west of that water, Daṇḍapāṇi always protects.
In that [direction], to the east, south, and north, are Tāra, Kāla, and the son of Śilāda (Nandikeśvara).
On the full-moon day, specifically on Śivarātri.
Whoever drinks that water which has been offered with faith from the three marks into the heart-lotus—those best of men have achieved their life's purpose. (222)
Near Avimukta, one should worship Arthya, the Lord of Liberation who bestows the intellect of liberation;
and to the north of that, one should worship Karuṇeśa, the abode of compassion. (223)
Svarṇākṣeśa is to the east of that [temple], and Jñānada is to its north;
Saubhāgyagaurī should be worshipped for the attainment of abundant good fortune.
To the south of Viśveśa, Nikumbheśa should be diligently worshipped as the bringer of security to the sacred field; behind him is Vighnanāyaka.
Virūpākṣa, the destroyer of all obstacles who bestows excellent success, should be worshipped specifically on the fourth lunar day; he is to be honored in the southeast from Nikumbheśa.
To the south of that is Śukreśa, who increases one's sons and grandsons;
to the north of that is the great liṅga known as Devayānīśvara.
To the east of Śukreśa, the deity known as Kaceśa is to be worshipped;
having sipped water at Śukrakūpa, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
The water that has been drunk with faith should be offered to the three Liṅgas; this is "the drinking of that water," which is to be construed with the preceding verse.
Bhavānī and Īśa are auspicious deities to be saluted, located to the west of Śukreśa.
Those two always provide food and drink to their own devotee.
Alarkeśa, situated to the east of Śukreśa, is to be worshipped;
Madālaseśvara is there to the east of that, the remover of all obstacles.

O Brahmin, having slain the Lord of Laṅkā, Raghunātha installed that supreme Liṅga, the Lord of the lords of Gaṇas, which bestows all spiritual perfections. By touching that Liṅga, even Brahmā is instantly purified.
There is another [liṅga] there, the noble Tripurāntaka, which bestows great merit.
To the west of that is the auspicious Dattātreyeśvara Liṅga;
to its south is Harikeśeśa, and beyond that is Gokarṇeśa.
In front of that lake is the sin-destroying [site], and behind it is Dhruveśvara;
in front of that is the Dhruvakuṇḍa, which is supremely pleasing to the ancestors.
By Raghu—that is, by Viṣṇu known as Rāma, born in the lineage of Raghu. As it is stated in the Āraṇyaka Parvan:
"To the high-souled Daśaratha was born one named Rāma;
he was Viṣṇu himself in bodily form for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa."
In the reading "Raghunātha," the meaning is quite clear.
To the north of that is Piśāceśa, the remover of the state of being a Piśāca.
Pitrīśa is in that direction of Yama; in front of him is the Pitṛkuṇḍa.
There, the great-grandfathers of those men who perform the Śrāddha rite shall be satisfied.
In front of Dhruveśa is Tāreśa; he is indeed Vaidyanātha himself.
To the southwest of that is the Liṅga of Manu, which supremely increases one's lineage;
and there is the Priyavrateśvara Liṅga situated in front of Vaidyanātha.
To the south of that is the region of Mucukunda; at its side is Gautameśvara.
To the west of that is Bhadreśa, and to the south of that is Ṛṣyaśṛṅgin.
Brahmeśa is to the east of that, and Parjanyeśa is situated to the northeast of it.
To the east of that is Nahuṣeśa, and in front of it is Viśālākṣī. || 23.9 ||
The Viśālākṣīśvara Liṅga is located right there; it bestows the foundation of the sacred field.
To the south of that is the Jarāsaṃdheśvara Liṅga, which destroys fever.
In front of that, the Hiraṇyākṣa Liṅga is to be worshipped; it bestows gold.
To the west of that is Gayādhīśa, and to the west of that is Bhagīratha;
O Sage, to the east of that is Dilīpeśa, and to the west of Brahmeśa.
There, the Liṅga together with the Kuṇḍa bestows the desired fruits upon the one who bathes there.
There is the Viśvāvasu-liṅga; Muṇḍeśa is to its east;
Vidhīśa is to its south; and Vājimedhaka is to its south.
Having bathed at Daśāśvamedhika and beheld that supreme liṅga, a human being obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices. || 244 ||

North of that is Mātṛtīrtha, which removes the fear of rebirth for one who bathes there. Whether it be a woman or even a man, whoever performs a bath there obtains their desired fruit through the grace of the Mothers.
To the south of your pond is the supreme Puṣpadanteśvara.
In that direction of Agni (the southeast), there are numerous liṅgas of the hosts of celestial sages (devarṣis).
To the south of Puṣpadanta is Siddhīśa, who bestows supreme perfection;
through worship with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), he shall grant supreme success in one's dreams.
The attainment of sovereignty shall come to men through the service of Hariścandreśa;
this is for you, O Agastya.
To the west of that is Naiṛteśa, then Aṅgiraseśa in the south;
to the south of that is Kṣemeśa, and then Citrāṅgeśa in the south.
To the south of that is Kedāra, which bestows the status of an attendant of Rudra.
In the southern region from Kedāra, hundreds and thousands of Liṅgas have been installed by kings of the lunar and solar dynasties.
To the south of Lolārka is the worshipped Sarvāśāpūraka;
to the west of that is the Karandhameśvara Liṅga, which yields great fruit;
and to its west is Mahādurgā, the destroyer of even the greatest difficulties.
And Śuṣkeśvara is to the south of that, worshipped by the river Śuṣkā;
Janakeśa is to the west of Taṭha, and Śaṅkukarṇa is to its north. To the east of that is the Mahāsiddhīśvara Liṅga, which bestows all perfections (siddhis).
Having bathed in the Siddhakuṇḍa and beheld the great Siddheśvara, a man [attains success].
A person reaches the furthest shore of all spiritual accomplishments at the Liṅga known as Vāyavya, located to the northwest of Śaṅkukarṇeśa. (255)
The remainder is that the one who fulfills all hopes is Arkavināyaka.
|| 251 || By the river named Asī, which was dry.
And in front of that is Vibhāṇḍeśa, and Kaholeśa to its north;
there is the Liṅga Dvāreśvara, and the auspicious goddess Dvāreśvarī.
From worshipping that [Liṅga], there shall arise perfection that bestows bliss and residence in the forest;
and there, O Sage, are the Gaṇas who are protectors, possessing various forms and weapons.
Right there is the Lord Hari, and then the Kātyāyana Liṅga.
Beside that is Jāṅgaleśa, and behind that is Mukuṭeśvara.
Right there is a pure pool (kuṇḍa) that bestows the fruit of all pilgrimages;
having bathed in the Mukuṭakuṇḍa and indeed beheld Mukuṭeśvara, [one attains the goal]. || 258-259 ||

By visiting all the *liṅgas*, one obtains that fruit which results from austerity (*tapas*) and yoga; that supreme earth bestows perfection (*siddhi*). O Sage, there are hundreds of thousands of *liṅgas* there for the sake of accomplishment.
O Goddess, the northern direction alone is dear to me in Vārāṇasī;
even there, my love for Pañcāyatana is supreme, O beloved. At the time of its origin and throughout its duration, I have always remained there.
The gift of a residence in Ānandāraṇya is the gift of a dwelling in Avimukta.
|| 257 || It is said that it is the northern direction because of its location in Trilocana.
The Ninety-seventh Chapter. 37.9 Thus, he who understands this is not defiled by sins.
Truth, truth, and again truth—this triple truth, O beloved, is found nowhere else. 263.
One who desires my state should go quickly to that very place;
O sage, I have described the lingas to you merely by way of indication.
Certain liṅgas were installed with devotion two or three times; they are not redundant, for they are to be honored everywhere with faith.
All these lingas, all these sacrificial pits, all these wells,
and all these tanks should be honored with faith by the wise.
From the sight and bathing at these [sites], the fruit becomes progressively greater;
this applies to the liṅgas, the wells, and the lakes located here as well. (267)
Who would be capable of counting the ponds and the images?
It is far better even to count the blades of grass situated within Ānandakānana. || 268 ||
Even the dwellers of heaven do not find it elsewhere—that which is the vessel for rebirth;
Kāśī consists of all sacred emblems and is the sole birthplace of all holy pilgrimage sites.
O Goddess, you alone— served by me until the end of this body— are seen to be the bestower of both heaven and liberation through the power of my ascetic penance. (270)

By its very nature, this Kāśī is my ground for the repose of happiness. Indeed, those who utter the name of Kāśī and those who rejoice in it are like my own Śākha, Viśākha, Skanda, Nandi, and Gajānana.
O Goddess, they alone are my devotees; they alone are my servants.
They alone are seekers of liberation here who dwell in Ānandavana. Great penance has been performed by them, and great vows have been observed by them.
And those who dwell in Ānandavana have given great gifts;
they have indeed bathed in all sacred fords and are initiated into all sacrifices.

Indeed, those who have practiced all dharmas and dwell in Ānandavana— even though they are but companions here in this final age— all those gods, asuras, serpents, and humans are for the sake of bearing the burden of the earth.
(275) By whomsoever [this] is practiced here in the final age, even as a friend, they are dwellers in Ānandavana.
Even an outcaste is better in Kāśī than one who has mastered the Vedas elsewhere.
The former has crossed to the further shore of saṃsāra, while the latter, though born of the lowest caste, remains below.
He alone is surely omniscient; he alone indeed possesses the supreme vision.
He who, having abandoned his earthly body, assumes an ethereal form in Kāśī—
by hearing this meritorious chapter, which contains the secrets of all sacred fords,
a man certainly attains the merit born of beholding Kāśī. (277-278)

Whoever recites this chapter every single day at dawn, by him all these sacred fords have been visited; it is not otherwise. That wise person who constantly chants this chapter, which consists entirely of *liṅgas*, [attains the fruit].
Neither Yama, nor his messengers, nor even sin afflicts such a person. || 280 ||
The fruit of the *brahmayajña* arises for that person of virtuous soul who,
being pure and with his mind fixed upon it, should recite this chapter;
he has bathed in all sacrificial pits and he has drunk the waters of all ponds.
He who recites this chapter here is a worshiper of all lingas. (282) What is the use of many other hymns that yield very meager fruits?
This chapter, which yields great fruit, should be recited by those who possess love for Me. (283)
Whatever fruit is indeed obtained here from the giving of great gifts when they have been bestowed, that is fully attained by reciting this Great Chapter just once. || 284 ||

"Having heard this meritorious chapter"—that is, having heard this sacred narrative. What is it? Having bathed in all the holy fords (tīrthas) and having beheld numerous Liṅgas... [Pt 4 Page 466]... [one attains the fruit].

Whatever fruit is obtained by mortals, that is surely attained through the recitation of this. This alone is the most intense austerity; this alone is the great recitation, O Sage, namely, that the chapter titled "The Series of Liṅgas of Kāśī" should be recited.
This recitation must not be given to one who bears malice toward me, nor to an atheist, nor to one devoted to reviling the Vedas; it must not be given, it must not be given, it must not be given.
By the recitation of this chapter, even the sin arising from the slaughter of a Brahmin [is destroyed].
Also, approaching those who should not be approached, as well as eating what is unfit to be eaten;
that which arises from violating the teacher’s wife, from the theft of gold, from the killing of mother or father, and from the slaughter of a cow or an embryo. (288–289)
Great sins, minor sins, and numerous sins— whether committed knowingly or unknowingly—
as well as secondary sins and those born of mind, speech, and body,
all go to complete destruction without exception by my command; of this there is no doubt.

By reciting this chapter, a wise man will surely obtain sons, grandsons, wealth, grain, a wife, and even land; indeed, he shall attain everything his heart desires, as well as heaven, liberation, and all forms of happiness— of this there is no doubt.
It is called *japa* because it is recited; thus ends the chapter.
|| 287 || Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter in the commentary on the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa* composed by Śrī Rāmānanda.
While the Lord was thus narrating this story before the Goddess, Nandin arrived, prostrated himself, and made this request: || 2.93 ||
The completion of the construction of the great palace has been achieved;
this chariot is ready, and the gods, beginning with Brahmā, have assembled.
The lotus-eyed Lord, mounted upon Tārkṣya, stands at the gate with his followers,
awaiting the opportune moment while placing the lords of sages at his forefront.
"Those of noble vows who dwell throughout the fourteen worlds have now assembled together, having heard of the great festival of entry.
Skanda said:
Having heard these words of Nandin, the Lord, accompanied by the Goddess,
ascended a divine chariot and departed from Triviṣṭapa.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Centers of the Field," in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
[Pt 4 Page 468] || Now begins the ninety-eighth chapter. ||
Vyāsa said: Listen, O highly fortunate Sūta,
to how the great festival of Śambhu was described by Skanda when he was questioned by the pot-born Agastya.
Skanda said: Listen, O one of great wisdom, to the narrative concerning the entry of Śambhu,
which generates joy for the three worlds and strikes terror into those who commit great sins.
Having come from Mount Mandara on the Damanaka festival in the month of Caitra,
Śambhu reached the dense forest of bliss and wandered here and there.
This much is explained in the ninety-eighth chapter.
In the glorious Muktimaṇḍapa, there was a meeting with the illustrious Viśveśvara.
He introduces the narration of the great festival of Viśveśvara with the words, "Listen, O Sūta! [Verse 1]. Regarding "Kumbhasambhave":
it means for Kumbhasambhava; or alternatively, one who arises perfectly from a pitcher (kumbha) is Kumbhasambhu, and for him [it is said].
[Verse 2]. "Prāveśikīm" means connected with the entry, that is to say, related to it. "Taṅkinīm" means destructive. [Verse 2].
Regarding "on the Damanaparvan," this means on the thirteenth day of the waxing moon of Caitra, known as Damanatrayodaśī. As for the phrase "even having attained":
although supreme bliss was produced by the very attainment of Ānandavana, nevertheless he wandered here and there; such is the meaning.
[Pt 4 Page 469]
Then, when the temple had attained perfection amidst the playful splendor of the Fortune of Liberation,
the Lord entered the inner sanctum from the seat of Virajas.

On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ūrja (Kārttika), coinciding with the conjunction of Mercury and the asterism Rādhā (Jyeṣṭhā), when the Moon was situated in its seventh house and the remaining planets were in their exaltations;
while musical instruments were being played and all the quarters of the sky were serene. || 5 ||
The Veda of the Brahmins has eclipsed all other sounds.
In that festive celebration of Śambhu’s entry, the entire interior of the Bhūrloka and Bhuvarloka resounded with echoes, and all were filled with joy;
hosts of Gandharvas sang and throngs of Apsaras danced.
The celestial bards (cāraṇas) offered hymns of praise, and the hosts of deities rejoiced from the stainless seat,
the abode of the Three-eyed Lord.
Fragrant breezes blew and clouds rained down flowers; all were adorned with auspicious ornaments, and all spoke auspicious words. All beings, both stationary and moving, became overflowing with joy.
Among all the gods and asuras, as well as among the gandharvas and uragas.
Among the Vidyādharas, Sādhyas, Kinnaras, and humans—
among all those born as both female and male— the four shone forth, and indeed the four alone shone forth.
O Sage, at every step the goals of human endeavor were exceedingly free from obstacles; however, at that time, the sky was reddened by the dense masses of incense smoke.
Even today, the infinite blue-black luster never abandons [the Lord] at any time;
all those lamps which were then awakened for the purpose of the lustration ceremony [remain so]. (13)
Their lights still shine in the sky even today in the guise of stars;
and on every palace, there are variegated banners of various forms. (14)
Washed by the radiance of beautiful banners, they shone at every temple of Śiva;
in some places those skilled in song sang, and in others dancers danced. (15)
The connection is as follows: that redness which is connected with a certain blueness—that is the blueness. Or, it may be understood as "extended.
Furthermore, four kinds of musical instruments are played here and there.
In every street, the ground was slippery with splashes of sandalwood paste.
In every courtyard, beautiful rows of colored cloths—shining with many hues of green, white, madder-red, blue, and yellow—were displayed. || 16–17 ||
The ground surfaces were paved with jewels, and the gate-towers shone brightly; the rows of mansions, radiant with plaster, truly earned the name "saudha" (white-plastered).
O Pot-born One, whatever auspicious things are celebrated here— even those that are insentient— appeared at that time as if they were sentient;
for that day was indeed the birth-day of all of them.
Then the God of gods, having arrived, entered the pavilion of liberation (Muktimaṇḍapa).
*Chaṭās* are throws or drops [of flowers].
(16) *Raṅgamālās* are garlands made for the occasion of a festival.
(17) [They are placed] at the tops of the *gopuras*, facing the outer gates. (18)
That very day on which the Lord of the Universe entered became the day of birth for all of them.
Then the God of gods was consecrated by the four-faced Brahmā along with the hosts of great sages.
Seated upon an auspicious throne, accompanied by Bhavānī and surrounded on all sides by throngs of Kumāras. || 21 ||
Then, with countless jewels, many fine silken garments, and various radiant garlands of desired fragrances,
the hosts of gods and those lords of great serpents joyfully worshipped Maheśa;
as did the mines of jewels, the best of mountain kings, and others of meritorious intellect, each according to their own means.
O Pot-born One, Śambhu, the Lord, was there worshipped and honored with the lustration rite (nīrājana) by the hosts of Mothers.
Having first gratified all the lords of sages with their respective heart-felt and long-cherished desires,
Śiva— venerated by the entire host of immortals— then addressed Brahmā and spoke to Viṣṇu.
"Please sit here"—this was preceded by a similar [request]—for you are my sole cause for all sovereignty;
even though you remain at a distance, you alone are near to me, and there is no one other than you who can accomplish my purpose. (25)
By you, the most excellent of kings, Divodāsa, was instructed with such proper guidance that he attained supreme perfection; thus, my entire desire has been fulfilled.
(26) The "multitudes of youths" refers to the hosts of Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya, or Sanaka and the others. (21)
"O Viṣṇu, choose a boon—whatever you desire; indeed, there is nothing here that cannot be granted to you.
This Ānandavana which has been obtained by me, the cause for its attainment therein is you and that Gaṇeśa. (27)
"Nothing in the three worlds is as dear to me as this ground of supreme bliss,
Vārāṇasī— the mine of the elixir of Brahman, where those who sleep long [in saṃsāra] find no further rebirth.
Having heard these words of the Lord of the World, Viṣṇu spoke to Maheśa, the bestower of boons.
O wielder of the Pināka bow, if you are pleased, then may I not be far from your feet.
Having heard these words of Madhusūdana, Purāri, being exceedingly pleased, said:
"O Murāri, may you always remain here in my presence, this abode of Nirvāṇa-ramā.
Even one who, having first failed to worship you, should worship me here with devotion—"
O Lotus-and-Discus-handed One, his desired goal will certainly not be accomplished by me, who am far inferior to the Supreme.
The word "but" (tu) has the sense of "and" (ca), and it is connected with the phrase "Gaṇeśaḥ ca" (and Gaṇeśa). || 27 ||
[This refers to] those who have long slept, having abandoned their vital breaths.

|| 28 || [It is] the abode of the beauty of Nirvāṇa, the seat of the Fortune of Liberation—that is to say, the Pavilion of Liberation. The sense is that, because you are the Lord of Fortune (Lakṣmīpati), it is fitting for you to dwell in the residence of the Fortune of Liberation. || 30 ||
"O Acyuta,
by this boon, may there be happiness for me everywhere while I remain here in the Pavilion of Liberation. [Pt 4, Page 474]

Dakṣeśa, Pārvatīśa, and likewise Paśupatīśvara;

First the celestial river [Ganges], and then the Lord of the Universe—
certainly for him who dwells in Kāśī, every day that passes by is in vain.

Vyāsa said:
O Sūta, having heard this supreme greatness of Kāśī from the Skanda Purāṇa,
a man does not go to hell even after committing a thousand sins.

O Sūta, whatever merit is acquired by bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas), that shall be attained simply by listening to the Kāśī-khaṇḍa; of this there is no doubt. Having given all possible gifts and having performed numerous sacrifices, [that merit is likewise attained].
Whatever merit is obtained by mortals through performing fierce austerities and attaining great fruit—that is certainly gained simply by hearing this section; of this there is no doubt. (108–109)
Whatever fruit is obtained by studying the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs,
that same fruit is attained by men upon hearing the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*.
Just as ancestors are satisfied by the offering of *śrāddha* at Gayā, [so too are they satisfied by this].
In the same way, by hearing this, the ancestors of men are satisfied.
By those of steady intellect, all the Purāṇas have been heard;
and by those who have heard the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the pinnacle of all auspicious things, [all else has been heard].
All dharmas have been heard by those who are a singular mass of great merit—
by those of steady mind who have heard the supreme majesty of Kāśī. (113)
For this alone is proclaimed as the supreme worship of the gods;
O twice-born ones, one should recite this entire section and it should be heard with faith.
Whoever hears even a single narrative born from the Kāśī-khaṇḍa has,
without a doubt, heard all the treatises on Dharma.
It is the sole generator of great righteousness and the expounder of the supreme goal.
This Kāśīkhaṇḍa is remembered as the cause for attaining all desires.
For men, liberation is not at all far off through hearing this;
all the ancestors are gratified upon hearing this excellent section. 117.
All the immortals, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, are delighted;

From this hearing of the greatness [of Vārāṇasī], there is no doubt regarding Vārāṇasī. || 11.9 ||
The wise person of supreme merit who, with a steady mind, causes this incomparable majesty of Kāśī to be heard— whether in its entirety or even only in half— [attains the highest goal].
Whether it be a quarter [of the verse], half of that, or even a single [word], such an explanation is considered supreme. (120)
He is to be saluted with effort and worshipped like one's own chosen deity;
